## 1. Project introduction

Most "AI + Firebase" samples skip Firestore rules, trust the client to police its own data, and stop
at a single prototype file. This kit is built around the parts that decide whether an AI feature
survives real users: **who may read a document, what happens when the model returns malformed JSON,
where the API key lives, and how any of it is tested before production.**

The kit deliberately implements the same product through two back ends:

- **Spark mode** — the browser calls Gemini REST directly with a key the user supplies in the Setup
  tab. The key lives in `sessionStorage` for that tab only: never committed, never bundled, never
  written to Firestore. This mode needs no billing account, and it is what runs at
  <https://fb-ai-starter-kit.web.app>.
- **Blaze mode** — the same endpoints as Cloud Functions 2nd gen: Zod validation, per-user rate
  limits, server-only `GEMINI_API_KEY`, conversation persistence. Kept in `functions/` as the
  production upgrade path.

Both modes share one contract (`apps/web/src/lib/api.ts` keeps the original callable-shaped function
names), so switching modes is a configuration change, not a rewrite.

## 2. Problem statement

Building an AI feature on Firebase usually raises the same five problems:

| Problem                  | Typical shortcut                                     | What this kit does                                                                          |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| API key exposure         | Key inlined into the production bundle               | Spark mode: user-supplied key kept in `sessionStorage` only. Blaze mode: server-only secret |
| Unbounded cost           | No limits on prompt size, history, or call frequency | Zod length caps, message-history caps, Firestore-backed per-user rate limits                |
| Data leakage             | Shared collection with client-side filtering         | `users/{uid}/**` ownership rules, enforced and unit-tested                                  |
| Unvalidated model output | Raw JSON parsed in the UI                            | Schema-constrained structured output validated before it reaches React                      |
| Untestable setup         | Manual clicking through the console                  | Emulator Suite, mocked model, 51 unit tests, 22 rules tests, 14 end-to-end emulator checks  |

## 3. Key features

**Authentication**

- Email/password sign-up, sign-in, password reset, session persistence, sign-out.
- Profile bootstrap on first login (`ensureUserProfile`) and profile updates with validated preferences.

**Firestore**

- Per-user profile, preferences, conversations, messages, and monthly usage counters.
- Security rules covering read/write separation, ownership, immutability of server-managed fields.

**Gemini**

- Server-side text generation, chat with history, and schema-constrained structured output.
- Mock mode for emulator/CI runs so tests never bill the API.

**Cloud Functions (2nd gen, TypeScript)**

- Nine callable endpoints with shared middleware: auth, App Check awareness, validation, rate
  limiting, structured error mapping, and request logging.

**Security**

- App Check integration points, strict schemas, rate limits, redacted logging, secret scanning
  script, hardened hosting headers, and a documented threat model.

**Developer experience**

- One-command emulator flow, mock AI mode, type-checking, linting, formatting, secret scanning,
  rules tests, emulator smoke test, and CI workflow.

## 4. Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Client["React 19 + Vite (browser)"]
    UI[Dashboard / Panels]
    SDK[Firebase Web SDK]
    AD[Auth state hook]
  end

  subgraph Firebase["Firebase project"]
    AUTH[Firebase Authentication]
    FS[(Cloud Firestore)]
    subgraph FNS["Cloud Functions v2"]
      MW[Auth + validation + rate limit]
      AIS[AI service]
      CONV[Conversation service]
    end
    APPCHECK[App Check]
  end

  GEMINI[Gemini API]

  UI --> SDK --> AD --> AUTH
  SDK --> FS
  UI -- "callable: HTTPS" --> MW
  MW --> APPCHECK
  MW --> AIS --> GEMINI
  MW --> CONV --> FS
  AIS --> FS
```

> **Spark mode difference.** In the default build the `Cloud Functions v2` box above is not deployed.
> The browser keeps the same API surface but calls `generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta`
> directly with the user's key, and writes conversation history to Firestore under the same rules.
> The diagram describes Blaze mode; see [`docs/FREE_PLAN_DEPLOYMENT.md`](docs/FREE_PLAN_DEPLOYMENT.md)
> for the client-side request path.

Request path for an AI call (Blaze mode):

1. The React panel calls a callable function with the user's ID token.
2. Middleware verifies authentication (and App Check when configured), then parses the payload with a
   strict Zod schema.
3. A Firestore transaction increments the per-user, per-endpoint counter for the current minute; the
   request is rejected with `resource-exhausted` when the limit is exceeded.
4. The AI service calls Gemini with the server-only key — or returns a deterministic mock response in
   mock mode.
5. Usage counters are updated, the response is validated, and a structured result returns to the UI.

Full details: [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md).

## 5. Technology stack

| Layer           | Choice                                   | Version              |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| UI              | React + Vite + TypeScript                | React 19.3, Vite 8.3 |
| Firebase client | `firebase` Web SDK                       | 13.x                 |
| Functions       | `firebase-functions` v2, Node 22         | 7.x                  |
| Admin           | `firebase-admin`                         | 14.x                 |
| Gemini          | `@google/genai`                          | 3.x                  |
| Validation      | `zod`                                    | 4.x                  |
| Styling         | Tailwind CSS                             | 4.1                  |
| Tests           | `vitest`, `@firebase/rules-unit-testing` | 5.x / 6.x            |
| Tooling         | ESLint, Prettier, TypeScript 5.9         | latest               |

## 6. Screenshots

Screenshots of the local demo are stored in [`docs/screenshots/`](docs/screenshots/). They are
captured from the running application against the emulator suite — no mock-ups.

| Setup screen (no Firebase config yet)          | Dashboard after sign-in                         |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| ![Setup screen](docs/screenshots/01-setup.png) | ![Dashboard](docs/screenshots/02-dashboard.png) |

A screenshot of the dashboard is rendered by signing a throwaway account up against the Auth
emulator; the AI responses visible on it come from `AI_MOCK_MODE=true`, not a billed Gemini call.

Captured from the live Spark deployment (<https://fb-ai-starter-kit.web.app>), signed in with a
throwaway account and no Gemini key configured:

| Live sign-in                               | Live dashboard (six panels)                       |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| ![Sign-in](docs/screenshots/shot-auth.png) | ![Dashboard](docs/screenshots/shot-dashboard.png) |

Mobile layout of the same deployment: ![Mobile](docs/screenshots/shot-mobile.png)

## 7. Prerequisites

- Node.js **22.x or 24.x** (the Functions runtime is Node 22) and npm 10+
- Java **21** for the Firestore emulator
- A Firebase project — the free **Spark** plan is enough for the default build; Cloud Functions v2
  (`functions/`) requires the Blaze plan
- A Gemini API key from Google AI Studio
- Firebase CLI (`npm i -g firebase-tools`) — or use `npx firebase-tools`

## 8. Installation

```bash
git clone https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/firebase-ai-starter-kit.git
cd firebase-ai-starter-kit

npm run setup          # installs apps/web and functions dependencies
cp .env.example .env   # then fill in your Firebase web config
cp .firebaserc.example .firebaserc
```

`npm run setup` installs both workspaces. Nothing else is required to run the tests.

## 9. Firebase configuration

1. Create a project in the [Firebase console](https://console.firebase.google.com/).
2. **Authentication â†’ Sign-in method â†’** enable _Email/Password_.
3. **Firestore Database â†’** create a database in production mode (rules are deployed from this repo).
4. **Project settings â†’ General â†’ Your apps â†’** add a Web app and copy the config values into `.env`.
5. Put your project id into `.firebaserc`:

```json
{
  "projects": { "default": "your-project-id" },
  "targets": {
    "your-project-id": { "hosting": { "web": ["web"] } }
  }
}
```

6. Enable App Check (optional but recommended) — register the web app with reCAPTCHA Enterprise and
   set `VITE_APPCHECK_SITE_KEY`.

## 10. Gemini configuration

The key never reaches the browser. Store it as a Functions secret:

```bash
firebase functions:secrets:set GEMINI_API_KEY
```

Then reference it from the function options (already wired in `functions/src/endpoints/ai.ts`).
For local runs, either put the key in `functions/.env` or use mock mode:

```bash
# .env (repo root, git-ignored)
AI_MOCK_MODE=true   # only honoured when FUNCTIONS_EMULATOR is set
```

## 11. Environment variables

**Web (`apps/web/.env.local`)**

| Variable                            | Required | Description                                        |
| ----------------------------------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `VITE_FIREBASE_API_KEY`             | yes      | Web API key from the Firebase console              |
| `VITE_FIREBASE_AUTH_DOMAIN`         | yes      | `<project>.firebaseapp.com`                        |
| `VITE_FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID`          | yes      | Project id                                         |
| `VITE_FIREBASE_STORAGE_BUCKET`      | yes      | `<project>.appspot.com`                            |
| `VITE_FIREBASE_MESSAGING_SENDER_ID` | yes      | Sender id                                          |
| `VITE_FIREBASE_APP_ID`              | yes      | Web app id                                         |
| `VITE_FUNCTIONS_REGION`             | no       | Defaults to `us-central1`                          |
| `VITE_APPCHECK_SITE_KEY`            | no       | Enables App Check when set                         |
| `VITE_USE_EMULATORS`                | no       | `true` connects Auth/Firestore/Functions emulators |
| `VITE_EMULATOR_HOST`                | no       | Defaults to `127.0.0.1`                            |

**Functions**

| Variable                       | Required         | Description                                              |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `GEMINI_API_KEY`               | yes (production) | Secret used by the AI service                            |
| `GEMINI_MODEL`                 | no               | Defaults to `gemini-2.5-flash`                           |
| `AI_MOCK_MODE`                 | no               | `true` returns deterministic mock output (emulator only) |
| `AI_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS`         | no               | Default output cap (default 1024)                        |
| `AI_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS`   | no               | Requests per window (default 20)                         |
| `AI_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECONDS` | no               | Window length (default 60)                               |

`.env`, `.env.local`, and service-account files are git-ignored; `npm run check:secrets` fails the
build if a key-looking string is committed.

## 12. Local development

```bash
npm run emulators     # Auth :9099, Firestore :8080, Functions :5001, UI :4000
npm run dev           # builds functions in watch mode, then starts Vite
```

Useful scripts:

| Command                              | Purpose                                                     |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm run dev`                        | Vite dev server + Functions watch build                     |
| `npm run emulators`                  | Start the Emulator Suite                                    |
| `npm run build`                      | Type-check and build web + functions                        |
| `npm run typecheck` / `npm run lint` | Static checks                                               |
| `npm test`                           | Unit tests (functions + web)                                |
| `npm run test:rules`                 | Firestore rules tests against the emulator                  |
| `npm run test:emulator`              | End-to-end smoke test of the deployed-like function surface |
| `npm run test:live`                  | Optional live Gemini test (requires a key)                  |
| `npm run verify`                     | Secrets scan + lint + typecheck + tests + build             |
| `npm run deploy`                     | Build and deploy (requires approval — see Deployment)       |

## 13. Authentication guide

```ts
import { getAuth, signInWithEmailAndPassword } from 'firebase/auth';

const auth = getAuth();
await signInWithEmailAndPassword(auth, email, password);
```

- The web app wraps the SDK in `useAuth()`; it exposes `user`, `loading`, `signUp`, `signIn`,
  `resetPassword`, and `signOut`.
- On first authenticated call the UI invokes `ensureUserProfile`, which creates
  `users/{uid}` with defaults if it does not exist.
- Security rules require `request.auth.uid == uid` for every document under `users/{uid}`.

## 14. Firestore guide

```
users/{uid}
  displayName, email, bio, createdAt, updatedAt
  preferences { theme, defaultModel, saveHistory }
  usage/{YYYY-MM} { month, requests, tokens, byEndpoint{}, mocked, updatedAt }
  conversations/{conversationId}
    title, model, messageCount, lastMessagePreview, createdAt, updatedAt
    messages/{messageId} { role, text, model, tokens, createdAt }
```

Rules at a glance:

- Every path is owner-scoped: `request.auth.uid` must equal the `{uid}` segment, and `list` is gated
  the same way, so collections cannot be enumerated.
- Profiles accept only user-editable fields on update (`displayName`, `bio`, `preferences`,
  `updatedAt`); `role` can never be escalated and profiles cannot be deleted.
- Messages are **append-only** (no update, delete allowed), conversation counters must be
  non-decreasing, and both are length-capped.
- `usage_events` is append-only and immutable once written; in Spark mode the authenticated owner
  writes its own events, and every field is validated against the call it claims to describe.
- `rateLimits/*` is unreadable and unwritable by clients — in Blaze mode it belongs to the server
  only. Everything else falls through to a deny-all rule.

Full rules: [`firestore/firestore.rules`](firestore/firestore.rules). Indexes:
[`firestore/firestore.indexes.json`](firestore/firestore.indexes.json).

## 15. Gemini integration guide

One call site, two implementations:

```ts
// identical in both modes — apps/web/src/lib/api.ts owns the difference
import { generateText } from './lib/api';

const { text } = await generateText({ prompt: 'Explain Firestore rules in 3 bullets.' });
console.log(text);
```

| Endpoint             | Purpose                 | Spark mode (client)                       | Blaze mode (functions)          | Highlights                                                     |
| -------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `generateText`       | One-shot completion     | Gemini REST with the user's key           | `aiGenerateText` callable       | Optional system instruction, temperature, token cap            |
| `chat`               | Multi-turn conversation | REST + Firestore writes under rules       | `aiChat` callable               | Persists history, caps history length, returns conversation id |
| `generateStructured` | Schema-constrained JSON | `responseSchema` + Zod re-validation      | `aiGenerateStructured` callable | Returns a validated `ArticleBrief` object                      |
| `usageSummary`       | Usage readout           | Firestore `count()` / `sum()` aggregation | `aiUsageSummary` callable       | No unbounded reads                                             |

`generateStructured` uses a Gemini response schema so the model cannot return free-form JSON, and the
result is re-validated with Zod before it reaches React — in both modes. Errors share one envelope
(`{ code, message }`), so panel error handling does not branch on the mode.

## 16. Cloud Functions guide

```
functions/src
  index.ts                 endpoint registration
  config.ts                region, models, limits, mock mode
  middleware/              auth, handler wrapper, rate limiting
  validation/              Zod schemas and JSON schema for structured output
  ai/                      provider abstraction, Gemini client, service layer
  services/conversations.ts conversation + usage persistence
  endpoints/               callable endpoints
  utils/                   errors, logging
```

Every endpoint is wrapped by `withHandler`, which provides:

- authentication (and App Check when configured)
- Zod parsing with `invalid-argument` mapping
- rate limiting via `enforceRateLimit`
- `AppError` â†’ HttpsError mapping, and internal errors reduced to a generic message
- structured logs with the uid and endpoint name, never the prompt text

See [`docs/api-reference.md`](docs/api-reference.md) for request/response shapes and error codes.

## 17. Security documentation

- **Key isolation** — Gemini is only reachable from Cloud Functions.
- **Authentication** — every callable rejects anonymous callers.
- **App Check** — optional enforcement hooks; the demo logs verification state.
- **Validation** — strict Zod schemas on every input; prompt and history caps.
- **Rate limiting** — Firestore-backed, per-user, per-endpoint windows.
- **Logging** — prompts and keys are never logged; errors are redacted before they reach the client.
- **Secret scanning** — `scripts/check-secrets.mjs` runs locally and in CI.
- **Headers** — hosting sets `X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`, and a
  restrictive `Permissions-Policy`.

Details: [`docs/security.md`](docs/security.md) and [`SECURITY_AUDIT.md`](SECURITY_AUDIT.md).

## 18. Testing

```bash
npm run test:unit       # 51 unit tests (validation, errors, rate limit, AI service, Gemini client)
npm run test:rules      # 22 Firestore rules tests (emulator + rules-unit-testing)
npm run test:emulator   # 14 end-to-end checks (auth, callables, chat persistence, ownership)
npm run test:live       # optional, requires GEMINI_API_KEY
npm run verify          # the full gate used by CI
```

Test strategy and CI details: [`docs/testing.md`](docs/testing.md).

## 19. Deployment

### Spark mode — no billing account

```bash
firebase login
firebase use --add                       # select your Spark project
npm run build:web                        # builds apps/web/dist with .env.production
firebase deploy --only hosting:web
firebase deploy --only firestore:rules
```

Live result of exactly this sequence: <https://fb-ai-starter-kit.web.app>. Step-by-step console
clicks, the Firestore/Auth setup, the hosting target wiring and the post-deploy verification:
[`docs/FREE_PLAN_DEPLOYMENT.md`](docs/FREE_PLAN_DEPLOYMENT.md).

### Blaze mode — server-side functions

```bash
firebase login
firebase use --add                  # select your project
firebase functions:secrets:set GEMINI_API_KEY
npm run build
firebase deploy --only firestore:rules,firestore:indexes,functions,hosting
```

Deployment is intentionally manual: the repository never deploys on push without review. See
[`docs/deployment.md`](docs/deployment.md) for the full runbook, including rollback steps.

## 20. Troubleshooting

| Symptom                                  | Cause                          | Fix                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Firebase: Error (auth/invalid-api-key)` | `.env.local` missing or stale  | Re-copy `.env.example`, restart Vite                     |
| `internal` from a callable               | Missing `GEMINI_API_KEY`       | Set the secret, redeploy functions                       |
| `resource-exhausted`                     | Rate limit hit                 | Wait for the window, or tune `AI_RATE_LIMIT_*`           |
| `permission-denied` on Firestore writes  | Writing server-only fields     | Only functions may write `usage/*`, counters, timestamps |
| Emulator cannot start Firestore          | Java < 21                      | Install JDK 21 and point `JAVA_HOME` at it               |
| `unavailable` on first call              | Functions not finished booting | Retry after the emulator reports the endpoints           |

More: [`docs/troubleshooting.md`](docs/troubleshooting.md).

## 21. Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. Please read [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md) and
[`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) first. Run `npm run verify` before opening a PR.

## 22. License

MIT — see [`LICENSE`](LICENSE).

## 23. Roadmap

See [`ROADMAP.md`](ROADMAP.md). Shipped: the hosted live demo on the Spark plan (2026-11-21).
Near-term: streaming responses, App Check enforcement, multi-model routing, and the Blaze deployment
of the server-side variant.

## 24. Project links

- Repository: https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/firebase-ai-starter-kit
- Live demo (Spark plan): https://fb-ai-starter-kit.web.app
- Project page (Marvis): https://marvis.web.app/projects/firebase-ai-starter-kit
- Documentation: [`docs/`](docs/)
- Author: Muhammad Hamid — https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations
- Contact: https://wa.me/923167417135

# issuefit

Score a GitHub issue before you spend a weekend on it.

`issuefit` answers three separate questions with evidence from the repository itself, then refuses to
pretend they are one number:

| Output | Question it answers | Evidence used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `merged_pr_probability` | Will an outside PR actually get merged here? | external merge rate, median time-to-merge, open-issue load, contributor-friendly labels |
| `maintainer_responsiveness` | Is anyone awake on the other side? | days since last push, maintainer reply in this thread, discussion volume, review speed |
| `stack_match` | Is this near my Python / MCP / LLM / FastAPI / Docker stack? | repository language plus keyword evidence in title, body and labels |

The fit score is `0.50 * merged_pr_probability + 0.35 * maintainer_responsiveness + 0.15 * stack_match`,
minus penalties for a thread with no reproduction detail (`-8`) and a repository untouched for more than
30 days (`-10`). It is clamped to 0-100. Every point comes from a named rule in
[`src/issuefit/score.py`](src/issuefit/score.py), and the CLI prints those rules back as `reasons`.

## Verdicts

Ordered by how hard the blocker is, because a high score does not rescue a blocked issue:

1. `rejected-not-fixable` — `dependency dashboard`, `dependencies`, `stale`, `question`, `support` labels.
2. `blocked-competing-pr` — an open PR already cross-references the issue (checked via the timeline API).
3. `needs-reproduction` — labelled `bug` but the thread has no steps/stack trace/expected-vs-actual.
4. `qualified` — score is at or above 60 and none of the blockers apply.
5. `watch` — everything else.

## Install

```bash
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

## Run the demo (offline, no token)

```bash
issuefit demo
issuefit demo --json
```

The demo scores a bundled fixture whose payload shapes are copied from real GitHub API responses but
whose values are synthetic. It is a demonstration, not a benchmark.

issuefit score --repo example-org/ha-mcp --issue 3166

```

1. `rejected-not-fixable` — `dependency dashboard`, `dependencies`, `stale`, `question`, `support` labels.

## Install

```bash

```

## Run the demo (offline, no token)

```bash
issuefit demo
issuefit demo --json
```

The demo scores a bundled fixture whose payload shapes are copied from real GitHub API responses but
whose values are synthetic. It is a demonstration, not a benchmark.

## Score live issues

```bash
export ISSUEFIT_TOKEN=...            # or GITHUB_TOKEN / GH_TOKEN; needs public read, repo read for private repos
issuefit score --repo example-org/ha-mcp --issue 3166
issuefit scan --query "mcp in:title is:issue is:open" --limit 15 --min-score 60 --out scored.json
```

`scan` writes the **full** scored list to `--out` (rejected and blocked issues included) and prints only
what clears `--min-score`, so nothing is silently dropped.

```console
$ issuefit demo
issuefit demo - fixture evaluated as of 2026-11-21T14:00:00+00:00 (no network, no token)

score  verdict               repo                        issue                                                     merge%  resp%  stack%
93.4   qualified             example-org/ha-mcp          #3166 [FEATURE] bulk entity update: optional compact r    94      90     100
76.8   blocked-competing-pr  example-org/agent-sdk       #7052 [Bug]: glob tool returns nothing for patterns wi    73      72     100
67.3   needs-reproduction    example-org/support-desk    #473 Problems connecting FastAPI app to the platform      92      41     100
66.1   rejected-not-fixable  example-org/design-system   #1204 Dependency Dashboard                                85      65      60

Top candidate reasoning:
  - repo baseline 40
  - external merges 6/8 (75%) -> +19
  - median merge 2.0h -> +20
  - 14 open issues -> +8
  - contributor-friendly label ['enhancement'] -> +7
  - pushed 0.1d ago -> +30
  - maintainer already replied -> +20
  - 4 comments -> +5
  - open-issue load 14 -> +15
  - review speed 2.0h -> +20

```

## Design notes

- **Two stdlib-only layers.** `signals.py` derives facts, `score.py` turns facts into points. Anything
  that needs the network lives in `github.py`, so the scoring engine is testable as pure functions.
- **Injected clock.** `derive_signals(issue, now=...)` means freshness scoring never depends on the day
  the test runs.
- **Insiders are excluded** from merge-rate evidence (`OWNER`, `MEMBER`, `COLLABORATOR`), otherwise a
  maintainer-only repository looks like it merges everything.
- **No fabricated metrics.** The package ships no claims about accuracy, precision, or stars. Only the
  rule table above.

## Limitations

- A score is a prior, not a prediction. It cannot see whether the requested change conflicts with a
  roadmap the maintainers never wrote down.
- `merged_pr_probability` uses the last 60 closed PRs as its sample; very high-volume repositories with
  mixed policies will look noisier.
- Issues whose body is a screenshot image will score low on reproduction detail.

```bash
python -m pytest -q
ruff check .
ruff format --check .
```

CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs both on Linux and Windows for Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13, then
builds the Docker image and executes the demo inside it.

readme.excerpt:
# Google Services MCP

A permission-controlled [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) gateway that gives AI agents scoped,
auditable access to **Google Drive, Sheets, Gmail, Calendar and Docs** — with OAuth scopes, a server-side permission
policy, mandatory confirmation for destructive actions, rate limiting and a JSONL audit trail.

The design goal is blunt: an agent should be able to *read* your workspace by default, and only *change* it when a human
operator deliberately widened the policy. The policy lives in the server, not in the prompt, so no amount of prompting
can talk its way past it.

```
agent ──MCP──▶ tool wrapper ──▶ 1. rate limit ──▶ 2. permission policy ──▶ 3. Google API
                                    │                                         │
                                    └── 4. redact + truncate ◀────────────────┘
                                                     │
                                                     └──▶ audit.jsonl
```

## Highlights

- **Default read-only.** `read_only` mode blocks every write/destructive tool before a network call is made.
- **Per-service, per-action flags.** `drive.share`, `gmail.send`, `calendar.delete`, … each have their own switch.
- **Two-key outbound email.** Sending requires `permissions.allow_email_send: true` *and* `gmail.send: true` *and*
  `confirm: true` on the call itself.
- **Dry-run by default.** Writes preview their effect unless the caller passes `dry_run: false`; deletions need
  `confirm: true` as well.
- **44 tools** across five services, each with an MCP `ToolSpec` (operation, policy key, scopes, annotations).
- **Untrusted content handling.** Gmail/Drive/Docs text is wrapped and control characters stripped before it reaches the
  model, so a malicious document cannot smuggle instructions.
- **Local file sandbox.** Drive upload/download are confined to `files.download_dir`; path traversal is rejected.
- **Audit without payloads.** `logs/audit.jsonl` records tool, service, outcome, duration, correlation id — never
  message bodies or tokens.

## Install

```bash
git clone https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/google-services-mcp.git
cd google-services-mcp
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\activate            # Windows
# source .venv/bin/activate         # macOS / Linux
pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

Requirements: Python 3.11+, an OAuth client (Desktop app) from Google Cloud Console with the Drive, Sheets, Gmail,
Calendar and Docs APIs enabled.

## Configure

```bash
cp config/config.example.yaml config/config.yaml
cp .env.example .env
```

Every flag in `permissions.services` maps to a policy key used by the tools. Widening one widens what the agent can do:

| Service | Policy keys | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `drive` | `read`, `create`, `update`, `upload`, `share`, `delete` | `delete` also needs `confirm=true` per call |
| `sheets` | `read`, `write`, `create`, `delete` | `delete` removes a whole sheet (irreversible) |
| `gmail` | `read`, `draft`, `send`, `modify`, `trash` | `send` needs `allow_email_send` + `confirm=true` |
| `calendar` | `read`, `create`, `update`, `delete` | deleting an event also needs `confirm=true` |
| `docs` | `read`, `create`, `update` | updates are append/insert/replace-text only |

`permissions.mode` adds a global gate on top: `read_only` (reads only), `read_write` (flag-driven), `restricted`

repositories.readme_full_content:
# Google Services MCP

A permission-controlled [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) gateway that gives AI agents scoped,
auditable access to **Google Drive, Sheets, Gmail, Calendar and Docs** — with OAuth scopes, a server-side permission
policy, mandatory confirmation for destructive actions, rate limiting and a JSONL audit trail.

The design goal is blunt: an agent should be able to *read* your workspace by default, and only *change* it when a human
operator deliberately widened the policy. The policy lives in the server, not in the prompt, so no amount of prompting
can talk its way past it.

```
agent ──MCP──▶ tool wrapper ──▶ 1. rate limit ──▶ 2. permission policy ──▶ 3. Google API
                                    │                                         │
                                    └── 4. redact + truncate ◀────────────────┘
                                                     │
                                                     └──▶ audit.jsonl
```

## Highlights

- **Default read-only.** `read_only` mode blocks every write/destructive tool before a network call is made.
- **Per-service, per-action flags.** `drive.share`, `gmail.send`, `calendar.delete`, … each have their own switch.
- **Two-key outbound email.** Sending requires `permissions.allow_email_send: true` *and* `gmail.send: true` *and*
  `confirm: true` on the call itself.
- **Dry-run by default.** Writes preview their effect unless the caller passes `dry_run: false`; deletions need
  `confirm: true` as well.
- **44 tools** across five services, each with an MCP `ToolSpec` (operation, policy key, scopes, annotations).
- **Untrusted content handling.** Gmail/Drive/Docs text is wrapped and control characters stripped before it reaches the
  model, so a malicious document cannot smuggle instructions.
- **Local file sandbox.** Drive upload/download are confined to `files.download_dir`; path traversal is rejected.
- **Audit without payloads.** `logs/audit.jsonl` records tool, service, outcome, duration, correlation id — never
  message bodies or tokens.

## Install

```bash
git clone https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/google-services-mcp.git
cd google-services-mcp
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\activate            # Windows
# source .venv/bin/activate         # macOS / Linux
pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

Requirements: Python 3.11+, an OAuth client (Desktop app) from Google Cloud Console with the Drive, Sheets, Gmail,
Calendar and Docs APIs enabled.

## Configure

```bash
cp config/config.example.yaml config/config.yaml
cp .env.example .env
```

Every flag in `permissions.services` maps to a policy key used by the tools. Widening one widens what the agent can do:

| Service | Policy keys | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `drive` | `read`, `create`, `update`, `upload`, `share`, `delete` | `delete` also needs `confirm=true` per call |
| `sheets` | `read`, `write`, `create`, `delete` | `delete` removes a whole sheet (irreversible) |
| `gmail` | `read`, `draft`, `send`, `modify`, `trash` | `send` needs `allow_email_send` + `confirm=true` |
| `calendar` | `read`, `create`, `update`, `delete` | deleting an event also needs `confirm=true` |
| `docs` | `read`, `create`, `update` | updates are append/insert/replace-text only |

`permissions.mode` adds a global gate on top: `read_only` (reads only), `read_write` (flag-driven), `restricted`
(only names in `allowed_tools`), `custom` (flags only, no mode-level short-circuit).

## Authorise

```bash
google-services-mcp auth login               # opens a browser, stores the refresh token
google-services-mcp auth login --console     # headless: paste the code
google-services-mcp auth login --write       # request write scopes too
google-services-mcp auth status              # token presence, expiry, granted scopes
google-services-mcp auth logout              # revoke at Google and delete locally
```

Tick the scopes you actually intend to use. A token that was granted read-only scopes cannot perform writes even if the
policy allows them — the server fails fast with `INSUFFICIENT_SCOPES` instead of a confusing 403.

## Run

```bash
google-services-mcp serve                        # stdio (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Marvis, …)
GSMCP_TRANSPORT=streamable-http google-services-mcp serve
```

Register with an MCP client (stdio):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "google-services": {
      "command": "D:\\GitHub Profile\\google-services-mcp\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe",
      "args": ["-m", "google_services_mcp", "serve", "--config", "D:\\GitHub Profile\\google-services-mcp\\config\\config.yaml"]
    }
  }
}
```

`streamable-http` binds to loopback by default. Do **not** expose it directly: it has no built-in user authentication —
put an authenticating reverse proxy in front of it, or keep the transport on `stdio`.

## CLI

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `serve` | Run the MCP server over the configured transport. |
| `auth login / status / logout` | Manage the OAuth credential (never prints tokens). |
| `policy` | Print the effective permission matrix. |
| `doctor` | Config, credential, path and tool-allow-list diagnostics as JSON. |

## Tools

44 tools, all prefixed by service. See [docs/tools.md](docs/tools.md) for the full reference with policy keys and
arguments.

- **Drive** — `drive_search_files`, `drive_list_files`, `drive_get_file`, `drive_read_file`, `drive_download_file`,
  `drive_upload_file`, `drive_create_folder`, `drive_copy_file`, `drive_move_file`, `drive_rename_file`,
  `drive_share_file`, `drive_trash_file`, `drive_delete_file`, `drive_list_permissions`
- **Sheets** — `sheets_get_spreadsheet`, `sheets_read_range`, `sheets_batch_read`, `sheets_update_range`,
  `sheets_append_rows`, `sheets_clear_range`, `sheets_create_spreadsheet`, `sheets_add_sheet`, `sheets_delete_sheet`
- **Gmail** — `gmail_get_profile`, `gmail_list_labels`, `gmail_search_messages`, `gmail_get_message`,
  `gmail_list_threads`, `gmail_create_draft`, `gmail_send_email`, `gmail_modify_labels`, `gmail_trash_message`
- **Calendar** — `calendar_list_calendars`, `calendar_list_events`, `calendar_get_event`,
  `calendar_check_availability`, `calendar_create_event`, `calendar_update_event`, `calendar_delete_event`
- **Docs** — `docs_get_document`, `docs_create_document`, `docs_append_text`, `docs_insert_text`, `docs_replace_text`

## Security model

Read [docs/security.md](docs/security.md) and [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). Short version:

1. Tools are only reachable if registered, and each registration carries an explicit `ToolSpec`.
2. `PermissionPolicy.check()` runs inside the wrapper before any HTTP call; denial is audited as `denied`.
3. Scopes are validated per service; missing scopes raise `INSUFFICIENT_SCOPES` with the missing list.
4. Destructive tools require `confirm: true`; writes default to `dry_run: true`.
5. Returned Google content is treated as data: wrapped, control-stripped, truncated, never executed.

## Retry and rate-limit behaviour

Every Google API call goes through `google_services_mcp.retry.execute_with_retry`:

- **What is retried.** Only `429`, `500`, `502`, `503`, `504` (and transport errors with no HTTP status) are retried,
  and only for idempotent operations. Non-idempotent calls (`gmail_send_message`, event creation without a stable id)
  fail fast — a duplicate side effect is worse than a visible error.
- **How long we wait.** When Google sends `Retry-After`, it is honoured in **both** RFC 9110 forms: `delay-seconds`
  (`Retry-After: 7`) and `HTTP-date` (`Retry-After: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 12:00:30 GMT`). Anything above
  `RETRY_AFTER_CEILING` (120 s) is clamped and logged as `retry_after_clamped`, because a single MCP tool call must not
  block for minutes. Without a hint, back-off is exponential from `backoff_base_seconds` with ±25 % jitter, capped at
  `backoff_max_seconds`.
- **How many attempts.** `max_retries` (default 3) plus the initial attempt; the last failure surfaces as a typed
  `GoogleServicesMCPError` whose `retryable` flag tells the client whether a retry is worth trying.

```bash
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest tests\test_retry.py -q   # 15 cases, no network, no real sleeping
```

## Development

```bash
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest -q
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m ruff check .
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m ruff format --check .
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m google_services_mcp --config config\config.example.yaml policy
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\gen_tools_doc.py   # regenerate docs/tools.md from ToolSpec metadata
```

CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs the same commands on Ubuntu and Windows for Python 3.11 and 3.12, and fails if
`docs/tools.md` is out of date.

When adding a tool: declare a `ToolSpec`, register it in the service module, add a permission flag in `config.py` if it
introduces a new operation, then rerun `scripts/gen_tools_doc.py`.

Layout:

```
google_services_mcp/
  config.py        settings models + YAML/env loading
  permissions.py   policy + ToolSpec
  tools/           one module per service + registry/wrapper
  services/        typed Google API adapters
  oauth/           token manager, scopes, authorisation flows
  audit.py         JSONL audit log with rotation
  security.py      redaction, truncation, sandboxing, untrusted wrapping
```

## License

MIT — see [LICENSE](LICENSE).

# Gemini Agent Automation Toolkit

[![tests](https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/gemini-agent-automation-toolkit/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/gemini-agent-automation-toolkit/actions/workflows/tests.yml)
[![Python 3.10+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%2B-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green.svg)](LICENSE)

A small, modular Python toolkit for building **reliable** Google Gemini agents: validated tool
calling, Pydantic structured outputs, retries with backoff, human approval for sensitive actions,
multi-step workflows and redacted execution logging.

It is deliberately opinionated and dependency-light — a thin, testable layer over the official
[`google-genai`](https://github.com/googleapis/python-genai) SDK instead of another framework.

- Project page: **https://marvis.web.app/projects/gemini-agent-automation-toolkit.html**
- Repository: **https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/gemini-agent-automation-toolkit**

---

## Why this toolkit

Most "Gemini wrapper" packages stop at a single API call. Real agents need the boring parts:
tools that validate their own arguments, outputs that fail loudly instead of silently, retries that
do not duplicate side effects, a human in the loop before anything destructive happens, and logs you
can hand to a security reviewer.

| Capability | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| Agent engine | `Agent(...).run(prompt)` with instructions, context, usage metadata and typed results |
| Tools | `@tool` decorator, JSON schema generation, argument validation, recursion and call limits |
| Structured output | Pydantic schemas validated on the way out, with explicit `StructuredOutputError` |
| Reliability | Exponential backoff with jitter, transient/permanent error classification, timeouts |
| Human approval | Policies, single-use tokens bound to arguments, expiry, safe failure when unavailable |
| Workflows | Ordered steps, state passing, per-step retries, approval checkpoints, execution history |
| Observability | Structured JSON or plain logs, secrets and API keys redacted, token usage recorded |

Everything is in-memory by design; nothing is persisted unless you persist it yourself.

## Install

```bash
pip install gemini-agent-toolkit
```

From source (development):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/gemini-agent-automation-toolkit.git
cd gemini-agent-automation-toolkit

```

Python 3.10+ is required. The only runtime dependencies are `google-genai` and `pydantic` v2.

## Quick start

Set your key once (never commit it):

```bash
set GEMINI_API_KEY=your-key        # PowerShell: $env:GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key"
```

```python
from gemini_agent_toolkit import Agent

agent = Agent(
    name="Research Assistant",

)

result = agent.run("Explain how AI agents work in three sentences.")
print(result.output)
print(result.usage)  # token usage when the API reports it
```

@tool
def calculate_total(price: float, quantity: int) -> float:
    """Calculate a purchase total."""
    return price * quantity


agent = Agent(
    name="Shopping Assistant",

    tools=[calculate_total],

# Gemini Agent Automation Toolkit

[![tests](https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/gemini-agent-automation-toolkit/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/gemini-agent-automation-toolkit/actions/workflows/tests.yml)

[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green.svg)](LICENSE)

A small, modular Python toolkit for building **reliable** Google Gemini agents: validated tool
calling, Pydantic structured outputs, retries with backoff, human approval for sensitive actions,
multi-step workflows and redacted execution logging.

It is deliberately opinionated and dependency-light — a thin, testable layer over the official
[`google-genai`](https://github.com/googleapis/python-genai) SDK instead of another framework.

- Project page: **https://marvis.web.app/projects/gemini-agent-automation-toolkit.html**
- Repository: **https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/gemini-agent-automation-toolkit**

---

## Why this toolkit

Most "Gemini wrapper" packages stop at a single API call. Real agents need the boring parts:
tools that validate their own arguments, outputs that fail loudly instead of silently, retries that
do not duplicate side effects, a human in the loop before anything destructive happens, and logs you
can hand to a security reviewer.

| Capability | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| Agent engine | `Agent(...).run(prompt)` with instructions, context, usage metadata and typed results |
| Tools | `@tool` decorator, JSON schema generation, argument validation, recursion and call limits |
| Structured output | Pydantic schemas validated on the way out, with explicit `StructuredOutputError` |
| Reliability | Exponential backoff with jitter, transient/permanent error classification, timeouts |
| Human approval | Policies, single-use tokens bound to arguments, expiry, safe failure when unavailable |
| Workflows | Ordered steps, state passing, per-step retries, approval checkpoints, execution history |
| Observability | Structured JSON or plain logs, secrets and API keys redacted, token usage recorded |

Everything is in-memory by design; nothing is persisted unless you persist it yourself.

## Install

```bash
pip install gemini-agent-toolkit
```

From source (development):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/gemini-agent-automation-toolkit.git
cd gemini-agent-automation-toolkit
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\activate      # Windows
pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

Python 3.10+ is required. The only runtime dependencies are `google-genai` and `pydantic` v2.

## Quick start

Set your key once (never commit it):

```bash
set GEMINI_API_KEY=your-key        # PowerShell: $env:GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key"
```

```python
from gemini_agent_toolkit import Agent

agent = Agent(
    name="Research Assistant",
    instructions="You are a helpful research assistant.",
)

result = agent.run("Explain how AI agents work in three sentences.")
print(result.output)
print(result.usage)  # token usage when the API reports it
```

## Tools

```python
from gemini_agent_toolkit import Agent, tool


@tool
def calculate_total(price: float, quantity: int) -> float:
    """Calculate a purchase total."""
    return price * quantity


agent = Agent(
    name="Shopping Assistant",
    instructions="Help users calculate totals.",
    tools=[calculate_total],
)

result = agent.run("Calculate the total for 5 items costing 20 each.")
```

The model proposes a tool call; the toolkit validates arguments against the generated schema,
executes the function, feeds the real result back to the model, and records the call. A proposal is
never reported as an executed call.

Useful decorator options:

```python
@tool(requires_approval=True, approval_reason="Deletes user data")
def delete_file(file_path: str) -> str: ...


@tool(idempotent=True, timeout=5.0, tags=("files",))
def read_file(file_path: str) -> str: ...
```

## Structured output

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from gemini_agent_toolkit import Agent


class ResearchResult(BaseModel):
    title: str
    summary: str
    key_points: list[str]


agent = Agent(name="Research Agent", instructions="Produce structured research summaries.")
result = agent.run("Explain the benefits of Python automation.", output_schema=ResearchResult)

print(result.output.summary)  # a validated ResearchResult instance
```

Validation failures raise `StructuredOutputError` with the offending payload attached, so you can
decide to retry, repair or surface the problem — the toolkit will not hand you a dict that only
looks like your model.

## Retries, timeouts and error handling

```python
agent = Agent(name="Reliable Agent", max_retries=3, timeout=30)

from gemini_agent_toolkit import RetryPolicy, is_transient

policy = RetryPolicy(max_attempts=4, base_delay=0.5, max_delay=8.0, jitter=0.1)
```

Only transient conditions (rate limits, 5xx, network errors, timeouts) are retried; authentication
and validation errors fail immediately. Side-effecting tools are guarded by an idempotency cache and
an execution guard so a retry cannot silently run the same call twice. Exhausted retries raise
`RetryExhaustedError`.

## Human approval

```python
from gemini_agent_toolkit import Agent, tool, PendingPolicy


@tool(requires_approval=True)
def delete_file(file_path: str) -> str:
    """Delete a file after human approval."""
    import os

    os.remove(file_path)
    return f"deleted {file_path}"


agent = Agent(
    name="File Management Agent",
    tools=[delete_file],
    approval_policy=PendingPolicy(),  # safe default is DenyAllPolicy
)

result = agent.run("Delete the old report.")
if result.status is RunStatus.PENDING_APPROVAL:
    request = result.pending_approvals[0]
    print(request.tool_name, request.arguments, request.expires_at)
    # ... human decides ...
    agent.approval.approve(request.token)  # or .reject(request.token)
    result = agent.resume(result.execution_id)
```

Guarantees:

- An approval-gated tool never executes before approval.
- Tokens are single-use and bound to a fingerprint of the arguments, so approving `a.txt` cannot
  authorise `b.txt`.
- Requests expire (`AgentConfig.approval_ttl_seconds`, default 900s) and expired tokens are rejected.
- The default policy denies everything; `AllowAllPolicy` exists but must be requested explicitly.
- If the approval mechanism is unavailable, execution fails closed with `ApprovalUnavailableError`.

## Workflows

```python
from gemini_agent_toolkit import Workflow, WorkflowRunner

workflow = (
    Workflow(name="report")
    .add_step("collect", lambda state: {"rows": 42})
    .add_step("summarise", lambda state: f"{state['collect']['rows']} rows collected")
)

result = WorkflowRunner(workflow).run()
print(result.status, result.outputs["summarise"])
print([record.name for record in result.history])
```

Steps receive the running state dict, return a value stored under the step name, and can require
approval or carry their own retry policy. A failing step stops the run with `StepFailedError`
captured on the result.

## Logging and observability

```python
from gemini_agent_toolkit import Agent, AgentConfig

agent = Agent(
    name="Audited Agent",
    config=AgentConfig(log_level="DEBUG", json_logs=True),
)
```

Records include execution id, agent name, model, timings, status, tool calls and results, retries,
approval decisions, errors and token usage. API keys, bearer tokens, passwords and other secrets are
redacted by `redact()` before anything is written; token *counts* stay readable so cost tracking
still works. Logs go through the standard `logging` module, so you can route them anywhere later.

## Configuration

`AgentConfig` is an immutable dataclass; anything can be overridden per agent or via keyword
arguments (`Agent(..., model=..., max_retries=..., timeout=...)`).

| Field | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model` | `gemini-3.8-flash` | Generation model (never hardcoded elsewhere) |
| `temperature` / `top_p` | `None` | Optional sampling controls |
| `max_output_tokens` | `2048` | Output cap |
| `timeout` | `60.0` | Per-request timeout in seconds |
| `max_retries` | `3` | Retry attempts for transient failures |
| `max_tool_calls` | `8` | Tool calls allowed per run |
| `max_tool_iterations` | `6` | Model↔tool round trips per run |
| `max_repeated_tool_calls` | `2` | Guards against tool loops |
| `approval_ttl_seconds` | `900` | Approval token lifetime |
| `log_level` / `json_logs` | `INFO` / `False` | Logging behaviour |

The API key comes from `GEMINI_API_KEY` or an explicit `api_key=` argument — never from source.

## Project layout

```
gemini_agent_toolkit/
├── agent.py          # run / resume orchestration
├── client.py         # thin google-genai adapter + LLMClient protocol for mocking
├── config.py         # AgentConfig, defaults, env handling
├── context.py        # in-memory conversation context
├── models.py         # typed results: AgentResult, WorkflowResult, ApprovalRequest ...
├── tools/            # registry, executor, @tool decorator
├── outputs/          # Pydantic structured-output helpers and validators
├── reliability/      # retry, timeout, idempotency/recovery guards
├── approval/         # policies and approval manager
├── logging/          # execution logger + redaction
└── workflows/        # step runner
```

Design notes live in [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md); the ecosystem survey behind the
design is in [docs/RESEARCH.md](docs/RESEARCH.md); planned work is in [docs/ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md).

## Examples

| File | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| `examples/basic_agent.py` | Minimal agent, usage metadata |
| `examples/tool_calling_agent.py` | Registered tools and real execution |
| `examples/structured_output.py` | Pydantic schema validation |
| `examples/human_approval.py` | Pending approval → approve → resume |
| `examples/retry_handling.py` | Backoff, transient vs permanent errors |
| `examples/multi_step_workflow.py` | Multi-step workflow with history |

Examples require `GEMINI_API_KEY` (except `retry_handling.py` and `multi_step_workflow.py`, which run
entirely offline against a stub client).

## Development

```bash
pytest -q          # 85 tests, no network access required
ruff check .
mypy gemini_agent_toolkit
```

Tests never call the real API: a `StubClient` implements the same `LLMClient` protocol as
`GeminiClient`, so retries, approvals and tool loops are all exercised deterministically.

## Status and limitations

- Version `0.1.0` — the API is usable today but may still change before `1.0.0`.
- Context is in-memory only; there is no built-in persistence or vector memory.
- No streaming API yet (see the roadmap).
- Workflows are intentionally minimal: no branching, parallelism or distributed execution.
- Model availability differs per tier; `gemini-3.8-flash` is a default, not a promise.

## Contributing and security

Contributions are welcome — read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and our
[Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Please report vulnerabilities privately as described in
[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) rather than in a public issue.

readme.excerpt:
# sarif-verify

Validate a SARIF 2.1.0 log **before** GitHub code scanning sees it.

`upload-sarif` fails late and vaguely: a `ruleIndex` that disagrees with
`ruleId` silently mislabels findings, an absolute artifact URI gets the whole
upload rejected, and a `startLine` of `0` drops the annotation without any
error. `sarif-verify` catches those mistakes locally, in under a second, with
no network access and no runtime dependencies.

```
$ sarif-verify check results.sarif
OK   results.sarif | 0 error(s), 0 warning(s)

$ sarif-verify check broken.sarif
ERROR result-rule-index: ruleIndex 0 points at 'missing-key', not 'empty-value' [runs[0].results[0].ruleIndex]
ERROR uri-relative: uri 'C:/repo/.env' is not repository relative [runs[0].results[0].locations[0].physicalLocation.artifactLocation.uri]
FAIL broken.sarif | 2 error(s), 0 warning(s)
```

## Why not just use the schema?

A JSON-schema check tells you the document is shaped correctly. It does not tell
you the document will *work*. The checks here encode the code-scanning contract
instead:

repositories.readme_full_content:
# sarif-verify

Validate a SARIF 2.1.0 log **before** GitHub code scanning sees it.

`upload-sarif` fails late and vaguely: a `ruleIndex` that disagrees with
`ruleId` silently mislabels findings, an absolute artifact URI gets the whole
upload rejected, and a `startLine` of `0` drops the annotation without any
error. `sarif-verify` catches those mistakes locally, in under a second, with
no network access and no runtime dependencies.

```
$ sarif-verify check results.sarif
OK   results.sarif | 0 error(s), 0 warning(s)

$ sarif-verify check broken.sarif
ERROR result-rule-index: ruleIndex 0 points at 'missing-key', not 'empty-value' [runs[0].results[0].ruleIndex]
ERROR uri-relative: uri 'C:/repo/.env' is not repository relative [runs[0].results[0].locations[0].physicalLocation.artifactLocation.uri]
FAIL broken.sarif | 2 error(s), 0 warning(s)
```

## Why not just use the schema?

A JSON-schema check tells you the document is shaped correctly. It does not tell
you the document will *work*. The checks here encode the code-scanning contract
instead:

| Code | Level | What it catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `document-type` | error | Top level is not a JSON object |
| `version` | error | `version` is missing or not `2.1.0` |
| `runs` | error | `runs` is missing, empty, or not an array |
| `driver-name` | error | `run.tool.driver.name` is empty (upload rejected) |
| `driver-version` | warning | Tool version missing, so annotations cannot be traced to a release |
| `rules-id` | error | A rule has no usable `id` |
| `rules-duplicate` | error | Two rules share an `id`, making `ruleIndex` ambiguous |
| `column-kind` | warning | `columnKind` outside `utf16CodeUnits` / `unicodeCodePoints` |
| `result-message` | error | A result has no `message.text`, so the annotation renders blank |
| `result-rule` | error | `ruleId` is not declared in `driver.rules` |
| `result-rule-index` | error | `ruleIndex` is out of range or disagrees with `ruleId` |
| `result-level` | error | `level` outside `none` / `note` / `warning` / `error` |
| `result-location` | warning | No location, or no `artifactLocation.uri` |
| `uri-relative` | error | Absolute path, `file://` URI, or `..` traversal |
| `region-lines` | error | `startLine` is not a positive integer, or `endLine` precedes it |

Errors fail the run; warnings fail it only under `--strict`.

## Install

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/sarif-verify.git
# or, from a checkout
pip install -e .
```

Requires Python 3.11+. No third-party dependencies.

## Usage

```bash
sarif-verify check results.sarif                 # one file
sarif-verify check a.sarif b.sarif              # several files, exit 1 if any fails
sarif-verify check results.sarif --strict       # warnings become failures
sarif-verify check results.sarif --json         # machine-readable report
sarif-verify check - < results.sarif            # stdin
sarif-verify checks                             # list every check with help text
sarif-verify version
```

Exit codes: `0` clean, `1` findings, `2` unreadable file or invalid JSON.

### In a GitHub Actions workflow

Run it as the step immediately before the upload, so a malformed log fails with
a readable message instead of an opaque `upload-sarif` error:

```yaml
jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install git+https://github.com/hamids-ai-automations/sarif-verify.git
      - run: envscope check --sarif results.sarif      # produces the log
      - run: sarif-verify check --strict results.sarif # fails fast if malformed
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with:
          sarif_file: results.sarif
```

### In Python

```python
from sarif_verify import validate

report = validate(document, source="results.sarif")
if not report.ok:
    for finding in report.errors:
        print(finding.code, finding.path, finding.message)
```

`validate` never raises on malformed input; it returns a `Report` with
`findings`, `errors`, `warnings`, `ok`, `stats()` and `to_dict()`.

## Docker

```bash
docker build -t sarif-verify .
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" sarif-verify check /work/results.sarif
```

The image has `sarif-verify` as its entrypoint, so the usual Docker pattern
applies: arguments after the image name are passed to the CLI. The image
self-tests at build time (the bundled clean log must pass, the demo must exit
`1`), and starting it without arguments validates `/app/fixtures/good.sarif`,
so `docker run --rm sarif-verify` proves the tool works with zero setup.

## Working demo

```bash
python -m sarif_verify.demo
```

The demo builds a deliberately broken log in memory - wrong `ruleIndex`,
undeclared `ruleId`, absolute URI, `startLine: 0` - and prints the findings,
exiting `1` exactly as CI would. `fixtures/good.sarif` is the clean counterpart.

## Development

```bash
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v   # stdlib only, no extra installs
make demo                                 # same as python -m sarif_verify.demo
```

CI runs the suite on Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13, plus a Docker build and a
self-check of `fixtures/good.sarif`.

## Scope

This is a contract validator, not a full SARIF JSON-schema implementation. It
checks the fields that decide whether an upload succeeds and whether annotations
land in the right place; it does not validate `fixes`, `codeFlows`, `graphs`, or
external `$schema` references. A clean run means "this log will upload", not
"this log is semantically ideal".

readme.excerpt:
# WhatsApp Attribution Router

[![CI Quality Assurance & Test Suite](https://github.com/hamid-digitalmarketer/whatsapp-attribution-router/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/hamid-digitalmarketer/whatsapp-attribution-router/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
[![Python: 3.11+](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.11+-brightgreen.svg)](backend/)
[![JavaScript: ES6+](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-ES6+-yellow.svg)](src/)

> **"Turn WhatsApp Clicks into Trackable, Campaign-Attributed Leads."**  
> An open-source JavaScript and Python toolkit that captures UTM campaign parameters, generates attributed WhatsApp click-to-chat links, and synchronizes lead events with Google Sheets, GoHighLevel CRM, or outbound webhooks.

---

## The Business Problem

Performance marketers and digital agencies spend thousands of dollars every month on **Meta Ads (Click-to-WhatsApp)**, **Google Search Ads**, and paid social campaigns. 

However, the moment a prospect leaves a landing page and jumps into the WhatsApp messaging interface, **standard analytics break into a complete black box**:

1. **Lost Campaign Context:** Sales reps answering WhatsApp messages have no idea which ad, keyword, or campaign prompted the inquiry.
2. **Attribution Blind Spots:** Advertising algorithms (Meta CAPI, Google Ads Smart Bidding) optimize blindly on button clicks rather than actual qualified conversations or closed revenue.
3. **Disorganized Inbound Volume:** High-ticket leads get lumped together with casual, unqualified queries without CRM lead tagging or offline conversion loops.

---

## The Solution

**WhatsApp Attribution Router** bridges the gap between web analytics and direct chat apps:

- **Client-Side Parameter Capture:** Captures `utm_source`, `utm_medium`, `utm_campaign`, `utm_content`, `utm_term`, `gclid`, and `fbclid` with zero third-party cookies or fingerprinting.
- **Dynamic WhatsApp Routing:** Formats official WhatsApp click-to-chat links (`https://wa.me/...`) with prefilled messages referencing the exact campaign name and an opaque lead reference token (`lead_ref`).
- **Parallel Server-Side Dispatch:** Dispatches an event payload via `navigator.sendBeacon` or async fetch to a lightweight Python FastAPI gateway.
- **Downstream Synchronization:** Automatically logs click rows to **Google Sheets**, syncs contacts and attribution tags to **GoHighLevel CRM**, and signs outbound webhooks for agency automations.

---

## Architecture & Data Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Client ["Browser / Landing Page"]
        Visitor(["Visitor arrives via Ad"]) --> Page["Landing Page (with UTM parameters)"]
        Page --> Router["WhatsApp Attribution Router (JS)"]
        Router --> Capture["Capture & Normalize UTMs"]
        Capture --> Storage["Session / Local Storage (Consent-Aware)"]
        Storage --> Click{"Visitor Clicks WhatsApp CTA"}
        Click -->|1. Generate Prefilled URL| WA_App["WhatsApp Mobile / Web App"]
        Click -->|2. Send Event via Beacon| FastAPIGateway["Python FastAPI Gateway"]
    end

    subgraph Backend ["Server-Side Gateway (Python)"]
        FastAPIGateway --> Security["Rate Limiter & 512KB Size Cap"]
        Security --> Dedup["Deduplication Engine (48h Window)"]
        Dedup --> Dispatcher["Integration Dispatcher"]
    end

    subgraph Integrations ["Downstream Marketing Tech"]
        Dispatcher --> GSheets["Google Sheets API v4"]
        Dispatcher --> GHL["GoHighLevel CRM (v2 Contacts)"]
        Dispatcher --> Webhook["Generic Outbound Webhook (HMAC-SHA256)"]
    end

    subgraph Conversion_Loop ["Downstream Conversion Loop"]
        WA_App --> CustomerMsg["Customer Sends WhatsApp Message"]
        CustomerMsg --> SalesRep["Sales Representative Identifies lead_ref"]
        SalesRep --> CRM_Update["POST /api/v1/leads (Status: qualified)"]
        CRM_Update --> GHL
        CRM_Update --> GSheets
    end
```

---

##

# ConversionBridge

Privacy-First Server-Side Conversion Tracking for Meta Ads & Google Analytics 4.

--- ## 📌 Executive Summary **ConversionBridge** is an enterprise-grade, open-source Python and Firebase solution for capturing consent-aware first-party conversion events and dispatching them directly to **Meta Conversions API (CAPI)** and **Google Analytics 4 (GA4) Measurement Protocol** via server-to-server integrations. Modern performance marketing suffers from severe signal degradation caused by iOS App Tracking Transparency (ATT), browser ad-blockers, ITP cookie lifespan caps, and third-party cookie restrictions. Browser-only tracking routinely misses **15% to 30% of conversions**, distorting return on ad spend (ROAS) and crippling algorithmic bidding. ConversionBridge restores measurement integrity by moving conversion delivery to a trusted, secure first-party server environment—enforcing user consent, eliminating duplicate transactions, and protecting customer privacy. --- ## 🏗️ System Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph Clients["First-Party Client Applications"] Web["Web Application / Checkout"] Backend["E-Commerce / CRM Server"] Mobile["Mobile App Backend"] end subgraph Gateway["ConversionBridge Gateway (FastAPI / Firebase Functions v2)"] Ingest["POST /api/v1/events"] AuthRate["Authentication & Sliding-Window Rate Limiting"] Validate["Event Validator (Timestamps, Schema, Data Formats)"] Consent["Consent Engine (Fail-Closed Policy)"] Dedup["Deduplication Engine (48-Hour Idempotency)"] Storage[("Storage Backend\nMemory / Cloud Firestore")] end subgraph Destinations["Advertising & Measurement Platforms"] Meta["Meta Conversions API\nGraph API v20.0"] GA4["Google Analytics 4\nMeasurement Protocol"] end Web -->|Conversion Event| Ingest Backend -->|Purchase / CRM Deal| Ingest Mobile -->|In-App Conversion| Ingest Ingest --> AuthRate AuthRate --> Validate Validate --> Consent Consent -->|Consent Permitted| Dedup Consent -.->|Consent Denied| BlockedConsent["Log Skipped (Consent)"] Dedup <--> Storage Dedup -->|Unique Event| Dispatcher["Multi-Channel Dispatcher"] Dedup -.->|Duplicate ID| BlockedDedup["Suppress Duplicate"] Dispatcher -->|SHA-256 Hashed Customer Signals| Meta Dispatcher -->|Client ID & Event Parameters| GA4 ``` --- ## ✨ Key Capabilities - **Unified Multi-Channel Gateway**: Ingests a single standardized first-party event and dispatches to Meta CAPI, GA4, or both in parallel. - **Fail-Closed Consent Architecture**: Gated by explicit consent flags (`consent.advertising` for Meta, `consent.analytics` for GA4). If consent is missing or rejected, events are safely suppressed. - **Cryptographic PII Protection**: Automatically normalizes and generates one-way SHA-256 hashes for customer emails, phone numbers, and physical addresses per platform specifications. Unhashed technical context (`_fbp`, `_fbc`, IP, User-Agent) is preserved. - **Cross-Channel Deduplication**: Supports a 48-hour deduplication window using isolated storage keys (`meta:Lead:1001` vs `ga4:Lead:1001`) to prevent duplicate retries while preserving independent delivery. - **Dual Runtime Support**: Operates as a native ASGI application (FastAPI / Uvicorn) for Docker/Cloud Run and as an HTTP Cloud Function on **Firebase Cloud Functions for Python (v2)**. - **Dry-Run Test Endpoint**: Dedicated `POST /api/v1/events/test` route validates schemas, simulates consent rules, and generates safe wire-format previews without transmitting live advertising data. - **Built-in Security Defenses**: API key/Bearer token protection, sliding-window rate limiting (120 req/min), body size limits (512 KB), and automated secret redaction in logs. --- ## 🛠️ Technology Stack | Layer | Technologies | |---|---| | **Backend Framework** | Python 3.11 / 3.12, FastAPI, Pydantic v2, Pydantic-Settings | | **Serverless Runtime** | Firebase Cloud Functions for Python (v2), Google Cloud Functions | | **HTTP Client** | HTTPX (Asynchronous, connection pooling, timeout controls) | | **Persistence & State** | Google Cloud Firestore (Distributed Serverless), In-Memory (Dev/Test) | | **Quality & Testing** | Pytest, Pytest-Asyncio, Ruff (Linter & Formatter), MyPy | | **CI / DevOps** | GitHub Actions CI, Firebase CLI, Google Secret Manager | --- ## 📦 Directory Structure ``` conversionbridge/ ├── app/ │ ├── __init__.py │ ├── main.py # FastAPI app & Firebase Functions v2 handler │ ├── config.py # Pydantic Settings configuration │ ├── routes/ │ │ ├── events.py # POST /api/v1/events & POST /api/v1/events/test │ │ ├── health.py # GET /health │ │ └── status.py # GET /api/v1/destinations/status │ ├── schemas/ │ │ └── events.py # Pydantic data models & validators │ ├── services/ │ │ ├── event_processor.py # Multi-destination dispatcher coordinator │ │ ├── consent.py # Privacy & consent evaluation engine │ │ ├── deduplication.py # Cross-channel deduplication service │ │ └── validation.py # Deep schema & integrity validator │ ├── destinations/ │ │ ├── base.py # BaseDestination abstract interface │ │ ├── meta.py # Meta Conversions API adapter │ │ └── ga4.py # GA4 Measurement Protocol adapter │ ├── security/ │ │ ├── authentication.py # API Key & Bearer token verification │ │ ├── rate_limit.py # Sliding-window rate limiter │ │ └── secrets.py # Secret masking & SHA-256 hashing │ └── storage/ │ ├── base.py # StorageBackend abstract interface │ ├── memory.py # Thread-safe in-memory cache │ └── firestore.py # Google Cloud Firestore transactional storage ├── tests/ │ ├── test_events.py # API routes & validation tests │ ├── test_consent.py # Consent engine & privacy tests │ ├── test_deduplication.py # Deduplication & TTL window tests │ ├── test_meta.py # Meta CAPI adapter tests │ ├── test_ga4.py # GA4 adapter & debug mode tests │ └── test_security.py # Auth, rate limiting & secret redaction ├── examples/ │ ├── python_client.py # Python backend integration script │ ├── javascript_client.js # Browser / Node.js integration script │ ├── sample_event.json # Standard sample payload │ ├── sample_lead_event.json # B2B lead generation payload │ └── sample_purchase_event.json # E-commerce transaction payload ├── docs/ │ ├── architecture.md # Detailed subsystem architecture │ ├── meta-setup.md # Meta Business Manager & token setup │ ├── ga4-setup.md # GA4 Data Stream & API secret setup │ ├── deployment.md # Firebase & Cloud Run deployment guide │ ├── privacy-security.md # GDPR/CCPA compliance & security posture │ ├── troubleshooting.md # Diagnostic guide & common error fixes │ └── integration-guide.md # Webhook & CMS implementation patterns ├── .github/workflows/ci.yml # Automated CI linting & test pipeline ├── firebase.json # Firebase Cloud Functions configuration ├── firestore.rules # Firestore backend security rules ├── firestore.indexes.json # Compound index & TTL definitions ├── .env.example # Environment configuration template ├── pytest.ini # Pytest async runner configuration ├── ruff.toml # Ruff linter rules ├── LICENSE # MIT License └── README.md ``` --- ## 🚀 Quick Start Guide ### 1. Clone & Set Up Virtual Environment ```bash git clone https://github.com/hamid-digitalmarketer/conversionbridge.git cd conversionbridge python -m venv venv # Windows: venv\Scripts\activate # macOS/Linux: source venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements-dev.txt ``` ### 2. Configure Local Environment Copy the example environment file and add your credentials: ```bash cp .env.example .env ``` Key environment settings: ```ini ENVIRONMENT=development REQUIRE_API_KEY=false STORAGE_BACKEND=memory # Meta Conversions API META_ENABLED=true META_PIXEL_ID=123456789012345 META_ACCESS_TOKEN=EAAG_your_token_here # GA4 Measurement Protocol GA4_ENABLED=true GA4_MEASUREMENT_ID=G-XXXXXXXXXX GA4_API_SECRET=your_api_secret_here ``` ### 3. Run Automated Tests & Linting ```bash # Run 38 unit & integration tests pytest -v # Run code style and linter checks ruff check . ``` ### 4. Start Local Development Server ```bash python -m uvicorn app.main:app --port 8080 --reload ``` Interactive OpenAPI documentation will be accessible at `http://localhost:8080/docs`. --- ## 📡 API Usage & Example Payloads ### Ingest a Conversion Event (`POST /api/v1/events`) ```bash curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/events \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "event_name": "Lead", "event_id": "lead_20261019_001", "event_time": 1729304859, "event_source_url": "https://example.com/consultation", "action_source": "website", "consent": { "analytics": true, "advertising": true }, "user_data": { "email": "customer@example.com", "phone": "+15551234567", "first_name": "Sarah", "last_name": "Connor", "country": "us", "client_id": "123456789.1729304859", "fbp": "fb.1.1729304859.1029384756" }, "custom_data": { "value": 150.00, "currency": "USD", "content_name": "Growth Strategy Audit" }, "destinations": ["meta", "ga4"], "test_mode": false }' ``` #### Successful JSON Response: ```json { "success": true, "event_id": "lead_20261019_001", "event_name": "Lead", "results": [ { "destination": "meta", "status": "sent", "status_code": 200, "message": "Meta accepted event successfully (events_received: 1)", "event_id": "lead_20261019_001", "payload_preview": null }, { "destination": "ga4", "status": "sent", "status_code": 204, "message": "GA4 accepted event via Measurement Protocol (HTTP 204/200)", "event_id": "lead_20261019_001", "payload_preview": null } ], "timestamp": 1729304860 } ``` --- ## 🔒 Security & Privacy Guarantees 1. **One-Way SHA-256 Hashing**: Direct customer identifiers (`email`, `phone`, `names`) are never sent in plaintext over external networks. 2. **Fail-Closed Privacy**: Omitting consent causes ConversionBridge to block outbound requests before network transmission. 3. **SSRF Prevention**: All external HTTP requests route exclusively to predefined platform endpoints (`graph.facebook.com` and `google-analytics.com`). Arbitrary URLs are strictly rejected. 4. **Zero Persistent PII**: Deduplication records store only hashed routing keys and timestamps. Customer details are not permanently retained in the database. --- ## ⚠️ Important Technical Limitations - **Attribution vs. Event Acceptance**: Receiving an HTTP 200/204 response from Meta or Google confirms successful receipt of the data. It **does not guarantee** that Meta or Google will attribute that conversion to an advertising campaign. Attribution depends on platform match keys, auction models, and user conversion windows. - **Privacy Policy Compliance**: Server-side tracking does not eliminate the legal obligation to obtain user consent under GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, and relevant data privacy legislation. - **GA4 Reporting Latency**: Events sent to GA4 Measurement Protocol appear in DebugView immediately, in Realtime reports within minutes, and in standard attribution reports within 24 to 48 hours. --- ## 🗺️ Product Roadmap - [x] Dual Meta Conversions API & GA4 Measurement Protocol adapters. - [x] Fail-closed privacy & consent management engine. - [x] Cross-channel deduplication with Firestore & Memory storage. - [x] Dual runtime (Uvicorn ASGI + Firebase Functions v2). - [ ] TikTok Events API adapter. - [ ] Google Ads Enhanced Conversions for Leads direct API integration. - [ ] BigQuery raw event archiving pipeline. --- ## 🤝 Contributing & License Contributions are welcome! Please review [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and our [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) guidelines. Released under the [MIT License](LICENSE). Copyright © 2026 Muhammad Hamid. --- ## Let's Build Better Conversion Tracking Need reliable server-side conversion tracking for your business? I can help implement Meta Conversions API, Google Analytics 4 Measurement Protocol, lead tracking, purchase events, and custom conversion measurement workflows. Whether you're running an e-commerce store, generating leads, managing paid advertising campaigns, or building a SaaS product, let's discuss a tracking setup tailored to your requirements. Contact me directly on WhatsApp to discuss your project. 💬 **WhatsApp**: [+92 316 7417135](https://wa.me/923167417135)
