Every estimate says how much to trust it: `exact`, `upper_bound` or `heuristic`. A heuristic is never called exact. ## Configuration Copy [`gulliver.example.toml`](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/gulliver.example.toml) to `gulliver.toml`: ```toml default_connection = "local" [connections.local] engine = "duckdb" path = "warehouse.duckdb" [connections.bq] dsn = "bigquery://my-project?location=EU" dataset = "analytics" price_per_tib_usd = 6.25 [budget] max_query_usd = 1.00 # hard stop for one query approval_over_usd = 0.25 # above this a human runs `gulliver approve ` rehearse_over_usd = 0.10 # above this a rehearsal is required first day_usd = 10.00 # total per day (local ledger) max_runtime_s = 900 max_output_rows = 200 # rows handed back to the agent session_usd = 3 # per agent session (optional) agent_day_usd = 5 # per agent per day (optional) ``` The example file also shows the settings for the read-only gate (`allowed_paths`, `allow_remote`, `allow_functions`), the result guard (`policy`), the runaway guard, `[lint]`, `[review]` and `[approval]`. An unknown top-level key or section is refused, so a typo such as `[budjet]` cannot silently fall back to the default budget. ### A read-only Postgres role Gulliver refuses writes itself, but a role that can only read is a good second layer. Run this once as an admin and put `gulliver_ro` in the DSN: ```sql CREATE ROLE gulliver_ro LOGIN PASSWORD 'change-me'; GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE app TO gulliver_ro; GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO gulliver_ro; GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO gulliver_ro; ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO gulliver_ro; -- tables created later ALTER ROLE gulliver_ro SET statement_timeout = '15min'; -- the server stops runaway queries too ALTER ROLE gulliver_ro SET default_transaction_read_only = on; ``` Or skip the file: `GULLIVER_DSN`, `GULLIVER_MAX_QUERY_USD`, `GULLIVER_DAY_USD` and friends. Credentials never go in the config: Gulliver uses each engine's own environment variables and credential chains (Google ADC, `SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD`, `PGPASSWORD`, ...). The agent only ever sees connection *names*. ## Safety model - **Read-first.** Only `SELECT` (and `WITH ... SELECT`) runs by default. `DELETE`, `UPDATE`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `ALTER`, `MERGE`, several statements at once and unparsable SQL are refused by a parser, not a regex. - **A SELECT is not automatically safe.** Functions with side effects (`pg_terminate_backend`, `set_config`, `nextval`), SQL hidden in a string (`dblink_exec`, DuckDB `query()`, BigQuery `EXTERNAL_QUERY`) and file or URL access (`pg_read_file`, `read_csv('~/.aws/credentials')`) are refused with codes [GS001-GS004](#scale-lint-rules), anywhere in the statement. - **DuckDB is sandboxed in the engine.** Every DuckDB connection runs with `allowed_directories` set to the database folder and the current folder (or `allowed_paths`), external access off, extension auto-loading off and the configuration locked, so the agent cannot `SET` it back. For Postgres, BigQuery and Snowflake the parser is Gulliver's only check, so also use a [read-only role](#a-read-only-postgres-role). `gulliver selftest security` runs the bypass test set that ships with Gulliver (151 cases) and checks the sandbox live. - **Writes need two keys.** `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` and `INSERT ... SELECT` run only when the call says `allow_write` **and** a human set `allow_write = true` on that connection. Rehearsals never write. - **Budgets fail closed.** Over the per-query, per-day, per-session, per-agent, bytes or runtime limit means `block`. Money above the approval limit needs `gulliver approve `, a CLI command for humans that is not exposed as an MCP tool (or, when the human turned it on, a form in the MCP client that the agent cannot fill). - **Rows are data, not instructions.** Run results are marked `untrusted: true`, secrets are masked, personal data is flagged, and text that reads like instructions to an AI is listed in `data_warnings`. - **Engine-side caps** where they exist: BigQuery `maximum_bytes_billed`, Snowflake and Postgres statement timeouts, a DuckDB interrupt timer. - **Local state only.** Receipts, the spend ledger and approvals live in `./.gulliver/` as JSON, hash-chained so `gulliver audit verify` can detect edits. No telemetry. The threat model is in [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/SECURITY.md); the full list of what the gate refuses is in [docs/features/security.md](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/docs/features/security.md). > **Breaking change in 0.3.0.** DuckDB connections can no longer read files outside the database folder and the > current folder, read remote URLs, or auto-load extensions. If you read Parquet or CSV files elsewhere, add the > folder to `allowed_paths` (or the bucket to `allow_remote`) on the connection in `gulliver.toml`. When the > database folder or the current folder is `/`, your home folder or above it, it is left out of the default; > set `allowed_paths` then. `sandbox = false` turns the engine sandbox off (the parser still checks). > Queries that call the refused functions get `block`; `allow_functions` lifts that per connection. ## How the prediction works Each rung measures runtime, output rows and (where the engine reports it) bytes. Gulliver fits `metric = a * fraction^k` in log-log space and reads off the value at 100%. - `k ≈ 1`: grows with the data (scans, filters, key joins against a full table). - `k ≈ 0`: flat (aggregations). Group counts saturate, so grouped results are capped by what was observed and the planner estimate. - `k > 1.3`: grows faster than the data: a big sort, or (with `--sample all`) a join between two sampled sides that multiplies rows. Flagged. In the default mode a multiplying join keeps `k ≈ 1` and is flagged by size instead: output much larger than the biggest input table. Runtime first subtracts the fixed per-query overhead (measured with `SELECT 1`). Confidence is `high`, `medium` or `low`, with a range of x0.7-1.5, x0.5-2 or x0.25-4. After a real run, the receipt shows predicted vs actual. Use `gulliver calibration --days 30 -c NAME` to see how often the recorded ranges covered real rows, runtime and cost at each confidence level. Omit `-c` to include every connection. The window includes today in UTC. This reads receipts without running SQL. It uses the linked rehearsal for older runs and counts runs with no usable range separately. Local engines have no cost data. The median and geometric mean use actual/predicted, and the worst ratio is the one farthest from 1 on a multiplicative scale. A zero prediction counts toward range coverage when it has bounds, but it has no ratio. Use `--json` or read the default report at `gulliver://calibration` in MCP. By default only the **largest** table is sampled and the others stay complete, which keeps key joins honest. When the query reads that table more than once (a self-join, an `IN (SELECT ...)` on the same table, a CTE used twice), only the first occurrence is sampled and the others are read in full on every rung. Two samples of one table drawn with the same seed would hold the same rows, so every row would meet itself and small rungs would come out too big. With one side sampled the output grows linearly and the prediction stays unbiased; the price is a full read of the other side per rung. A result much larger than the biggest input table is flagged as a join that multiplies rows. On the 5M-row demo self-join, five seeds predicted 252M-257M rows against 254,966,150 real ones. `--sample all` samples every table and every occurrence, each with its own seed. That is cheaper, but a join between two sampled sides grows with fraction² and the noise of both samples multiplies, so those predictions get `low` confidence. When a table is read more than once, `--method auto` uses row (bernoulli) sampling. When the smallest rung reads fewer than 2,000 rows, the range is widened one level. For BigQuery the money prediction uses the exact dry-run bytes of the full query. **Limits, honestly:** block (system) sampling is cheap but can be skewed on clustered data; use `--method bernoulli` when that matters. On DuckDB a system sample takes whole 2,048-row vectors and is not repeatable even with a seed, so `--method auto` always uses bernoulli on DuckDB (a local scan costs nothing); on BigQuery and Snowflake it keeps the cheap system sample for tables of a million rows or more. Extrapolating 10x always has uncertainty; Gulliver shows it instead of hiding it. Databricks, ClickHouse and Spark are not supported yet. ## Pipeline tools These reuse the same connections, budget gate and receipts. Every query they run is generated, parsed, estimated and gated like your own queries. ### Impact: what breaks if a column changes ```bash gulliver impact raw.events.amount --models models/ # or --manifest target/manifest.json ``` ``` Changing raw.events.amount affects 4 model(s): stg_events: amount <- raw.events.amount fct_revenue: revenue <- stg_events.amount user_ltv: ltv <- stg_events.amount country_report: revenue <- fct_revenue.revenue ``` Plain `*.sql` files and dbt models (`{{ ref() }}`, `{{ source() }}`, `{{ config() }}`, `{% if %}`) both work. Columns used only in filters or joins are reported too, and `SELECT *` models are flagged because their shape follows the source. `gulliver lineage --models models/` prints the whole graph. ### Drift: schema changes since last time ```bash gulliver snapshot # remember tables, columns and row counts gulliver drift --models models/ # later: what changed, and which models it breaks gulliver drift --save # accept the new schema ``` Removed and retyped columns are `warn` and are mapped to impacted models; row counts that move more than 20% are listed too. ### Diff: prove two queries return the same rows ```bash gulliver diff --left "select * from fct_orders" --right "select * from fct_orders_v2" --key order_id gulliver diff --left orders --right orders --key id -c postgres_prod --right-connection snowflake_new ``` Each side is reduced inside its engine to 256 buckets of (row count, sum of MD5 row hashes) keyed by the key's hash, so it scales to billions of rows and costs about one scan per side. Only buckets that differ are opened (with a finer second pass when they are big) to list keys that are missing, extra or changed and which columns differ. MD5 is the same on every engine, so you can diff across engines; values are compared as text, so cast or round in your queries where engines format numbers or timestamps differently. Use it after a refactor, a migration or an incremental switch. Diff key samples join parts with `|`, escaping `~` as `~~` and embedded `|` as `~p`. Parts without these characters are unchanged. The same escaping keeps composite uniqueness checks from confusing distinct values. ### Translate: SQL between dialects ```bash gulliver translate --from snowflake --to bigquery -f model.sql gulliver translate --from duckdb --to postgres --check -c pg "select ..." # also preflight on the target ``` Functions the translator does not know are copied as-is and listed as warnings, so nothing is silently wrong. ### Incremental: stop rebuilding everything ```bash gulliver incremental -f models/user_ltv.sql --time-column ts --unique-key user_id --period 1d ``` | Strategy | When | What it generates | |---|---|---| | `append` | no aggregation | read only rows newer than the target's max (merge on `unique_key` for late updates) | | `partition_overwrite` | grouped by a time grain | dbt `microbatch` config: recompute the recent periods (+ lookback) | | `merge_recompute` | grouped (or windowed) by an entity key | recompute only the keys that got new rows, merge on the key | | `not_safe` | LIMIT, totals over everything, windows without PARTITION BY | keeps the full rebuild and says why | It also measures the saving on the real source ("each run would read about 172,800 of 5,000,000 rows, 96.5% fewer") and, on billed engines, compares dry-run bytes, telling you when you need to partition or cluster the source to turn fewer rows into less money. Prove the result with `gulliver diff`. ### Check: data quality in one scan ```bash gulliver check events --unique event_id --not-null user_id,amount \ --accepted "event_type=view|click|cart|buy" --range "amount=0:10000" --fresh ts=24h --max-change 30 ``` All checks become one aggregate query (one scan), budget-gated like any other. Status `fail` (exit code 4) when a check fails, so it drops into CI or an orchestrator. Row-count history is kept per target, so `--max-change` catches a load that suddenly lost half its rows. Add `--samples N` (1-20; MCP `samples`) to see the most frequent offending values and their row counts for failed unique, accepted-values and range checks. A composite key shows every key column; single-column uniqueness ignores NULLs, while composite keys include them. This is off by default: each failed supported check adds one scan, separately estimated, budget-gated and recorded in the spend ledger. Passing checks, not-null, freshness and row-count checks add no sample query. If a sample query is blocked, needs approval or fails, `samples_skipped` explains why and the check status and counts stay available. Samples use the same connection result policy (mask/hash/deny), output limits and untrusted-data envelope as query previews; receipts contain the guarded values. Composite-key serialization collisions remain tracked in #36. ```bash gulliver check events --unique user_id --accepted "event_type=view|click" --samples 5 ``` ### Top: the most expensive repeated queries ```bash gulliver top # the connection's own query history gulliver top --source csv:history.csv --days 30 ``` It reads Gulliver's receipts, `pg_stat_statements`, BigQuery `JOBS_BY_PROJECT`, Snowflake `QUERY_HISTORY` or a CSV/JSONL export, groups the queries by shape (literals become `?`), and ranks them by cost or runtime. The top groups get lint, a rewrite that returns exactly the same rows, and a saving per month labeled `exact` (both estimates are BigQuery dry runs) or `heuristic`. Repeated aggregates that could read a summary table are listed too. Reading the history is a query like any other, so it goes through the budget gate. Details and limits: [docs/features/top.md](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/docs/features/top.md). ## Auto-fix ```bash gulliver fix "select event_type, count(*) from events where date(ts) = '2025-01-02' group by 1" ``` ``` GV005 [returns exactly the same rows] before: CAST(ts AS DATE) = '2025-01-02' after: ts >= '2025-01-02' AND ts < '2025-01-03' why: Filters the raw column ts by range, so partitions, indexes and min/max statistics can skip data. ts is TIMESTAMP, so the rows are the same. ``` | Rewrite | Rule | Guarantee | Default | |---|---|---|---| | `DATE(ts) = d`, `ts::date`, `TO_DATE(ts)`, `DATE_TRUNC(day/month/quarter/year, ts)`, `YEAR(ts)`, `EXTRACT(YEAR ...)` with `=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `BETWEEN` → a range on the raw column | GV005 | `same` when the connection shows the column is a DATE or a TIMESTAMP without time zone | yes | | the same, when the column type is unknown | GV005 | `assumes` (same rows only if it is such a column) | `mode=all` | | `a.x NOT IN (SELECT y ...)` → `NOT EXISTS` | GV012 | `nulls`: same rows unless the subquery returns NULL | `mode=all` | | `COUNT(DISTINCT x)` → approximate distinct count | GV007 | `changes` (approximate) | `mode=all` | | `UNION` → `UNION ALL` | GV009 | `changes` (keeps duplicates) | `mode=all` | | unbounded `SELECT` → `LIMIT n` | GV002 | `changes` (fewer rows) | `mode=all` | `same` is a promise, so Gulliver keeps it narrow. It never rewrites a date filter on text columns, `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` (a day can start twice when the clocks change at midnight), intervals, `TRY_` and `BETWEEN SYMMETRIC` variants, filters with a time-zone or format argument, or periods that run past year 9999. A column only counts as typed when it clearly comes from one table with metadata, not from a CTE or subquery that could redefine it. Every `same` rewrite is tested against real data: DATE and TIMESTAMP columns, NULLs, `infinity`, the last microsecond of a day and leap days. What it will not do: guess a date range for a missing partition filter (GV004) or a join key for a cartesian join (GV003). Those need a decision, so they stay in `remaining`. Where it pays off: Postgres cannot use a plain index or range partitions on `ts` for `ts::date = ...`, and BigQuery, Snowflake and Parquet readers prune best on the raw column. DuckDB already optimizes this case on its own tables, so there the estimate stays the same. ### Test every rewrite: `--verify` Labels are reasoning; `--verify` adds evidence. It runs the original and each rewrite on small generated tables full of the data that breaks rewrites (NULLs, duplicates, date boundaries, infinity, daylight-saving jumps) in a private in-memory DuckDB, and shows the rows when they disagree, shrunk to a repro you can paste: ```text $ gulliver fix --mode all --verify "select o.id from orders o where o.customer_id not in (select customer_id from blocked)" GV012 [same rows unless a NULL is involved (in the subquery, or in the outer column)] tested: rows differ in 112 of 200 generated cases repro: CREATE TABLE "orders" ("id" INTEGER, "customer_id" INTEGER); INSERT INTO "orders" VALUES (0, NULL); ... ``` A test is not a proof, so labels never move up: an `assumes` change with no counterexample stays `assumes`. A counterexample against a `same` rewrite drops that change and says so (that would be a Gulliver bug). It reads none of your data and costs nothing. `gulliver_preflight` runs a quick version on the `autofix` it hands over. Details: [docs/features/verify.md](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/docs/features/verify.md). ## Guards for agents These run on every query, with no extra tool call. The settings live in `gulliver.toml`, so only the human can change them. ### Read-only gate ```console $ gulliver preflight "select * from read_csv('/etc/passwd')" --json "status": "block", "statement": {"kind": "block", "code": "GS004", "reason": "GS004 file-access: read_csv() reads '/etc/passwd', which is outside the allowed folders (/home/me/project). ..."} ``` | Code | Refuses | |---|---| | `GS001` server-control | `pg_terminate_backend`, `pg_reload_conf`, `SYSTEM$CANCEL_QUERY`, Snowflake `SYSTEM$` functions not known to be read-only | | `GS002` session-state | `set_config`, advisory locks, `nextval`/`setval`, large-object writes, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` | | `GS003` dynamic-sql | `dblink*`, `query_to_xml*`, DuckDB `query` / `query_table` / `postgres_query`, BigQuery `EXTERNAL_QUERY` | | `GS004` file-access | `pg_read_file`, `lo_import`, DuckDB `read_text`, `getenv`, `http_get`; any DuckDB path or URL outside the allowed folders, hidden files (`.env`, `.gulliver/`, also as a glob), `../` and symlinks that lead out | Names are matched in every part of the statement (CTEs, subqueries, UNION branches, the SELECT of a write), after removing quotes, schemas and escapes. On top of that, DuckDB runs in an engine sandbox (see the [Safety model](#safety-model)). It is a denylist plus a path allowlist, not a proof: functions defined in the database can call anything. Settings per connection: `allowed_paths`, `allow_remote`, `allow_functions`, `sandbox`. Details: [docs/features/security.md](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/docs/features/security.md). ### Result guard: personal data, untrusted rows and output size Every `gulliver_run` preview is checked before the agent or the receipt on disk sees it: - **Sensitive columns** by name (`email`, `iban`, `card_number`, `password`, `api_key`, Dutch names too), through your SQL (aliases, CTEs, `SELECT *`, a whole row as one value), and by validated value patterns (email, phone, IBAN mod-97, Luhn card numbers, BSN 11-check, IP, JWT, API-key shapes). - **Untrusted envelope.** The result has `untrusted: true`. Text that reads like instructions to an AI ("ignore previous instructions", `gulliver_*` tool names, hidden Unicode, base64) is listed in `injection` and `data_warnings`. - **Output size.** Long cells are cut (`max_cell_chars`, default 1,000) and a preview over `max_output_chars` (default 50,000) keeps fewer rows plus a `column_summary`, so one wide result does not fill the context. By default secrets are masked and personal data is shown but flagged (`status: warn`), so existing queries keep returning the same values. A `policy` per connection can `allow`, `warn`, `mask`, `hash`, `last4` or `deny` by kind, category or column; `deny` blocks at preflight. `gulliver inspect --sensitive` lists the columns that look sensitive, and lint rule GV014 flags them without a database. This is a mitigation, not a data-loss prevention product: the injection scan uses patterns, so the agent must still treat rows as data. Details: [docs/features/guard.md](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/docs/features/guard.md). ### Runaway guard: loops, per-agent and per-session budgets | Guard | Default | When it trips | |---|---|---| | `max_repeats` / `repeat_window_min` | 5 runs / 30 min | the same query runs again on tables that did not change: `block`, reason `loop`, with the last result in `cached` (free). When Gulliver cannot tell if the data changed: `needs_approval`, reason `repeat` | | `velocity_usd` / `velocity_window_min` | $2 / 10 min | one agent or session spends faster than this: `needs_approval`, reason `velocity` | | `session_usd` | off | one session spent its budget: `block`, reason `session_budget` | | `agent_day_usd` | off | one agent spent its budget for today: `block`, reason `agent_budget` | Cheap repeats (under $0.01 and under 1 GB) never count as a loop. The agent comes from MCP `clientInfo`, `--agent` or `GULLIVER_AGENT` (set by the human, it wins). Names are self-reported, so per-agent budgets are accounting, not a security boundary; the per-query and per-day limits always apply. Queries are tagged in the warehouse (Postgres `application_name`, Snowflake `QUERY_TAG`, BigQuery job labels), `gulliver spend --by agent` (or `day`, `table`, `session`, `task`) shows who spent what, and `gulliver audit verify` checks the hash chain over the ledger, receipts and approvals. Details: [docs/features/runaway.md](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/docs/features/runaway.md). ## In CI and on pull requests ### Lint every SQL file ```bash gulliver lint models/ queries/ # every *.sql file, dbt Jinja included, with line:col gulliver lint models/ --format sarif -o gulliver.sarif # GitHub Code Scanning; also github, gitlab, junit, json gulliver lint models/ --fail-on warn # exit 2 on warnings too (default: errors) gulliver fix --check models/ -c warehouse # exit 2 when a same-rows rewrite exists gulliver fix --write models/ -c warehouse # apply only same-rows rewrites, in place gulliver rules [--format text|markdown|json] # every rule with its severity and autofix ``` Accept a pattern on purpose with `-- gulliver: ignore GV001 reason` (or `ignore-file`); a typo in the rule list ignores nothing and is reported as GV901. Rules, severities and excludes go in `[lint]` in `gulliver.toml`. A pre-commit hook ships with the repo: ```yaml repos: - repo: https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver rev: main # or a release tag hooks: - id: gulliver-lint - id: gulliver-fix args: [--dsn, warehouse.duckdb] # column types are needed to prove same-rows rewrites ``` Fixes are applied as small text edits (comments, line endings and Jinja stay) and are only accepted when the edited statement re-parses to exactly the rewritten tree. Details: [docs/features/lint-ci.md](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/docs/features/lint-ci.md). ### `gulliver review` and the GitHub Action ```bash gulliver review --models models --base origin/main # lint + change type + impact gulliver --dsn bigquery://my-project review --models models --rehearse # + cost per month and row growth gulliver review --manifest-base prod/manifest.json --manifest-head target/manifest.json ``` For every changed model it reports new lint, the change type (`cosmetic`, `non_breaking`, `breaking`), the downstream models that use a removed or changed column, the scan and money per run and per month before vs after, and with `--rehearse` a `superlinear` flag when output rows now grow faster than the data. A `[review]` policy maps the flags to ok, warn or block (exit code 2). A missing base ref or base manifest blocks instead of reviewing everything. ```yaml on: pull_request permissions: { contents: read, pull-requests: write } jobs: review: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: { fetch-depth: 0 } - uses: laaielichter/Gulliver@main # pin a release tag or commit with: models: models # dsn: bigquery://my-project # cost estimates; credentials come from the job env ``` The action posts one PR comment and updates it on every push, writes the job summary, and fails the job on `block`. Classification is static, so a new LEFT JOIN on a unique key is still called breaking; prove it with `gulliver diff`. Details: [docs/features/review.md](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/docs/features/review.md). ## Scale lint rules | Rule | Name | Severity | |---|---|---| | GV001 | select-star | warn | | GV002 | unbounded-output | warn | | GV003 | cartesian-join | error (no condition) / warn (CROSS JOIN) | | GV004 | missing-partition-filter | error | | GV005 | function-on-filter-column | warn | | GV006 | order-without-limit | warn | | GV007 | exact-count-distinct | info | | GV008 | non-equi-join | warn | | GV009 | union-distinct | info | | GV010 | scalar-subquery-in-select | info | | GV011 | window-without-partition | warn | | GV012 | not-in-subquery | info | | GV013 | leading-wildcard-like (`%` or `_`) | info | | GV014 | sensitive-column-in-output | info (personal data, masked secret) / warn (unmasked secret) | | GV015 | fan-trap | warn | | GV016 | order-by-random | warn | | GV017 | deep-offset | warn | | GV018 | count-for-existence | info | | GV900 | parse-error (file lint only) | warn | | GV901 | unused-ignore (an unreadable or unused `gulliver: ignore`) | warn | `gulliver lint` works without any database; `gulliver rules` prints the list with descriptions. GV015 flags `SUM`, `AVG` or `COUNT` of a column from the one side of a join like `orders.id = order_items.order_id`, which repeats each order once per item; it only fires in that naming pattern, to keep false alarms rare. The read-only gate uses its own codes. A `GS` finding is always a `block` with the code in `statement.code`: | Code | Name | Refuses | |---|---|---| | GS001 | server-control | functions that stop sessions or change the server | | GS002 | session-state | functions that change settings, locks or sequences, and `FOR UPDATE` | | GS003 | dynamic-sql | functions that run SQL text the parser never sees | | GS004 | file-access | file and URL readers outside the allowed folders, hidden files, environment variables | ## CLI reference ``` gulliver status connections, budget, spend today (and your own, under caller) gulliver inspect [TABLE] [--sensitive] [--scan N] biggest tables, one table's columns, or sensitive columns gulliver lint SQL [--dialect D] scale lint of one query gulliver lint PATH... [--format text|json|sarif|github|gitlab|junit] [--fail-on error|warn|info|never] [--exclude GLOB] [--warn-unused-ignores] [--metadata] [-o PATH] files and folders (CI) [--baseline FILE] [--write-baseline [FILE]] report only findings not in the baseline gulliver rules [--format text|markdown|json] every lint rule: id, name, severity, autofix gulliver fix SQL [--dialect D] [--mode safe|all] [--limit N] [-o PATH] rewrite SQL, say what changes gulliver fix SQL --verify [--cases 200] [--seed 0] [--timezone TZ] test every rewrite on generated data gulliver fix --check | --write PATH... same-rows rewrites in files (CI) gulliver preflight SQL estimate + lint + gate, no execution gulliver rehearse SQL [--fractions 0.01,0.03,0.1] [--sample largest|all] [--method auto|system|bernoulli] gulliver run SQL [--max-rows N] [--allow-write] gulliver receipt [ID|latest] [--format markdown|json] [-o PATH] gulliver receipt --list [--limit N] [--status STATUS] [--json] gulliver approve ID [--note TEXT] (human only) gulliver demo [PATH] create a demo DuckDB database gulliver lineage --models DIR | --manifest FILE gulliver impact TABLE[.COLUMN] --models DIR | --manifest FILE gulliver snapshot | drift [--models DIR] [--save] gulliver diff --left SQL --right SQL --key k1,k2 [--right-connection NAME] [--columns a,b] gulliver translate SQL --to D [--from D] [--check] [-o PATH] gulliver incremental SQL [--time-column C] [--unique-key K] [--period 1d] [--lookback 1] gulliver check TARGET [--where W] [--unique K] [--not-null C] [--accepted C=a|b] [--range C=min:max] [--fresh C=24h] [--min-rows N] [--max-change PCT] [--samples 0-20] gulliver top [--source auto|receipts|pg_stat_statements|bigquery_jobs|snowflake_history|csv:FILE|jsonl:FILE] [--file PATH] [--days 7] [--limit 20] [--analyze 10] [--rank-by auto|cost|runtime|bytes|calls] [-o PATH] gulliver review [--models DIR] [--base REF] [--head REF] | [--manifest-base FILE --manifest-head FILE] [--rehearse] [--fail-on KINDS] [--max-increase-pct N] [--max-increase-usd N] [--runs-per-day N] [--format markdown|json] [-o PATH] gulliver selftest security [--corpus FILE] the bypass test set and the DuckDB sandbox gulliver spend [--by agent|day|table|session|task|connection|kind] [--days 7] [--format markdown|csv] [-o PATH] gulliver audit verify [--head HASH] check the hash chain over ledger, receipts and approvals gulliver prune [--older-than 30d] [--keep-last N] [--dry-run] clean up old receipts and expired approvals gulliver tools --format mcp|openai|gemini [--toolset core|pipeline|all|NAMES] gulliver mcp [--http] [--toolset core|pipeline|all|NAMES] start the MCP server ``` Exit codes: `0` ok, `1` error, `2` blocked (also: a lint finding at `--fail-on`, a rewrite found by `fix --check`, a review that says do not merge), `3` needs rehearsal or approval, `4` a check failed (data checks, `selftest`, `audit verify`). SQL can be an argument, `-f file.sql`, or `-` for stdin. Global flags: `--dsn`, `--config`, `-c NAME`, `--agent NAME`, `--json`. ## FAQ **Does Gulliver send my data or my SQL anywhere?** No. It runs on your machine and only talks to the databases you configure. Receipts, the spend ledger and approvals are JSON files in `./.gulliver/`. There is no telemetry. **Do I need a warehouse to try it?** No. `gulliver demo` builds a DuckDB database with 5 million events in seconds, and `gulliver lint` works without any database at all. **Which agents and models does it work with?** Any MCP client: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Claude Desktop, VS Code, Windsurf. Without MCP, use the CLI with `--json`, or `gulliver tools --format openai|gemini` for function calling. Every answer is short JSON with a `status` and a `next_step`, so smaller models can follow the loop too. **How accurate is the prediction?** It is a growth curve fitted on three samples, so it comes with a confidence level and a range (x0.7-1.5 when confidence is high, up to x0.25-4 when it is low). On BigQuery the money estimate uses the exact dry-run bytes of the full query. After a real run, the receipt shows predicted versus actual. Joins and skewed data can grow faster than the data; Gulliver flags that (growth exponent above 1.3) instead of hiding it. **Can the agent change or delete data?** Not by default. Only `SELECT` runs. Writes (`CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT`, `INSERT ... SELECT`) need both the call and a human-set `allow_write = true` on the connection, and the agent cannot approve its own runs. **How is this different from `EXPLAIN` or a BigQuery dry run?** Gulliver uses those for the preflight. On top of that it rehearses on samples to show how runtime and output rows grow, rewrites slow SQL with a stated guarantee, enforces a budget, and writes a receipt, in one JSON format across four engines. **Is the read-only gate enough on its own?** On DuckDB the engine sandbox does not depend on function names, so a file outside the allowed folders is refused by DuckDB itself. On Postgres, BigQuery and Snowflake the parser is Gulliver's only check, and functions or views defined in the database can call anything, so keep a read-only database role as well. Run `gulliver selftest security` to see the bypass test set pass on your install. **Will the agent see personal data from my tables?** Secrets (passwords, tokens, API keys) are masked by default. Personal data such as emails is shown but flagged in `data_warnings`, so queries like "find the customer with this email" keep working. Set a `policy` per connection to mask, hash or deny it. Masking happens on the preview after the query ran; the engine still reads and bills the data. **Can text in my data hijack the agent?** It can try. Gulliver marks every result `untrusted: true`, lists text that reads like instructions in `data_warnings`, and can redact it (`injection = "redact"`). The scan uses patterns, so a determined attacker can get past it; the envelope tells the agent to treat rows as data, never as instructions. **My agent keeps re-running the same query. Can Gulliver stop it?** Yes. After `max_repeats` identical runs on tables that did not change, `gulliver_run` returns `block` with reason `loop` and the last result for free. Budgets per session and per agent stop one agent from spending the whole day's budget. **Can I use it in CI without a warehouse?** Yes. `gulliver lint models/` and `gulliver review` (without `--dsn`) need no database. Add a connection to get partition checks, same-rows fixes and cost per pull request. **Is it ready for production on BigQuery and Snowflake?** Not yet. Both are beta and have been tested against fakes, not live accounts. DuckDB and Postgres are tested in CI, Postgres against a live server. Reports from real warehouses are very welcome. ## Roadmap Ideas for what comes next, not promises. Each one is open for help: - Live tests for BigQuery and Snowflake, so they can leave beta. The new query tags, history reads for `gulliver top` and review cost estimates on those engines are also tested only against fakes so far. - GS005: look up the user functions a Postgres query calls in `pg_proc`, and block those in untrusted languages or with `SECURITY DEFINER`. It needs a live-server test setup. - More same-rows rewrites in `gulliver_fix`, and more `--verify` coverage (window functions with ties are skipped today). - Stopping the engine job when a rehearsal is cancelled from the MCP client. - Databricks and ClickHouse engines. Have a case where an agent's SQL went wrong at scale? [Open an issue](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/issues/new/choose). Real examples shape the next lint rules. ## Contributing ```bash git clone https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver && cd Gulliver pip install -e ".[dev]" pytest ``` Contributions are welcome. Start with a [good first issue](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22), and read [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and the [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). See [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/AGENTS.md) for the agent-facing guide and [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/SECURITY.md) to report a vulnerability. Thanks to everyone who helps: ## License MIT, see [LICENSE](https://github.com/laaielichter/Gulliver/blob/main/LICENSE).

Your Data. Your Model. Your Hardware.

Turn clinical text into structured, de-identified insight on hardware you control.
OpenMed's core local runtime performs extraction and de-identification after required model artifacts are available. Model downloads, remote-provider adapters, telemetry-enabled paths, and user-configured integrations may use a network; review each model and dataset's terms.

PyPI package · Python 3.11+ · Model catalog · Research paper · Apache-2.0 SDK source

OpenMedKit · Apple Silicon / MLX · Android / ONNX Runtime Mobile · Browser / Transformers.js · Documentation

2,266 manifest entries  ·  35 model-backed PII languages  ·  Apache-2.0 SDK

English · 简体中文 · Español · Français · Deutsch · Italiano · Português · Nederlands · العربية · हिन्दी · తెలుగు · 日本語 · Türkçe · فارسی · Kiswahili

--- ## See it in action This iPhone example uses OpenMed's local runtime after the required model artifacts are available:

On iPhone via OpenMedKit: scan a clinical note, de-identify it, and extract clinical signals with Apple MLX processing locally in this configuration.


Real-time PII de-identification: in this configured local workflow, the Nemotron Privacy Filter redacts names, addresses, IDs, and billing data from a synthetic clinical discharge packet. (All values shown are synthetic.)
--- ## 30-second example ```python from openmed import analyze_text result = analyze_text( "Patient started on imatinib for chronic myeloid leukemia.", model_name="disease_detection_superclinical", ) for entity in result.entities: print(f"{entity.label:<12} {entity.text:<28} {entity.confidence:.2f}") # DISEASE chronic myeloid leukemia 0.98 # DRUG imatinib 0.95 ``` A clinical NER model using the local runtime after its required artifacts are available. --- ## Clinical brief in 30 seconds From a source checkout, run the CPU-only synthetic contract demonstration: ```bash python examples/v30_clinical_brief.py # Optional: --model mlx, with the pinned model already cached on Apple silicon. ``` It de-identifies an embedded note, extracts and grounds a finding, then prints a cited brief, verdicts and a value-free review packet. **NER/NLI providers are explicit synthetic test doubles, not trained-model or clinical validation.** No external note input is accepted. The MLX option may refuse unsupported output; it never bypasses the guards. See the [brief guide](docs/clinical/clinical-brief.md) and [demo script](docs/demo/clinical-brief.md) for the boundaries and local setup. --- ## Building with an agent? Start with the [consumer agent-usage guide](docs/agent-usage.md), or load the curated [llms.txt](https://openmed.life/docs/llms.txt) documentation index. For callable local interfaces, use the [MCP server](docs/mcp-clients.md), the typed [tool registry](openmed/mcp/tool_registry.py), or the [command-line interface](docs/agent-usage.md#command-line-interface). Ready-made cross-tool procedures live in the [repository skills catalog](skills/README.md). --- ## Why OpenMed? | Deployment consideration | OpenMed SDK boundary | | --- | --- | | Core runtime | Processes locally after required artifacts are available | | Optional network paths | Downloads, remote adapters, telemetry-enabled paths, and user integrations may use a network | | Validation | Deployment owners validate model and dataset terms, privacy behavior, and clinical fitness | | Interfaces | Python, Swift, Android, browser, and service surfaces where supported | - **Curated model catalog**: validate each model, license, and dataset for your use case. - **Safe Harbor-aligned configuration**: can target the 18 identifier categories; expert deployment review remains required, and use of the SDK does not itself establish HIPAA compliance. - **Supported execution paths**: CPU, CUDA, MLX, mobile, service, and browser adapters vary by environment and artifact. - **Deployment interfaces**: Python, containers, services, and batch workflows require configuration and validation. - **SDK source**: released under the Apache-2.0 License; model and dataset terms vary. --- ## On-device on Apple: Swift, MLX & iOS On supported Apple hardware, OpenMed can use **MLX** and **[OpenMedKit](swift/OpenMedKit)** for local processing after required artifacts are available. Model acquisition and any user-configured remote integrations remain separate network boundaries. ```swift // Add OpenMedKit to your app dependencies: [ .package(url: "https://github.com/maziyarpanahi/openmed.git", from: "3.2.0"), ] ``` Expected result: Swift Package Manager resolves OpenMedKit and makes `import OpenMedKit` available to your app target. - **MLX runtime** for PII token classification, the Privacy Filter family, experimental GLiNER-family zero-shot tasks, and Python MLX-LM text generation with Laneformer; includes a CoreML fallback path for supported token-classification artifacts. - **Portable model naming where supported**: an MLX model name can fall back to a matching PyTorch checkpoint when that mapping and artifact are available on non-Apple hardware. - **Python on Apple Silicon** too: `pip install --upgrade "openmed[mlx]"`. Guides: [MLX backend](docs/mlx-backend.md) · [OpenMedKit (Swift)](docs/swift-openmedkit.md) · [CoreML export](docs/coreml-export.md)

MLX on Apple Silicon: 24–33× faster than CPU PyTorch for the Privacy Filter: median latency per inference step, lower is better.
--- ## On-device on Android — Kotlin & ONNX Runtime Mobile OpenMedKit also ships as a native Android/Kotlin library for local document intake, OCR handoff, PII redaction, and token-classification inference through **ONNX Runtime Mobile**. Mobile model repositories include stable tensor names, dynamic sequence axes, tokenizer files, labels, and Android-ready fp32, fp16, INT8, and optional `.ort` outputs. Add the scoped JitPack repository in `settings.gradle.kts`: ```kotlin dependencyResolutionManagement { repositories { google() mavenCentral() maven { url = uri("https://jitpack.io") content { includeGroup("com.github.maziyarpanahi") } } } } ``` Then use the immutable OpenMed `v3.2.0` release: ```kotlin dependencies { implementation("com.github.maziyarpanahi:openmed:v3.2.0") } ``` See the [Android installation guide](android/README.md) for local builds and publishing details. ```kotlin val model = OpenMedKit.fromDirectory(modelDir) val entities = model.analyzeText("Patient Alice Nguyen was seen in cardiology.") ``` - **Android ONNX profile** emits `model.onnx`, `model_fp16.onnx`, `model_int8.onnx`, tokenizer assets, labels, and `openmed-onnx.json`. - **ORT Mobile support** records the minimal-build operator configuration when ONNX Runtime conversion tooling is installed. - **Kotlin parity tests** keep tokenizer offsets, span boundaries, and decoder output aligned with the Python runtime. Guides: [Android ONNX export](docs/export-onnx-android.md) · [Android span parity](docs/android-parity.md) · [OpenMedKit Android](android/openmedkit) ### The same ONNX model on Python CPU ```python from openmed import OnnxModel model = OnnxModel.from_pretrained( "OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-ClinicalE5-Small-33M-v1-onnx-android" ) entities = model("Patient Alice Nguyen was seen in cardiology.") ``` ### The same ONNX model in the browser ```bash npm install openmed @huggingface/transformers ``` ```typescript import { loadOnnxModel } from "openmed"; const model = await loadOnnxModel( "OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-ClinicalE5-Small-33M-v1-onnx-android", ); const entities = await model("Patient Alice Nguyen was seen in cardiology."); ``` --- ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Clinical text"] --> B["OpenMed
(local-first)"] B --> C["Medical entities"] B --> D["PII detected"] B --> E["De-identified text"] style B fill:#0D6E6E,stroke:#0A5656,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff style C fill:#D6EBEB,stroke:#0D6E6E,color:#0E1116 style D fill:#F7DCD8,stroke:#C5453A,color:#0E1116 style E fill:#F5E27A,stroke:#A9A088,color:#0E1116 ``` Rendered result: a local clinical-text pipeline that returns medical entities, PII findings, and de-identified text without sending data to a cloud API. --- ## Agent Skills — build with OpenMed from your coding agent The [`skills/`](skills/) catalog ships portable [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) for on-device de-identification, clinical NER, FHIR export, evaluation, and the healthcare workflows around them. The same `SKILL.md` folders work in **Claude Code**, **OpenAI Codex**, **OpenCode**, and compatible agents; the installer uses each client's skills directory plus the cross-client `~/.agents/skills` convention. ```bash git clone https://github.com/maziyarpanahi/openmed && cd openmed ./install-skills.sh # installs for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and ~/.agents/skills ``` Then ask your agent for the pipeline using synthetic placeholders: > Build a local OpenMed pipeline that de-identifies a synthetic discharge note and extracts medication entities. It loads the right skills and produces an on-device pipeline (`openmed.deidentify(...)` → `openmed.analyze_text(...)`). After the one-time model download, run that pipeline locally on real notes; do not paste real PHI into a cloud-hosted agent prompt. See the **[skills catalog and 30-second example](skills/README.md)**. --- ## Quick start ```bash # Core + Hugging Face runtime (Linux, macOS, Windows; CPU or CUDA) pip install --upgrade "openmed[hf]" # Add the REST service pip install --upgrade "openmed[hf,service]" # Apple Silicon acceleration (MLX) pip install --upgrade "openmed[mlx]" ``` Expected result: ```text Successfully installed openmed-... ```
**Python API** ```python from openmed import analyze_text result = analyze_text( "Patient received 75mg " "clopidogrel for NSTEMI.", model_name= "pharma_detection_superclinical", ) print([(e.label, e.text) for e in result.entities]) ``` Example output: ```text [('DRUG', 'clopidogrel'), ('CONDITION', 'NSTEMI')] ``` **REST service** ```bash python -m openmed.service.logging \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 ``` Example output: ```text INFO: Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8080 GET /health -> 200 OK ``` `GET /health` `POST /analyze` `POST /pii/extract` `POST /pii/deidentify` **Batch** ```python from openmed import BatchProcessor p = BatchProcessor( model_name= "disease_detection_superclinical", group_entities=True, ) results = p.process_texts([...]) print(len(results), sum(len(r.entities) for r in results)) print([(e.label, e.text) for e in results[0].entities[:1]]) ``` Example output: ```text 3 7 [('DISEASE', 'leukemia')] ```
**Browser / WebGPU** Package ONNX token-classification exports for in-browser inference through Transformers.js: ```bash python -m openmed.onnx.convert \ --model dslim/bert-base-NER \ --output dist/example-onnx \ --include-transformersjs ``` Example output: ```text Exported Transformers.js bundle to dist/example-onnx ``` ```javascript import { pipeline } from "@huggingface/transformers"; const detector = await pipeline( "token-classification", "/models/openmed-pii/transformersjs", { device: "webgpu" }, ); const entities = await detector("Patient Casey Example called 212-555-0198."); console.log(entities.slice(0, 2)); ``` Example output: ```javascript [ { entity: "NAME", word: "Casey Example", score: 0.99 }, { entity: "PHONE", word: "212-555-0198", score: 0.98 }, ] ``` [Transformers.js export guide](docs/export-transformersjs.md) **Offline / air-gapped?** Point `model_name` (or `model_id`) at a local directory and OpenMed loads it without contacting the Hugging Face Hub: ```python from openmed import OpenMedConfig, analyze_text result = analyze_text( "Patient presents with chronic myeloid leukemia and Type 2 diabetes.", model_id="./models/OpenMed-NER-DiseaseDetect-SuperClinical-434M", config=OpenMedConfig(device="cpu"), ) for entity in result.entities: print(f"{entity.label:<12} {entity.text:<28} {entity.confidence:.2f}") ``` Example output: ```text DISEASE chronic myeloid leukemia 0.98 DISEASE Type 2 diabetes 0.96 ``` Because `model_id` points to a local directory, this example does not contact the Hugging Face Hub or any external model provider. --- ## Models A curated registry of specialized medical NER models; browse the [full catalog](https://openmed.life/docs/model-registry). | Model | Specialization | Entity types | Size | |-------|----------------|--------------|------| | `disease_detection_superclinical` | Disease & conditions | DISEASE, CONDITION, DIAGNOSIS | 434M | | `pharma_detection_superclinical` | Drugs & medications | DRUG, MEDICATION, TREATMENT | 434M | | `pii_superclinical_large` | PII & de-identification | NAME, DATE, SSN, PHONE, EMAIL, ADDRESS | 434M | | `anatomy_detection_electramed` | Anatomy & body parts | ANATOMY, ORGAN, BODY_PART | 109M | | `gene_detection_genecorpus` | Genes & proteins | GENE, PROTEIN | 109M | --- ## Privacy: PII detection & de-identification ```python from openmed import extract_pii, deidentify text = "Patient: John Doe, DOB: 01/15/1970, SSN: 123-45-6789" # Extract PII with smart merging (prevents tokenization fragmentation) result = extract_pii(text, model_name="pii_superclinical_large", use_smart_merging=True) print([(e.label, e.text) for e in result.entities]) # De-identify with the method you need print(deidentify(text, method="mask").deidentified_text) print(deidentify(text, method="replace").deidentified_text) print(deidentify(text, method="hash").deidentified_text) print(deidentify(text, method="shift_dates", date_shift_days=180).deidentified_text) ``` Example output: ```text [('NAME', 'John Doe'), ('DATE', '01/15/1970'), ('SSN', '123-45-6789')] Patient: [NAME], DOB: [DATE], SSN: [SSN] Patient: Emily Chen, DOB: 03/22/1985, SSN: 456-78-9012 Patient: 6b8f...c4a1, DOB: 48b1...91de, SSN: 3f13...e912 Patient: John Doe, DOB: 07/14/1970, SSN: 123-45-6789 ``` - **Smart entity merging** keeps `01/15/1970` whole instead of fragmenting it. - **Policy-aware pipelines** add HIPAA/GDPR/research profiles, calibrated thresholds, signed audit reports, redaction previews, and minimum-necessary action selection. - **Faker-backed obfuscation** with custom clinical-ID providers (CPF, CNPJ, BSN, NIR, Codice Fiscale, NIE, Aadhaar, Steuer-ID, NPI). - **HIPAA boundary**: Safe Harbor-aligned categories and configurable thresholds are implementation aids; expert deployment review remains required, and SDK use alone does not establish compliance. - **Batch and streaming PII**: extract or de-identify across many documents with `BatchProcessor(operation="extract_pii" | "deidentify", batch_size=16)` or incremental streaming helpers.

Batch processing: up to 3.3× higher throughput on CPU and 2.2× on MLX vs. one document at a time.
[Complete PII notebook](examples/notebooks/PII_Detection_Complete_Guide.ipynb) · [Smart merging](docs/pii-smart-merging.md) · [Anonymization quickstart](docs/anonymization.md#quickstart-choosing-a-method)
Privacy Filter family: three model families on the OpenAI Privacy Filter architecture
Same model code (gpt-oss-style sparse-MoE transformer with local attention, sink tokens, RoPE+YaRN, tiktoken `o200k_base`), different training data. All route through the **same** `extract_pii()` / `deidentify()` API; only `model_name=` changes. `openai/privacy-filter` is a Hugging Face model identifier for local weights; using it here does not call the OpenAI API. | Variant | PyTorch (CPU + CUDA) | MLX (Apple Silicon) | MLX 8-bit | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **OpenAI Privacy Filter** | [`openai/privacy-filter`](https://huggingface.co/openai/privacy-filter) | [`OpenMed/privacy-filter-mlx`](https://huggingface.co/OpenMed/privacy-filter-mlx) | [`…-mlx-8bit`](https://huggingface.co/OpenMed/privacy-filter-mlx-8bit) | | **Nemotron-PII fine-tune** | [`OpenMed/privacy-filter-nemotron`](https://huggingface.co/OpenMed/privacy-filter-nemotron) | [`…-nemotron-mlx`](https://huggingface.co/OpenMed/privacy-filter-nemotron-mlx) | [`…-nemotron-mlx-8bit`](https://huggingface.co/OpenMed/privacy-filter-nemotron-mlx-8bit) | | **OpenMed Multilingual** | [`OpenMed/privacy-filter-multilingual`](https://huggingface.co/OpenMed/privacy-filter-multilingual) | [`…-multilingual-mlx`](https://huggingface.co/OpenMed/privacy-filter-multilingual-mlx) | [`…-multilingual-mlx-8bit`](https://huggingface.co/OpenMed/privacy-filter-multilingual-mlx-8bit) | ```python from openmed import extract_pii text = "Patient Sarah Connor (DOB: 03/15/1985) at MRN 4471882." variants = { "baseline": extract_pii(text, model_name="openai/privacy-filter"), "nemotron": extract_pii(text, model_name="OpenMed/privacy-filter-nemotron"), "mlx": extract_pii(text, model_name="OpenMed/privacy-filter-mlx"), } print([(e.label, e.text) for e in variants["baseline"].entities]) ``` Example output: ```text [('NAME', 'Sarah Connor'), ('DATE', '03/15/1985'), ('ID', '4471882')] ``` On non-Apple-Silicon hosts, MLX model names are automatically substituted with the matching PyTorch checkpoint (with a one-time warning): reuse one model name where a matching backend artifact is available. See [Privacy Filter architecture & backend routing](docs/anonymization.md#privacy-filter-family).
--- ## Multilingual PII (42 supported routes; 35 model-backed) Extraction and de-identification support **42 supported PII language codes**: `am`, `ar`, `as`, `bn`, `cs`, `da`, `de`, `el`, `en`, `es`, `fa`, `fr`, `gu`, `he`, `hi`, `id`, `it`, `ja`, `kn`, `ko`, `ml`, `mr`, `nl`, `no`, `or`, `pa`, `pl`, `pt`, `ro`, `ru`, `sv`, `sw`, `ta`, `te`, `th`, `tr`, `uk`, `ur`, `vi`, `xh`, `zh`, and `zu`, with **the registry-backed PII model catalog** in total. Russian routing currently uses a documented multilingual default-model placeholder. Bengali, Chinese, and Tamil have dedicated registry entries. An optional, user-configured Indic NER family can serve Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil, and Telugu. Set `OPENMED_INDIC_NER_MODEL`; OpenMed never bundles or automatically selects those optional weights. OpenMed also includes validator-backed national-ID coverage for additional ID-only locales such as Latvian, Slovak, Malay, Filipino, and Finnish. See the [per-language guide](docs/languages.md) for each code's default PII model, Faker locale, and a before/after de-identification example. ```bash python -c "from openmed import extract_pii; print([(e.label, e.text) for e in extract_pii('Dr. Pedro Almeida, CPF: 123.456.789-09, email: pedro@hospital.pt', lang='pt').entities])" ``` Example output: ```text [('NAME', 'Pedro Almeida'), ('ID', '123.456.789-09'), ('EMAIL', 'pedro@hospital.pt')] ```
Show per-language examples (Portuguese, Dutch, Hindi, Arabic, Japanese, Turkish)
```python from openmed import extract_pii portuguese = extract_pii("Paciente: Pedro Almeida, CPF: 123.456.789-09, telefone: +351 912 345 678", lang="pt", use_smart_merging=True) dutch = extract_pii("Patiënt: Eva de Vries, BSN: 123456782, telefoon: +31 6 12345678", lang="nl", use_smart_merging=True) hindi = extract_pii("रोगी: अनीता शर्मा, फोन: +91 9876543210, पता: नई दिल्ली 110001", lang="hi", use_smart_merging=True) arabic = extract_pii("المريضة ليلى حسن، الهاتف +20 10 1234 5678، الرقم القومي 29801011234567.", lang="ar", use_smart_merging=True) japanese = extract_pii("患者 佐藤 花子、電話 +81 90 1234 5678、マイナンバー 1234 5678 9012.", lang="ja", use_smart_merging=True) turkish = extract_pii("Hasta Ayşe Yılmaz, telefon +90 532 123 45 67, TCKN 10000000146.", lang="tr", use_smart_merging=True) for r in (portuguese, dutch, hindi, arabic, japanese, turkish): print([(e.label, e.text) for e in r.entities]) ``` Example output: ```text [('NAME', 'Pedro Almeida'), ('ID', '123.456.789-09'), ('PHONE', '+351 912 345 678')] [('NAME', 'Eva de Vries'), ('ID', '123456782'), ('PHONE', '+31 6 12345678')] [('NAME', 'अनीता शर्मा'), ('PHONE', '+91 9876543210'), ('ADDRESS', 'नई दिल्ली 110001')] [('NAME', 'ليلى حسن'), ('PHONE', '+20 10 1234 5678'), ('ID', '29801011234567')] [('NAME', '佐藤 花子'), ('PHONE', '+81 90 1234 5678'), ('ID', '1234 5678 9012')] [('NAME', 'Ayşe Yılmaz'), ('PHONE', '+90 532 123 45 67'), ('ID', '10000000146')] ```
--- ## REST API A Docker-friendly FastAPI service with request validation, shared pipeline preload, and unified error envelopes. ```bash pip install --upgrade "openmed[hf,service]" python -m openmed.service.logging --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 # or with Docker docker build -t openmed:local . docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -e OPENMED_PROFILE=prod openmed:local ``` Example output: ```text INFO: Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8080 ``` ```bash curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/pii/extract \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"text":"Paciente: Maria Garcia, DNI: 12345678Z","lang":"es"}' ``` Abbreviated example response: ```json { "text": "Paciente: Maria Garcia, DNI: 12345678Z", "entities": [ {"text": "Maria Garcia", "label": "NAME", "confidence": 0.99, "start": 10, "end": 22}, {"text": "12345678Z", "label": "ID", "confidence": 0.98, "start": 29, "end": 38} ], "model_name": "OpenMed/privacy-filter-multilingual" } ``` **Model lifecycle and service controls:** free memory on demand with `GET /models/loaded`, `POST /models/unload`, and a `keep_alive` idle window; v1.8 also includes API-key/JWT auth, no-PHI request logging, tracing, gRPC, async jobs, webhooks, warm pools, dynamic batching, request coalescing, rate and concurrency limits, `/livez`, `/readyz`, and opt-in metrics: ```bash OPENMED_SERVICE_KEEP_ALIVE=10m python -m openmed.service.logging --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/models/unload -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"all":true}' ``` Example response: ```json { "unloaded": true, "released": {"models": 1, "tokenizers": 1, "pipelines": 1}, "active_models": {} } ``` See the full [REST service guide](docs/rest-service.md). --- ## Documentation Full guides at **[openmed.life/docs](https://openmed.life/docs/)**. AI agents can load the curated [llms.txt](https://openmed.life/docs/llms.txt) index or the inlined [llms-full.txt](https://openmed.life/docs/llms-full.txt) feed. Both are regenerated from the current documentation during every strict MkDocs build. | | | | |---|---|---| | [Getting Started](https://openmed.life/docs/) | [Analyze Text](https://openmed.life/docs/analyze-text) | [Model Registry](https://openmed.life/docs/model-registry) | | [FAQ](docs/faq.md) | [Anonymization](docs/anonymization.md) | [Batch Processing](https://openmed.life/docs/batch-processing) | | [Configuration Profiles](https://openmed.life/docs/profiles) | [REST Service](docs/rest-service.md) | [MLX Backend](docs/mlx-backend.md) | | [Transformers.js Export](docs/export-transformersjs.md) | [FHIR Interop](docs/fhir-interop.md) | [HL7 v2 De-identification](docs/hl7v2-deidentification.md) | | [OpenMed 3.2.0 Migration Guide](docs/migration/3.1-to-3.2.md) | [OpenMed 2.2.0 Release Notes](docs/release/v2.2.0.md) | [Examples](docs/examples.md) | | [Release Streams](docs/release/semver-and-channels.md) | [Generative Model Policy](docs/generative-model-policy.md) | [Contributing](docs/contributing.md) | | [Security Policy](SECURITY.md) | [Compliance Posture](docs/compliance.md) | [Extension Plugin SDK](docs/plugin-sdk.md) | | [v1 to v2 Migration](docs/migration.md) | [MCP Client Connections](docs/mcp-clients.md) | [African Developer Onboarding](docs/africa-onboarding.md) | --- ## Meet the mascot OpenMed's guardian is a fluffy Persian cat styled as a tiny **Avicenna (Ibn Sina)**: the great Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was the world's standard medical text for some 600 years. He keeps watch over the open book of medical knowledge, in a palette built around Persian turquoise (*fīrūza*): a local-first guardian for your most private data.
--- ## Contributing Contributions welcome: bug reports, feature requests, and PRs alike. Please read the [Contributing guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) and our [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) first. - [Open an issue](https://github.com/maziyarpanahi/openmed/issues) - [Contributing guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) · [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) · [Maintainers](MAINTAINERS.md) · [Security policy](SECURITY.md) - **Translations welcome**: help complete the other-language READMEs linked in the switcher at the top. --- ## Security Found a vulnerability? OpenMed redacts PHI, so a **redaction bypass or PHI/PII leak is a security issue**: please report it **privately**, never as a public issue. See **[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md)** for the responsible-disclosure policy and the [private reporting form](https://github.com/maziyarpanahi/openmed/security/advisories/new). Never include real patient data in a report. --- ## Credits OpenMed builds on excellent open-source work: particular thanks to **OpenAI** (the [Privacy Filter](https://huggingface.co/openai/privacy-filter) architecture), **NVIDIA** (the [Nemotron PII dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-PII-v1)), **Hugging Face** (`transformers`, Transformers.js & the model ecosystem), **Apple** ([MLX](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx)), and the **[Faker](https://faker.readthedocs.io/)** maintainers. ## License The OpenMed SDK source is released under the [Apache-2.0 License](LICENSE). Third-party asset notices are recorded in [NOTICE](NOTICE). ## Citation ```bibtex @misc{panahi2025openmedneropensourcedomainadapted, title={OpenMed NER: Open-Source, Domain-Adapted State-of-the-Art Transformers for Biomedical NER Across 12 Public Datasets}, author={Maziyar Panahi}, year={2025}, eprint={2508.01630}, archivePrefix={arXiv}, primaryClass={cs.CL}, url={https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.01630}, } ``` Expected result: BibTeX-compatible citation metadata for referencing OpenMed in papers, posters, and derived documentation. --- ## Star History If OpenMed is useful to you, a star helps others discover it. readme.excerpt:
tsoa

 Pronounced so·uh OpenAPI-compliant REST APIs using TypeScript and Node ![build status](https://github.com/lukeautry/tsoa/actions/workflows/runTestsOnPush.yml/badge.svg) [![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/tsoa/latest)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tsoa)
## Goal - TypeScript controllers and models as the single source of truth for your API - A valid OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) spec (2.0 or 3.0 if you choose 😍) is generated from your controllers and models, including: - Paths (e.g. GET /users) - Definitions based on TypeScript interfaces (models) - Parameters/model properties marked as required or optional based on TypeScript (e.g. myProperty?: string is optional in the OpenAPI spec) - jsDoc supported for object descriptions (most other metadata can be inferred from TypeScript types) - Routes are generated for middleware of choice - Express, Hapi, and Koa currently supported, other middleware can be supported using a simple handlebars template - Validate request payloads ## Philosophy - Rely on TypeScript type annotations to generate API metadata if possible - If regular type annotations aren't an appropriate way to express metadata, use decorators - Use jsdoc for pure text metadata (e.g. endpoint descriptions) - Minimize boilerplate - Models are best represented by interfaces (pure data structures), but can also be represented by classes - Runtime validation of tsoa should behave as closely as possible to the specifications that the generated OpenAPI 2/3 schema describes. Any differences in validation logic are clarified by logging warnings during the generation of the OpenAPI Specification (OAS) and/or the routes. - Please note that by enabling OpenAPI 3 you minimize the chances of divergent validation logic since OpenAPI 3 has a more expressive schema syntax. ## Framework packages `@tsoa/runtime` does not install a web framework. Its framework packages are optional peer dependencies, so install the ones for the framework you use: | Framework | Packages | | --------- | ------------------------------------ | | Express | `express`, `@types/express` (4 or 5) | | Koa | `koa`, `@types/koa` (2 or 3) | | Hapi | `@hapi/hapi`, `@hapi/boom` | The generated Hapi routes import `boomify` and `isBoom` from `@hapi/boom`. `@hapi/hapi` depends on it, but list it in your own `package.json` as well: with pnpm or another strict layout, the routes cannot resolve it otherwise. Each framework's template service has its own entry point. The `@tsoa/runtime` and `tsoa` roots do not export them, so custom route templates (`routes.middlewareTemplate`) and classes that extend a template service import them from the subpath: ```ts import { ExpressTemplateService } from '@tsoa/runtime/express'; import { HapiTemplateService } from '@tsoa/runtime/hapi'; import { KoaTemplateService } from '@tsoa/runtime/koa'; ``` ## Getting Started - [Documentation](https://tsoa-community.github.io/docs/) - [API Reference](https://tsoa-community.github.io/reference/) - [Getting started guide](https://tsoa-community.github.io/docs/getting-started) ## Examples Check out the [guides](https://tsoa-community.github.io/docs/getting-started) See example controllers in [the tests](tests/fixtures/controllers) See example models in [the tests](tests/fixtures/testModel.ts) ## Help wanted ### Contributing code To contribute (via a PR), please first see the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/lukeautry/tsoa/tree/master/docs/CONTRIBUTING.md) ### Becoming a maintainer tsoa wants additional maintainers! The library has increased in popularity and has quite a lot of pull requests and issues. [Please post in this issue](https://github.com/lukeautry/tsoa/issues/236) if you're willing to take on the role of a maintainer.

repositories.name: sentryward
repositories.description: Self-hosted AI code reviewer with automated reviews, inline suggestions, and flexible support for cloud and local models.

readme.excerpt:
Self-hosted AI code review for GitHub pull requests and GitLab merge requests.

Quick start · How it works · Configuration · Changelog · Discussions

Sentryward is an AI code reviewer for GitHub pull requests and GitLab merge requests. Connect repositories, choose a model provider or Ollama, and run manual or automatic reviews with inline findings, walkthroughs, and commit statuses. The dashboard tracks reviews and findings across runs. > [!WARNING] > Sentryward is pre-1.0: minor releases may include breaking changes.
