Claude Desktop Add to your config file: - **macOS**: `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` - **Windows**: `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json` - **Linux**: `~/.config/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` ```json { "mcpServers": { "memory": { "command": "memory", "args": ["server"] } } } ``` Restart Claude Desktop. Your AI now remembers everything across sessions.
Claude Code ```bash claude mcp add memory -- memory server ``` Restart Claude Code. Memory tools will appear automatically.
Agent pipelines (REST API — LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, any HTTP client) ```bash MCP_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS_ACCESS=true memory server --http # REST API running at http://localhost:8000 ``` Store a memory with `POST /api/memories`, search with `POST /api/search`, retrieve by tag with `POST /api/search/by-tag`. Send `X-Agent-ID: ` on a store request and the server tags the memory `agent:`, which a tag search then scopes retrieval by. Worked examples per framework, the tag conventions and the async patterns: **[docs/agents/](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/tree/main/docs/agents)**
OpenCode ```bash MCP_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS_ACCESS=true memory server --http ``` The plugin ships as repository files for the local plugin directory, so clone the repository once even if you installed from PyPI. Install steps, the `/memory` slash command and the endpoint override: **[opencode/README.md](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/opencode/README.md)**
Codex (automatic memory hooks) Start the Memory Service HTTP API, then install the hooks from this repository: ```bash python3 codex/install_hooks.py ``` Restart Codex and review the hooks with `/hooks`. They retrieve project context, capture new learnings, and checkpoint outcomes before compaction and at session end. See [Codex hook setup](codex/README.md) for prerequisites, authentication, and project-local installation.
claude.ai and ChatGPT (browser — Remote MCP) Remote MCP puts persistent memory in the browser on any device, no desktop app required: OAuth 2.0 over HTTPS, self-hosted or cloud-hosted. Both claude.ai and ChatGPT (Developer Mode) connect to the same endpoint. Cloudflare Tunnel quick start, Let's Encrypt, nginx, Caddy and Docker production setups: **[Remote MCP Setup](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/docs/remote-mcp-setup.md)** · [5-minute tutorial](https://mcpmemory.services/blog/remote-mcp-tutorial.html)
Advanced: custom backends and team setup ```bash git clone https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service.git cd mcp-memory-service python scripts/installation/install.py ``` Choose from **SQLite** (local, fast, single-user), **Cloudflare** (cloud, multi-device sync), **Hybrid** (5ms local reads with background cloud sync — recommended for production) or **Milvus** (dedicated vector DB: Lite file, self-hosted, or Zilliz Cloud). For self-hosted team setups, the Hybrid backend can sync to another **HTTP MCP Memory Service** instead of Cloudflare using `MCP_HYBRID_SECONDARY_BACKEND=http`. For long-lived services, prefer Docker Milvus or Zilliz Cloud over Milvus Lite — [why](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/docs/milvus-backend.md#which-uri-to-use).
--- ## ⚡ Works With Your Favorite AI Tools - **Agent frameworks (REST):** LangGraph · CrewAI · AutoGen · OpenClaw/Nanobot · any HTTP client - **CLI and terminal (MCP):** Claude Code · Gemini CLI · OpenCode · Codex CLI · Goose · Aider · Amp - **Desktop and IDE (MCP):** Claude Desktop · VS Code · Cursor · Windsurf · Raycast · JetBrains · Zed - **Chat (MCP):** ChatGPT (Developer Mode) · claude.ai (Remote MCP over HTTPS) Full list, plus clients without OAuth such as Home Assistant: **[docs/integrations.md](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/docs/integrations.md)** --- ## ✨ Features ### Store and retrieve context - 🧠 **Persistent memory** — Keep decisions, notes, and project context across sessions and agents. - 🔍 **Semantic and keyword search** — Combine vector search with BM25; use `mode="ranked"` to weigh recency, access frequency, and quality. An optional fallback cascade tries exact and tag matching when semantic results are sparse. - 🏷️ **Scoped retrieval** — Filter by tags with AND/OR matching, natural-language time ranges, and store partitions (`default`, `docs`, or `all` for cross-store search). - 📝 **Optional search summaries** — Request `summarize=true` for query-aware summaries with validated source references. Requires `MCP_SEARCH_SUMMARIZE_ENABLED=true` and a configured LLM provider; unavailable summaries fall back to raw results. [Search API and examples](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/docs/mastery/api-reference.md) - 📄 **Document ingestion** — Import PDF, text, and Markdown with chunking for retrieval. Additional formats such as DOCX and PPTX require optional parsing tools. [Document ingestion guide](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/docs/document-ingestion.md) ### Capture and maintain knowledge - ⚡ **Automatic session capture** — Configurable Claude Code hooks retrieve context and save session learnings; the local `memory_harvest` tool extracts decisions, bugs, conventions, and lessons from transcripts. [Hooks setup](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/claude-hooks/README.md) · [Harvest configuration](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/docs/mastery/configuration-guide.md) - 💡 **Autonomous consolidation** — Schedule clustering, compression, association discovery, and controlled forgetting. Insight cards surface patterns, trends, and knowledge gaps. [Consolidation guide](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/docs/guides/memory-consolidation-guide.md) - 💭 **Beliefs and contradiction handling** — Derive confidence-scored beliefs from observations. Heuristic contradiction detection can mark older memories as superseded, hiding them from default retrieval while retaining them for explicit lookup. - 🤖 **Agent bootstrap profiles** — `get_bootstrap_profile` assembles behavioral context for a new agent within a token budget, with optional task-aware retrieval. Requires `MCP_BOOTSTRAP_ENABLED=true`; profiles are not isolated by project. - 🧬 **Knowledge graph and entities** — Explore typed causal relationships in the interactive graph. 🔗 Entity extraction links @mentions, #tags, URLs, and file paths to a queryable entity graph. [Knowledge graph guide](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/docs/features/knowledge-graph-dashboard.md) - 🏠 **Quality scoring** — Use your own OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including Ollama, LiteLLM, or vLLM. [Configuration guide](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/docs/mastery/configuration-guide.md) ### Run locally and share across devices - 🔒 **Local-first storage** — Local ONNX embeddings and SQLite storage keep core memory operations on your infrastructure. Optional LLM features use the providers you configure. - ☁️ **Cloud or self-hosted sync** — Use Cloudflare or another MCP Memory Service instance as a Hybrid secondary. Separately enabled delta-sync exchanges changes between hosts; it is off by default. [Self-hosted sync guide](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/docs/guides/self-hosted-sync-hub.md) - 📦 **Import, export, and migration** — Move memories through JSON import/export, including conversion of mem0 exports. [Import/export tools](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/scripts/sync/README.md) · [mem0 migration guide](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/docs/guides/mem0-import.md) - 💾 **Database backups** — Configure scheduled backups or trigger one manually through the HTTP API. Inspect backup status and available snapshots through the backup endpoints in the live API reference at `/api/docs`. - 📊 **Web dashboard** — Search, browse, visualize, and manage memories at `http://localhost:8000`. The dashboard has eight tabs — Dashboard, Search, Browse, Documents, Manage, Analytics, Quality, API Docs. [Two-minute walkthrough on YouTube](https://youtu.be/W34r8VFoSdQ) · [Web Dashboard Guide](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/wiki/Web-Dashboard-Guide) How it compares to Mem0, Zep and the MCP-native alternatives, benchmark results, and deployments people run in production: **[mcpmemory.services](https://mcpmemory.services)** --- ## 🛠️ Configuration Highlights ```bash memory launch # Start HTTP server in background (127.0.0.1:8000) memory launch --port 8192 # Custom port memory info # Status and health memory logs --lines 50 # Recent logs memory stop # Stop server ``` These commands are optimized for fast startup and avoid loading heavy ML dependencies unless needed. > ⚠️ **Security note:** the server binds to `127.0.0.1` (localhost only) by default. > `--host 0.0.0.0` / `MCP_HTTP_HOST=0.0.0.0` exposes the API to your network — do that > only in trusted environments with authentication and firewall rules, or behind TLS > termination or a VPN overlay. Backends, embedding models, quality scoring and every environment variable: **[Configuration Guide](https://github.com/doobidoo/mcp-memory-service/blob/main/docs/mastery/configuration-guide.md)** --- ## 📚 Documentation - repositories.description: Checks whether the "fixed" in your AI coding agent's commits is true. It takes each fix back out and runs your tests. Free, with no key.

readme.excerpt: [![GitHub Marketplace](https://img.shields.io/badge/Marketplace-Bite%20free%20check-blue?logo=github)](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/bite-free-check) **Would your tests catch it if the bug came back?** Bite checks whether an AI coding agent's "fixed" is actually true. **Try it now.** It's free, needs no key, and never changes your files. If you have Python, paste these two lines into any terminal window (PowerShell, cmd, Terminal): ``` python -m pip install bite-check python -m bite_check --free ``` Outside a project, Bite first shows a demo on a tiny made-up one. To check your own project, type the second line and a space, drag your project's folder into the window (that types its path), and press Enter. Have [pipx](https://pipx.pypa.io) or [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)? One line does it, no install: `pipx run bite-check --free` or `uvx bite-check --free`. (On Linux or a Mac, if pip says "externally managed", use one of those.) If your commits never say "fix", add `--any` to check every recent change. To keep Bite installed as a `bite` command, see [Try it in a minute](#try-it-in-a-minute). **Here for Hack Week or your first open-source PR?** These [good first issues](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/labels/good%20first%20issue) are small, and each one says where to look and when it's done. Comment on one to claim it. ## Why you need this When an AI fixes a bug for you, it often says "Fixed, and I added a test." If you don't read code, you can't tell if that's true. A test is a tiny robot that checks one thing, like "2 + 2 should be 4", and shouts when it isn't. A good test shouts if the bug ever comes back. A weak one stays quiet no matter what. Bite checks your robots. It puts the old bug back on purpose and watches whether any test shouts. It's like testing a smoke alarm with real smoke instead of trusting the little green light. If a test shouts, that fix is guarded. If they all stay quiet, the next change, by you or your AI, could bring the bug back and nobody would notice. Bite names that fix, so you can tell your AI: "add a test that fails without this fix." ## How it works It takes each recent fix back out of your code and runs your tests. If they still pass, nothing guards that fix, and Bite tells you which one. That free check needs no key and works with pytest, npm test, cargo test, go test, dotnet test, Maven and Gradle (Java and Kotlin): ``` pipx install bite-check bite --free ``` With your own API key it goes one step further: it writes one small test of the commit's exact claim and runs it. That is how it found a memory leak in [prosemirror-py](#the-catch-that-shows-what-its-for) that a commit said it had fixed. > "Reverting the claimed fix and making the change prove itself under a real test is exactly the kind of check that > should exist for every "fixed" commit." > > — [Ivan Zdravkov](https://zdravkov.info), [on DEV](https://dev.to/izdravkov/comment/3jdej) ## Try it in a minute Install once with [pipx](https://pipx.pypa.io), which gives Bite its own space so there's no venv to set up or activate: ``` python -m pip install --user pipx python -m pipx ensurepath ``` Close the terminal window and open a new one, then: ``` pipx install bite-check bite --demo ``` `bite --demo` builds a tiny made-up shop project in a temporary folder and runs the free check on it. repositories.readme_full_content: [![GitHub Marketplace](https://img.shields.io/badge/Marketplace-Bite%20free%20check-blue?logo=github)](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/bite-free-check) **Would your tests catch it if the bug came back?** Bite checks whether an AI coding agent's "fixed" is actually true. **Try it now.** It's free, needs no key, and never changes your files. If you have Python, paste these two lines into any terminal window (PowerShell, cmd, Terminal): ``` python -m pip install bite-check python -m bite_check --free ``` Outside a project, Bite first shows a demo on a tiny made-up one. To check your own project, type the second line and a space, drag your project's folder into the window (that types its path), and press Enter. Have [pipx](https://pipx.pypa.io) or [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)? One line does it, no install: `pipx run bite-check --free` or `uvx bite-check --free`. (On Linux or a Mac, if pip says "externally managed", use one of those.) If your commits never say "fix", add `--any` to check every recent change. To keep Bite installed as a `bite` command, see [Try it in a minute](#try-it-in-a-minute). **Here for Hack Week or your first open-source PR?** These [good first issues](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/labels/good%20first%20issue) are small, and each one says where to look and when it's done. Comment on one to claim it. ## Why you need this When an AI fixes a bug for you, it often says "Fixed, and I added a test." If you don't read code, you can't tell if that's true. A test is a tiny robot that checks one thing, like "2 + 2 should be 4", and shouts when it isn't. A good test shouts if the bug ever comes back. A weak one stays quiet no matter what. Bite checks your robots. It puts the old bug back on purpose and watches whether any test shouts. It's like testing a smoke alarm with real smoke instead of trusting the little green light. If a test shouts, that fix is guarded. If they all stay quiet, the next change, by you or your AI, could bring the bug back and nobody would notice. Bite names that fix, so you can tell your AI: "add a test that fails without this fix." ## How it works It takes each recent fix back out of your code and runs your tests. If they still pass, nothing guards that fix, and Bite tells you which one. That free check needs no key and works with pytest, npm test, cargo test, go test, dotnet test, Maven and Gradle (Java and Kotlin): ``` pipx install bite-check bite --free ``` With your own API key it goes one step further: it writes one small test of the commit's exact claim and runs it. That is how it found a memory leak in [prosemirror-py](#the-catch-that-shows-what-its-for) that a commit said it had fixed. > "Reverting the claimed fix and making the change prove itself under a real test is exactly the kind of check that > should exist for every "fixed" commit." > > — [Ivan Zdravkov](https://zdravkov.info), [on DEV](https://dev.to/izdravkov/comment/3jdej) ## Try it in a minute Install once with [pipx](https://pipx.pypa.io), which gives Bite its own space so there's no venv to set up or activate: ``` python -m pip install --user pipx python -m pipx ensurepath ``` Close the terminal window and open a new one, then: ``` pipx install bite-check bite --demo ``` `bite --demo` builds a tiny made-up shop project in a temporary folder and runs the free check on it. Two of its commits say they fixed something: one added a test for its fix, the other didn't. Bite takes each fix back out and runs the tests, and you see the difference: ``` 9661edcf ✅ noticed by test_discount_never_below_zero Fix discounts over 100% making the price negative e5c329ec ⚠️ NO TEST NOTICED Fix totals showing long decimals like 0.30000000000000004 ``` It needs nothing besides git, takes a few seconds, and doesn't touch your files. Then try it on your own project: ``` bite --free /path/to/your-repo ``` (Or type `bite --free ` and drag the project's folder into the window. From inside the project's folder, plain `bite --free` works too.) `bite` now works in any terminal window. `bite --free` needs no key and costs nothing. It takes each recent change back out, runs your tests, and lists the changes no test guards, plus any new test that still passes without its commit's code (it tests nothing). If something it needs is missing, like git or pytest, it says so and gives you the line that installs it. Each run ends with a one-page report, `bite_proof/report.html`, to open in your browser. To update Bite later, see [Updating Bite](#updating-bite). To test the claims themselves (the paid step), add one extra package and set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, then run `bite`: ``` pipx inject bite-check claude-agent-sdk ``` This step uses your own API key, and `--budget` caps what a run spends ($1 by default). It runs on Anthropic's Agent SDK, so it needs an API key and never uses a Claude login or plan (Anthropic's Agent SDK rule: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview). The commits Bite checks can come from any coding AI or person. Works with pytest, npm test, cargo test, go test, dotnet test, Maven and Gradle. Settings and limits: [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/blob/main/AGENTS.md), written so your coding AI (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot) can set Bite up for you. To work on Bite itself: clone it, `pip install -e .[test]`, then `python -m pytest`. ## When a check is slow Bite runs your tests several times for each change, so a slow test suite makes a slow check. Four ways to speed it up: - `bite --free --jobs 4` checks 4 changes at a time. If two checks get in each other's way (a shared file, a port), Bite runs the failed one again on its own before it counts, so a clash never shows up as a result. - Bite remembers the changes it checked with ✅ in `bite_proof/checked.json`, and skips them next time when the tests, settings and dependency files (requirements.txt, package-lock.json, go.sum, ...) are the same. Add, change or delete a test, or update a library, and those changes are checked again. `--again` checks everything anyway. The Action keeps that memory between runs for you. - `bite --free --shard 2/5` runs part 2 of 5. Run parts 1/5 to 5/5 on 5 machines at once and together they check every change, in about a fifth of the time. On GitHub Actions that's a matrix: ```yaml strategy: matrix: part: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] steps: # ... check out and install, as usual - run: bite --free --shard ${{ matrix.part }}/5 ``` - pytest: install pytest-xdist and put `test_command = python -m pytest -n auto` in `.bite.ini` to run the tests themselves 4 at a time. Or point `free_test_command` at a faster part of your tests. When each change takes over 3 minutes, Bite prints these tips at the end of the run. ## Updating Bite `bite --version` prints your version, and when a newer one is out it says so and gives you the line to paste. That line always gets the newest version: ``` pipx install --force bite-check --pip-args="--no-cache-dir" ``` Installed with pip instead of pipx? `python -m pip install --upgrade --no-cache-dir bite-check` Why not just `pipx upgrade bite-check`? Right after a release, pip can keep using the list of versions it saved earlier and say you're already on the latest. `--no-cache-dir` makes it ask PyPI fresh, and `--force` also replaces an older `bite` or `bite.exe` that's in the way. What changed in each version: [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). Which languages, test runners and places Bite works in: [SUPPORTS.md](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/blob/main/SUPPORTS.md). ## Check Claude's "fixed" live, in Claude Code Bite can also check the moment Claude says it fixed something, before you read "fixed!". Each time Claude finishes a turn that changed code, Bite takes the change back out of a copy of your project and runs your tests. If none of them notice, Claude is sent back once to add a test that fails without its change. If it stops again and still no test notices, you get a warning instead, so it never goes round in circles. It's the free check: no API key. In Claude Code, type: ``` /plugin marketplace add connabyss/bite /plugin install bite@bite ``` and install Bite itself if you haven't: ``` pipx install bite-check ``` `/bite` checks the changes since your last commit whenever you like. In a trial, Claude fixed a discount and then wrote `assert total([50, 50], 10) == 90`. That passes with or without the fix (100 - 10 and 100 × 90% are both 90), and Bite said so: ``` Bite ⚠️ the tests that came with this change (test_cart.py) don't notice it: with the change to cart.py taken out, they still pass. The "fixed" isn't proven yet. ``` Without the plugin, run `bite live` yourself after a change, or `bite live --hook` from any tool that runs a command when the AI stops (it reads Claude Code's Stop hook JSON). ## Check the "fixed" live, in any coding AI `bite mcp` gives your coding AI the same free check as a tool it can call, `check_fix`, through MCP, the plug most coding AIs share. Its description tells the AI to call it after fixing a bug and before saying "fixed". If no test notices the change, the AI is told to add one that fails without it. No API key; it works in a copy, so your files are never touched. It needs Bite 0.8.0 or newer ([Updating Bite](#updating-bite)). Add it once, in the place your coding AI keeps its MCP servers: | Coding AI | Where | What to add | |---|---|---| | Claude Code | a terminal | `claude mcp add bite -- bite mcp` | | Cursor | `.cursor/mcp.json` in the project (or `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for all) | `{"mcpServers": {"bite": {"command": "bite", "args": ["mcp"]}}}` | | Copilot in VS Code | `.vscode/mcp.json` in the project | `{"servers": {"bite": {"type": "stdio", "command": "bite", "args": ["mcp"]}}}` | | Windsurf | `~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json` | `{"mcpServers": {"bite": {"command": "bite", "args": ["mcp"]}}}` | | Codex CLI | a terminal | `codex mcp add bite -- bite mcp` | | Gemini CLI | `.gemini/settings.json` in the project (or `~/.gemini/settings.json`) | `{"mcpServers": {"bite": {"command": "bite", "args": ["mcp"]}}}` | Any other AI that takes MCP servers: the command is `bite`, the argument is `mcp`. If yours says it can't start `bite` (apps opened from the Dock or Start menu don't always see the folder pipx put it in), use the full path instead: `~/.local/bin/bite` on Mac and Linux, `C:\Users\\.local\bin\bite.exe` on Windows (`pipx list` shows it). The tool checks the folder Bite was started in; the AI can pass `folder` for another one, and `since` (for example `main`) to check a whole branch, not just what changed since the last commit. An AI that can run commands but takes no MCP servers can run `bite live` itself: it prints the same answer and exits with 1 when no test noticed the change. Put a line like "After you fix a bug, run `bite live` before you say it's fixed" in its rules file (AGENTS.md, .cursorrules, .github/copilot-instructions.md). ## Ask in plain words ``` bite ask "is last week's login fix guarded?" ``` Bite finds the commit(s) that match your words (their message and the files they changed, and the time if you name one: today, yesterday, this week, last week, the last 10 days) and runs its free check on each. The answer opens in a few words, then gives a short block per commit: ``` Yes, it's guarded. ✅ YES, A TEST NOTICED Fix login letting an empty password in 3f2a9c1, Oct 27 With it taken out, test_empty_password_is_refused fails. ``` When no test notices a fix, its block says ⚠️ NO TEST NOTICED. Where emoji can't show (output sent to a file or another program, or an old Windows console) the labels are the same words without them. Matching is free. Only when your words match nothing clearly, and you have an API key, a small AI call picks the commit instead (about a cent); `--free` never uses the key. `--last 200` looks further back. Coding AIs get the same thing through `bite mcp`, as the tool `ask_bite`. ## Run it on every pull request Easiest: [install the bite-check app](https://github.com/apps/bite-check) on the repos you want. Within an hour it opens one issue there with an "Add Bite" link that fills in the file below for you; you read it and click **Commit changes**. The app can only open issues: it can't read or change your code or workflows. Or add this file to your repo yourself as `.github/workflows/bite.yml`. On each pull request it runs the free check on that pull request's commits and shows a pass or fail check next to your other CI. It fails when a commit's change can be taken back out and your tests still pass. No key, no cost. It's also listed on the GitHub Marketplace as [Bite free check](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/bite-free-check). ```yaml name: bite on: pull_request permissions: contents: read pull-requests: write jobs: bite: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 with: ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} fetch-depth: 0 # install what your tests need here, e.g. for Python: - uses: actions/setup-python@v7 - run: python -m pip install pytest -r requirements.txt - uses: connabyss/bite@v1.0.3 ``` Options go under `with:`: `args` (extra `bite` options, e.g. `--serious`), `max-commits` (default 20), `fail-on-gap` (set to `false` to report without failing) and `comment` (set to `false` for no comment). It posts one comment on the pull request that says, per commit, whether a test noticed the change being taken out, and updates that same comment on later pushes. The rerun steps for each flagged commit are on the job's summary page. ### Have Bite write the missing test (opt-in, your own key) When no test noticed a change, Bite can write that test for you. Add your Anthropic API key as a repository secret named `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, then: ```yaml - uses: connabyss/bite@v1.0.3 with: write-tests: true anthropic-api-key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }} args: --budget 0.50 ``` For each change no test noticed (3 at most, `--suspects` changes that), a fresh AI worker writes one small test on a copy of the project. Bite then runs it itself: it must pass twice with the change in, and fail with the change taken out. Only then does it show up in the comment, folded, ready to paste in. Otherwise Bite throws it away and says so. `--budget` caps what a run spends ($1 by default). Pull requests from forks don't get secrets, so on those Bite runs the free check only. On your own computer: `bite --write-tests`. Every test Bite keeps is also a download: **bite-missing-tests** under Artifacts on the run's page, each file already in the folder it belongs in. **One click instead of a paste (opt-in):** add `open-pr: true` and Bite opens a small pull request into your pull request's branch with the test in it. Click **Merge** there and the test is in. It runs on your workflow's own token, not on any app, so your workflow needs: ```yaml permissions: contents: write # Bite puts the test on a branch of its own, bite/missing-tests- pull-requests: write ``` and, in your repository, Settings, Actions, General: tick **Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests**. Without that tick, Bite still puts the test on its branch and the comment links to open the pull request yourself. GitHub doesn't run your checks on a pull request a workflow opened, so they run once you merge it into your branch; Bite has already run the test both ways. Not on pull requests from forks. ## The comeback alarm: a fix that quietly came undone A fix with no test can be undone by a later commit, and nobody hears about it: a "simplify", a bad merge, an old copy pasted back. Every free check also looks at whether each fix is still in today's code. If a later commit put the old code back, Bite says so and names that commit: ``` e5c329ec 🔁 UNDONE BY A LATER COMMIT Fix totals showing long decimals like 0.30000000000000004 🔁 UNDONE BY A LATER COMMIT: e5c329ec "Fix totals showing long decimals like 0.30000000000000004": Commit e8b75da4 (“Simplify total()”) put the old code back, so this fix is gone from today's code. ``` `bite --demo comeback` shows it on a tiny made-up shop. It's free and runs no tests: Bite only checks whether the fix's own change would apply again to today's code (and can't be taken back out of it). It works for fixes a test noticed too, since a fix and its test can be deleted together. A later commit whose title says it's a revert was done on purpose, so that one gets a quiet note instead of the alarm. A fix rewritten into new code doesn't count as undone, and neither does one a later commit did another way (it took the fix's lines out but wrote its own code for the same thing in the same function). A revert or a tidy-up that came undone gets no alarm either. When a branch is merged after the undo, Bite names the commit that put the old code back, not the merge. ## Results for other tools `bite --json` prints the results as JSON, for scripts, dashboards and other bots; everything else Bite says goes to stderr. Every run also saves them in `bite_proof/results.json`. These names stay the same from release to release (a change to them would bump `schema`): - `outcome`: `noticed` (a test noticed every change), `gaps` (no test noticed at least one), `undone_later` (a later commit put the old code back for at least one fix), `tests_fail`, `no_tests`, `nothing_checked` or `error` (`message` says why). - `commits`: one per commit checked, with `sha`, `subject`, `result` (`noticed`, `no_test_noticed`, `its_tests_didnt_notice`, `undone_later`, `tests_fail`, `no_tests` or `skipped`), `label` and `detail` (the words Bite shows), and `why`, `missing_test` or `undone_by` (`sha` and `subject` of the commit that undid it) when there is one. - `false_done`: each claim the paid step proved false, with `sha`, `subject`, `bug` and `today`. - `score`: the Bite score (below), with `noticed`, `out_of` and `badge` (a README badge line). Left out when no change could be checked. A commit that bundles a tested change with an untested one gets `no_test_noticed` with the label PART NOT NOTICED, and its `detail` names the part. [TRICKS.md](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/blob/main/TRICKS.md) has that and the other tricks we tried on Bite. ## Bite-proof badge When every change Bite checked had a test that noticed it, Bite ends with "Bite-proof. Nice work." and prints a badge line you can paste into your README: [![Bite-proof ✅](https://img.shields.io/badge/Bite--proof-%E2%9C%85-black)](https://github.com/connabyss/bite) ## Bite score Every run ends with a score: of the changes Bite could check, how many a test noticed ("Bite score: 7/9"). Changes it skipped, or couldn't check because the tests already fail, don't count either way. The report page shows it as a ring, and the pull request comment adds it in one small line. Bite also prints a badge line with the score, for your README: [![Bite score: 7 of 9 changes noticed by a test](https://img.shields.io/badge/Bite%20score-7%2F9%20noticed-yellowgreen)](https://github.com/connabyss/bite) Next to the report page, `bite_proof/card.svg` is the score as a picture (1200x630, the size link previews use), with the Bite cat, to drop into a post or a chat. Bite remembers each run's score in `bite_proof/scores.json` and says how it moved: "up from 5/9 last run", "down from 8/9 last run", or "Bite-proof 3 runs in a row". A rerun at the same commit doesn't count twice, and pull request checks (`--since`) aren't remembered, since they look at different commits. Each run also saves `bite_proof/badge.json` in [shields.io's endpoint format](https://shields.io/badges/endpoint-badge), so a badge can follow your newest run wherever you publish that file. **A badge that keeps itself up to date (the Action, opt-in):** on every push to main, Bite checks your newest commits and keeps the score on a branch of its own, `bite-badge`, which holds only `badge.json`. Add this as `.github/workflows/bite-badge.yml`: ```yaml name: bite-badge on: push: branches: [main] permissions: contents: write # only for the bite-badge branch jobs: badge: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 with: fetch-depth: 0 # install what your tests need here, as in the pull request check - uses: connabyss/bite@v1.0.3 with: badge-branch: bite-badge max-commits: 10 ``` The job's summary page then shows the badge line for your README (put your own owner/repo in it): ``` [![Bite score](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2FOWNER%2FREPO%2Fbite-badge%2Fbadge.json)](https://github.com/connabyss/bite) ``` Bite makes the branch on the first run, and never touches a branch that holds anything else. On a push run the check never fails; it only updates the badge. Prefer a gentler wording for the warnings? `bite --roast` gives the same results, phrased differently. In a hurry? `bite --quick` checks each change with two test runs, as older versions did: it skips the piece-by-piece check, the flaky-test rerun and the deleted-test check ([TRICKS.md](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/blob/main/TRICKS.md) says what those catch). ## Famous repos Bite has checked | Project | Language | Changes checked | Noticed by a test | Real gaps | |---|---|---|---|---| | [Rich](https://github.com/Textualize/rich) | Python | 37 | 15 | 1 small: [`` keys in Markdown](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/commit/a9c4aaba) | | [Click](https://github.com/pallets/click) | Python | 37 | 30 | 1 small: [`help` on custom setting types](https://github.com/pallets/click/commit/405a5481) | | [qs](https://github.com/ljharb/qs) | JavaScript | 40 | 40 | none ✅ | | [chi](https://github.com/go-chi/chi) | Go | 27 | 21 | 2 small: [a test that only works in a terminal](https://github.com/go-chi/chi/commit/878fe71f), [XML compression](https://github.com/go-chi/chi/commit/d7b767bc) | | [serde_json](https://github.com/serde-rs/json) | Rust | 16 | 12 | none ✅ | | [FluentValidation](https://github.com/FluentValidation/FluentValidation) | C# | 9 | 5 | none ✅ | Checked Oct 30-31, 2026 with `bite --free`. Every bug fix Bite could check had a test (one of chi's only works in a terminal). We read each unnoticed change by hand. Apart from the gaps above, they were things a test can't catch, like type hints, speed-ups, Windows-only code or rewrites that work the same. **[The full scoreboard](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/blob/main/SCOREBOARD.md)** has 20 projects in 5 languages, with a link to every gap. ## The catch that shows what it's for In [fellowapp/prosemirror-py](https://github.com/fellowapp/prosemirror-py), commit `3614c96` (co-authored by Claude) says: > fix: add weakref callback to clean up resolve cache entries > > The cache used dict keyed by id(doc) with no cleanup, causing a slow memory leak in long-running processes. Added a weakref finalizer callback that removes the cache entry when the doc is garbage collected. Bite wrote this test of that claim and ran it: ```python def test_cache_entry_removed_after_doc_gc(): resolvedpos._resolve_cache.clear() d = doc(p("hello")) ResolvedPos.resolve_cached(d, 2) assert len(resolvedpos._resolve_cache) == 1 del d gc.collect() assert len(resolvedpos._resolve_cache) == 0 # fails: 1 == 0 ``` It fails on that commit and on today's code. The cache keeps each document alive through its cached positions, so the cleanup never runs. After 20,000 documents are resolved and dropped, the cache still holds all 20,000, using 35 MB. The commit looked right, read right, and passed its own tests. Reported with a repro in [#335](https://github.com/fellowapp/prosemirror-py/issues/335); a tested fix is open as [#336](https://github.com/fellowapp/prosemirror-py/pull/336). ## Fixed or merged upstream Each bug was reproduced with a standalone script in a clean environment before it was reported. | Project | What happened | |---|---| | pyclibrary | 7 bugs reported in [#92](https://github.com/MatthieuDartiailh/pyclibrary/issues/92). All 7 fixes reviewed and merged: [#93](https://github.com/MatthieuDartiailh/pyclibrary/pull/93), [#94](https://github.com/MatthieuDartiailh/pyclibrary/pull/94), [#95](https://github.com/MatthieuDartiailh/pyclibrary/pull/95), [#96](https://github.com/MatthieuDartiailh/pyclibrary/pull/96), [#97](https://github.com/MatthieuDartiailh/pyclibrary/pull/97), [#98](https://github.com/MatthieuDartiailh/pyclibrary/pull/98), [#99](https://github.com/MatthieuDartiailh/pyclibrary/pull/99). The maintainer [wrote](https://github.com/MatthieuDartiailh/pyclibrary/issues/92): "Thanks for the small and focused PR very nice to review." | | django-tailwind-cli | With one stylesheet, `tailwind watch` hid rebuild messages and build errors. Fix [#232](https://github.com/django-commons/django-tailwind-cli/pull/232) merged and released in [4.8.2](https://github.com/django-commons/django-tailwind-cli/releases/tag/v4.8.2). The maintainer [wrote](https://github.com/django-commons/django-tailwind-cli/pull/232): "Just about to release 4.8.2 with the fix included. Thanks for the contribution." | | srptools | 4 bugs reported in [#13](https://github.com/idlesign/srptools/issues/13). The maintainer fixed all 4 and closed it the same day. | | resolve-robotics-uri-py | URI lookup depended on the hash seed ([#26](https://github.com/gbionics/resolve-robotics-uri-py/issues/26)). Fixed by the maintainers in [#27](https://github.com/gbionics/resolve-robotics-uri-py/pull/27). The maintainer [wrote](https://github.com/gbionics/resolve-robotics-uri-py/issues/26): "Thanks a lot for the detailed issue report!" | | text-to-cad | A Claude commit added a Python 3.11 syntax check that can't catch the exact bug it was written for (nested same-quote f-strings). Bite sent a test that does catch it, [#708](https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad/pull/708), was merged and released in [0.8.2](https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad/releases/tag/v0.8.2); the maintainer then closed the remaining gaps in [#712](https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad/pull/712). | | west | Loading a manifest from data with a reserved project name crashed. Fix [#1013](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/west/pull/1013) approved by two maintainers and merged. | | midea-lan | A message encoder got the frame length wrong when no padding was needed. Fix [#251](https://github.com/wuwentao/midea-lan/pull/251) merged. The maintainer [wrote](https://github.com/wuwentao/midea-lan/pull/251): "Thank you @connabyss for submitting this PR and for finding and fixing the 8370 framing bug." | | mizani | Number labels picked too few decimals when values were close together (`[0, 10, 10.5]` showed as `10, 10`). Fix [#90](https://github.com/has2k1/mizani/pull/90) merged. The maintainer [wrote](https://github.com/has2k1/mizani/pull/90): "@connabyss, thank you." | | pamqp | Bite's free check found three past fixes that no test would notice breaking, including one where `Basic.Reject(requeue=False)` was flipped back to `True`. Tests for all three ([#86](https://github.com/gmr/pamqp/pull/86)) merged. | ## Sent, waiting for review | Project | Link | What happened | |---|---|---| | prosemirror-py | [#335](https://github.com/fellowapp/prosemirror-py/issues/335), [#336](https://github.com/fellowapp/prosemirror-py/pull/336), [#337](https://github.com/fellowapp/prosemirror-py/pull/337) | The leak above. A second Claude commit (`1e3339e`) let `Mapping` change a list the caller still owned; fix in #337. | | python-vcr-tests | [#18](https://github.com/keboola/python-vcr-tests/issues/18), [#19](https://github.com/keboola/python-vcr-tests/pull/19) | A Claude commit said its database recorder captures every query; only the last per cursor is saved. | | ChatSBOM | [#217](https://github.com/WangYihang/ChatSBOM/issues/217) | A Claude commit's stale-result guard is reset on every walk page, so a repo can be collected twice. | | llm | [#1828](https://github.com/simonw/llm/pull/1828) | A Claude commit fixed per-turn tool ids in `llm logs`, but its test never made a tool call, so it passed even with the bug. | | treg | [#1237](https://github.com/superdesigndev/treg/pull/1237) | A Claude commit's test for an org header passes even with the fix removed, so it guards nothing. | | claude-seo | [#392](https://github.com/AgriciDaniel/claude-seo/pull/392) | A Claude commit's `--release` check let a value with a trailing newline through. | | marshmallow-fastoneofschema | [#1](https://github.com/Kalepa/marshmallow-fastoneofschema/issues/1), [#2](https://github.com/Kalepa/marshmallow-fastoneofschema/pull/2), [#3](https://github.com/Kalepa/marshmallow-fastoneofschema/pull/3), [#4](https://github.com/Kalepa/marshmallow-fastoneofschema/pull/4) | 3 bugs, one fix each. | | django-modeltranslation | [#831](https://github.com/deschler/django-modeltranslation/pull/831) | Nested `auto_populate()` and `fallbacks()` blocks reset the setting to nothing on exit instead of restoring it. | | mypy_boto3_builder | [#395](https://github.com/youtype/mypy_boto3_builder/issues/395) | Reported, no reply yet. | | drf-pydantic | [#51](https://github.com/georgebv/drf-pydantic/issues/51) | Reported, no reply yet. | ## Limits, plainly - **Most claims hold.** Across all rounds so far, Bite tested 137 "fixed" claims that it could run tests for (all from commits made with Claude Code, the AI those rounds looked at). 8 were false (about 1 in 17), and 4 of those were still broken on today's code. On well-reviewed projects it usually finds nothing, and that's the right answer. - **Quiet is not a pass.** Bite only shows a failing test that the second check calls fair and real. That second check has thrown out more than 10 failing tests that weren't. A claim that holds proves that one claim, not that the commit has no other bugs. - **It needs the project's tests to run.** If they don't run on a clean copy, Bite can't check that commit. - **Bug hunting is weaker than claim checking.** In a 10-project overnight hunt, two blind AI judges rated 21 of 22 proven fixes as real bugs and none as wrong, but Bite found only 1 of the 10 bugs the maintainers fixed soon after. - **Small samples, AI judges.** The judges read code without running it. The human checks are the maintainers' fixes and merges listed above. ## Contributing Bug reports, fixes and AI-assisted PRs are all welcome. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). If Bite flagged something wrongly, or missed a claim you know was false, please [open an issue](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/issues/new/choose). Thank you to Bite's first contributors: - [@snehaapratap](https://github.com/snehaapratap) made the setup error messages point to steps that exist ([#18](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/pull/18)). - [@gauravjangra3165](https://github.com/gauravjangra3165) added macOS to the tests ([#19](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/pull/19)). - [@bfs2021](https://github.com/bfs2021) made the "check it yourself" steps work for commits that add a new file ([#37](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/pull/37), fixing [#27](https://github.com/connabyss/bite/issues/27)). # Protean

**Protean** is an opinionated Python framework for building event-driven applications with Domain-Driven Design — aggregates, CQRS, and event sourcing are first-class, and your domain logic stays independent of the database, broker, and API you run it on.

[![Python](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/protean?label=Python)](https://github.com/proteanhq/protean/)
[![Release](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/protean?label=Release&style=flat-square)](https://pypi.org/project/protean/)
[![Build Status](https://github.com/proteanhq/protean/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/proteanhq/protean/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![Coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/proteanhq/protean/graph/badge.svg?token=0sFuFdLBOx)](https://codecov.io/gh/proteanhq/protean)
[![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-20%2C000%2B-brightgreen)](https://docs.proteanhq.com/community/quality/)
[![Maintainability](https://img.shields.io/badge/maintainability-A-brightgreen)](https://docs.proteanhq.com/community/quality/)

**🗺️ Roadmap:** [where Protean is headed next](https://github.com/proteanhq/protean/discussions/1356), and the [current milestone](https://github.com/proteanhq/protean/milestones) for the issue-by-issue detail.

## Installation

Protean is available on PyPI:

```console
$ pip install protean
```

Protean officially supports Python 3.11+.

## Quick Start

A command flows to its handler, the aggregate raises an event, an event
handler reacts, and a projector keeps a read-optimized feed in sync, all
wired by the domain, independent of infrastructure:

```python
from protean import Domain, current_domain, handle
from protean.core.projector import on
from protean.fields import Identifier, String, Text

domain = Domain()


@domain.aggregate
class Post:
    title: String(max_length=100, required=True)
    body: Text(required=True)
    status: String(max_length=20, default="DRAFT")

    def publish(self):
        self.status = "PUBLISHED"
        self.raise_(PostPublished(post_id=self.id, title=self.title))


@domain.event(part_of=Post)
class PostPublished:
    post_id: Identifier(required=True)
    title: String(required=True)


@domain.command(part_of=Post)
class PublishPost:
    title: String(max_length=100, required=True)
    body: Text(required=True)


@domain.command_handler(part_of=Post)
class PostCommandHandler:
    @handle(PublishPost)
    def publish_post(self, command: PublishPost):
        post = Post(title=command.title, body=command.body)
        post.publish()
        current_domain.repository_for(Post).add(post)
        return post.id


@domain.event_handler(part_of=Post)
class PostEventHandler:
    @handle(PostPublished)
    def announce(self, event: PostPublished):
        print(f"Event handled: post published ({event.title})")


@domain.projection
class PublishedPostsFeed:
    """A read-optimized feed of published posts."""

    post_id: Identifier(identifier=True, required=True)
    title: String(max_length=100, required=True)


@domain.projector(projector_for=PublishedPostsFeed, aggregates=[Post])
class PublishedPostsFeedProjector:
    """Maintains the PublishedPostsFeed projection from Post events."""

    @on(PostPublished)
    def on_post_published(self, event: PostPublished):
        feed_entry = PublishedPostsFeed(post_id=event.post_id, title=event.title)
        current_domain.repository_for(PublishedPostsFeed).add(feed_entry)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    domain.config["command_processing"] = "sync"
    domain.config["event_processing"] = "sync"

    domain.init(traverse=False)

    with domain.domain_context():
        # Write: publish a post through the command.
        post_id = domain.process(
            PublishPost(title="Hello, Protean!", body="My first published post.")
        )
        post = domain.repository_for(Post).get(post_id)
        print(f"Post created: {post.title} (status: {post.status})")

class PublishPost:
    title: String(max_length=100, required=True)
    body: Text(required=True)


@domain.command_handler(part_of=Post)
class PostCommandHandler:
    @handle(PublishPost)
    def publish_post(self, command: PublishPost):
        post = Post(title=command.title, body=command.body)
        post.publish()
        current_domain.repository_for(Post).add(post)
        return post.id


@domain.event_handler(part_of=Post)
class PostEventHandler:
    @handle(PostPublished)
    def announce(self, event: PostPublished):
        print(f"Event handled: post published ({event.title})")


@domain.projection
class PublishedPostsFeed:
    """A read-optimized feed of published posts."""

    post_id: Identifier(identifier=True, required=True)
    title: String(max_length=100, required=True)


@domain.projector(projector_for=PublishedPostsFeed, aggregates=[Post])
class PublishedPostsFeedProjector:
    """Maintains the PublishedPostsFeed projection from Post events."""

    @on(PostPublished)
    def on_post_published(self, event: PostPublished):
        feed_entry = PublishedPostsFeed(post_id=event.post_id, title=event.title)
        current_domain.repository_for(PublishedPostsFeed).add(feed_entry)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    domain.config["command_processing"] = "sync"
    domain.config["event_processing"] = "sync"

    domain.init(traverse=False)

    with domain.domain_context():
        # Write: publish a post through the command.
        post_id = domain.process(
            PublishPost(title="Hello, Protean!", body="My first published post.")
        )
        post = domain.repository_for(Post).get(post_id)
        print(f"Post created: {post.title} (status: {post.status})")

        # Read: the projector has already filled the feed inline.
        feed = domain.view_for(PublishedPostsFeed).query.all()
        print(f"Published posts feed: {feed.total} row(s)")
        for entry in feed.items:
            print(f"  - {entry.title}")
```

## Reference application

For a fuller picture, [`examples/reference_app/`](examples/reference_app/) runs
the same blog domain behind a FastAPI app. See
[`app/README.md`](examples/reference_app/app/README.md) for setup and the
routes it exposes.

For a larger, multi-context example, see
[proteanhq/shopstream](https://github.com/proteanhq/shopstream), a shopping
platform built with Protean.

## Documentation

Online docs are available at [https://docs.proteanhq.com](https://docs.proteanhq.com).

### Versioning

Protean does not use strict semantic versioning. The promise is:
**Code that runs warning-free on 1.N runs unmodified on 1.N+1.** Every removal
is announced by a deprecation warning naming the release it lands in, at least
one release ahead, so you can turn "will this upgrade break us?" into a test run.
See the [versioning policy](https://docs.proteanhq.com/reference/versioning-policy/)
for the full contract.

## Quality

Every commit runs the in-memory core suite across 5 Python versions and all 5 backing services on the newest stable Python; the full adapter matrix across every version runs nightly.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Tests | 20,000+ ([quality report](https://docs.proteanhq.com/community/quality/)) |
| Linting | Zero violations (Ruff) |
| Complexity | Avg 3.38 cyclomatic (A grade) |
| Maintainability | A rank (95% of files) |
| CI Matrix | Python 3.11-3.14 + 3.15 prerelease; PostgreSQL, Redis, Elasticsearch, MessageDB, MSSQL on the newest stable per PR, full matrix nightly |

See the full [Quality Report](https://docs.proteanhq.com/community/quality/) for details.

## Contributing

> **Note**: Protean framework is not associated or related to [Protean eGov Technologies](https://www.proteantech.in/) or [Code for Gov Tech](https://codeforgovtech.in/) initiatives.

Protean is developed and maintained by a single maintainer. The contributions
that help most are **bug reports**, **real-world use cases**, and **adapter
packages** built against the public conformance suite.

- Have a question, or a real-world use case to share? [Start a discussion](https://github.com/proteanhq/protean/discussions). Questions are answered there, and the thread stays searchable for the next person who hits the same thing.
- Found a bug? [Open an issue](https://github.com/proteanhq/protean/issues). Clear, reproducible reports are the most valuable contribution you can make, and they are answered as a priority.
- Planning a non-trivial code change? Open an issue to discuss it first, before investing in a pull request. Unsolicited large PRs may not be merged. Small, obvious fixes are welcome directly.
- Building an adapter? Adapters live in their own packages, certified against the conformance suite. See the [contributing guide](https://docs.proteanhq.com/community/contributing/setup/).

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and the
[community](https://docs.proteanhq.com/community/) section for the full picture.

readme.excerpt: # FLIMAnalyzer [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.12%2B-blue)](https://github.com/uvaKCCI/flimanalyzer/blob/main/pyproject.toml) [![Tests](https://github.com/uvaKCCI/flimanalyzer/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/uvaKCCI/flimanalyzer/actions/workflows/tests.yml) [![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/uvaKCCI/flimanalyzer/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/uvaKCCI/flimanalyzer) [![Documentation Status](https://readthedocs.org/projects/flimanalyzer/badge/?version=latest)](https://flimanalyzer.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) [![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.23426563.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23426563) Python package for analysis of Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Microscopy (FLIM) data. Documentation: https://flimanalyzer.readthedocs.io ## Requirements * Python 3.12 or later * All Python dependencies, including [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org) and [Prefect](https://www.prefect.io), are declared in `pyproject.toml` and installed automatically. ## Installation ### From PyPI with uv (recommended) [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) creates a virtual environment in `.venv` (installing a matching Python if needed). Then install FLIMAnalyzer with its graphical user interface (GUI) into it: uv venv --python 3.12 source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate uv pip install "flimanalyzer[gui]" The `gui` extra installs the GUI. Without it, `uv pip install flimanalyzer` installs only what [batch mode](#run-flimanalyzer-in-batch-mode) needs, for example on a computing cluster. Add `dask` for the optional Dask support (see [Concurrent and distributed execution](#concurrent-and-distributed-execution)), e.g. `"flimanalyzer[gui,dask]"`. ### From PyPI with pip python3.12 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate pip install "flimanalyzer[gui]" ### PyTorch and the GPU Installed from PyPI, FLIMAnalyzer gets PyTorch from PyPI, which provides a different build on each platform: * **Linux:** the PyPI build includes CUDA, so an NVIDIA GPU is used if its driver is recent enough. * **Windows:** the PyPI build is CPU-only. For an NVIDIA GPU, install with `uv pip install "flimanalyzer[gui]" --torch-backend=cu128`, or with pip install the CUDA build first: `pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128`. See [pytorch.org](https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/) for other CUDA versions. * **macOS:** only Apple Silicon is supported, because current PyTorch versions are not available for Intel Macs. The PyPI build uses the Apple GPU (MPS). ### Latest development version To install the current state of the repository, clone it and let uv create the environment. `uv sync` installs FLIMAnalyzer with the GUI in editable mode, with the exact package versions from `uv.lock` (the versions the tests run with). On Windows and Linux (x86_64), it installs the CUDA 12.8 build of PyTorch: git clone https://github.com/uvaKCCI/flimanalyzer.git cd flimanalyzer uv sync Without the GUI, with the test dependencies, or with Dask support: uv sync --no-group gui uv sync --extra test uv sync --extra dask With pip, in a virtual environment in the cloned folder: `pip install -e ".[gui]"`. ### With Docker The Docker images run only [batch mode](#run-flimanalyzer-in-batch-mode). They don't include the GUI. Each release is published to the GitHub Container Registry: | Image | | |---|---| | `ghcr.io/uvakcci/flimanalyzer:`, `:latest` | with the CUDA build of PyTorch (x86_64, several GB) | | `ghcr.io/uvakcci/flimanalyzer:-cpu`, `:latest-cpu` | CPU only (x86_64 and ARM), much smaller | docker pull ghcr.io/uvakcci/flimanalyzer:latest-cpu To build an image from the repository instead: with the CUDA 12.8 build of PyTorch, with the build for another CUDA version (here 12.6)

Documentation: https://flimanalyzer.readthedocs.io ## Requirements * Python 3.12 or later * All Python dependencies, including [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org) and [Prefect](https://www.prefect.io), are declared in `pyproject.toml` and installed automatically. ## Installation ### From PyPI with uv (recommended) [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) creates a virtual environment in `.venv` (installing a matching Python if needed). Then install FLIMAnalyzer with its graphical user interface (GUI) into it: uv venv --python 3.12 source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate uv pip install "flimanalyzer[gui]" The `gui` extra installs the GUI. Without it, `uv pip install flimanalyzer` installs only what [batch mode](#run-flimanalyzer-in-batch-mode) needs, for example on a computing cluster. Add `dask` for the optional Dask support (see [Concurrent and distributed execution](#concurrent-and-distributed-execution)), e.g. `"flimanalyzer[gui,dask]"`. ### From PyPI with pip python3.12 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate pip install "flimanalyzer[gui]" ### PyTorch and the GPU Installed from PyPI, FLIMAnalyzer gets PyTorch from PyPI, which provides a different build on each platform: * **Linux:** the PyPI build includes CUDA, so an NVIDIA GPU is used if its driver is recent enough. * **Windows:** the PyPI build is CPU-only. For an NVIDIA GPU, install with `uv pip install "flimanalyzer[gui]" --torch-backend=cu128`, or with pip install the CUDA build first: `pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128`. See [pytorch.org](https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/) for other CUDA versions. * **macOS:** only Apple Silicon is supported, because current PyTorch versions are not available for Intel Macs. The PyPI build uses the Apple GPU (MPS). ### Latest development version To install the current state of the repository, clone it and let uv create the environment. `uv sync` installs FLIMAnalyzer with the GUI in editable mode, with the exact package versions from `uv.lock` (the versions the tests run with). On Windows and Linux (x86_64), it installs the CUDA 12.8 build of PyTorch: git clone https://github.com/uvaKCCI/flimanalyzer.git cd flimanalyzer uv sync Without the GUI, with the test dependencies, or with Dask support: uv sync --no-group gui uv sync --extra test uv sync --extra dask With pip, in a virtual environment in the cloned folder: `pip install -e ".[gui]"`. ### With Docker The Docker images run only [batch mode](#run-flimanalyzer-in-batch-mode). They don't include the GUI. Each release is published to the GitHub Container Registry: | Image | | |---|---| | `ghcr.io/uvakcci/flimanalyzer:`, `:latest` | with the CUDA build of PyTorch (x86_64, several GB) | | `ghcr.io/uvakcci/flimanalyzer:-cpu`, `:latest-cpu` | CPU only (x86_64 and ARM), much smaller | docker pull ghcr.io/uvakcci/flimanalyzer:latest-cpu To build an image from the repository instead: with the CUDA 12.8 build of PyTorch, with the build for another CUDA version (here 12.6), with the CPU-only build, or with Dask support: docker build -t flimanalyzer . docker build -t flimanalyzer:cu126 --build-arg TORCH_INDEX=https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu126 . docker build -t flimanalyzer:cpu --build-arg TORCH_INDEX=https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu . docker build -t flimanalyzer:dask --build-arg EXTRAS=dask . `TORCH_INDEX` replaces PyTorch with the build from that PyTorch package index, in the same PyTorch version (the one in `uv.lock`, currently 2.11.0). Choose the CUDA version that the NVIDIA driver of your computer supports. PyTorch 2.11.0 is available for CUDA 12.6 (`cu126`), 12.8 (`cu128`, the default), 12.9 (`cu129`) and 13.0 (`cu130`). `EXTRAS=gui` stops the build with an error, because the images do not support a display. ## Start FLIMAnalyzer with the GUI With uv, no activation is needed: uv run flimanalyzer In an activated environment: flimanalyzer To open data files (tab- or comma-separated) right away, each in its own window: uv run flimanalyzer -i results.txt more-results.csv Run `flimanalyzer --help` for all command line options. ## Using a GPU The autoencoder tools (Autoencoder: Train, Run and Augment Data, and the FLIM Data Augmentation Tuning and FLIM Feature Analysis workflows) have a **Device** setting, in the GUI and in batch mode: * `auto` (default): an NVIDIA GPU (`cuda`) if available, otherwise the Apple GPU (`mps`), otherwise the CPU. * `cpu`, `cuda` or `mps`: uses that device, or the CPU if it is not available. Which GPU can be used depends on the PyTorch build that was installed (see [Installation](#installation)). Trained models are saved so that they don't need a GPU, so a model trained on a GPU can also be used on a computer without one. ## Run FLIMAnalyzer in batch mode `flimbatch` imports data files and runs tools or workflows on them without opening the GUI, for example on a computing cluster. It takes its settings from a settings file saved in the GUI (File > Export Settings...): the import settings and the settings of each tool. A tool's dialog can add its settings to such a file with Save Settings..., which keeps the file's other sections. Load Settings... reads the tool's own section back. uv run flimbatch -i data/ -o results/ -c settings.json \ --run Summarize --run "Basic FLIRR Analysis" The imported table is saved as `results/Imported.txt`, and each tool's results in `results//`. A workflow column that is not in the data (for example `FAD a1%` for `FAD a1[%]`) is an error. `--allow-guesses` uses the closest column instead and lists it in the run summary. The exit code is 1 if a check or task failed. Run `flimbatch --help` for all options. `flimanalyzer --batch …` does the same as `flimbatch …`. On Windows, use `flimbatch`: `flimanalyzer` starts without a console there, so its messages are not shown. ### In Docker The image runs `flimbatch`. Make the folder with the data and the settings file available inside the container as `/work`: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" ghcr.io/uvakcci/flimanalyzer:latest-cpu \ -i data/ -o results/ -c settings.json --run Summarize --no-prefect-server * On Linux, add `-u $(id -u)` so that the result files belong to you. * With the CUDA image, add `--gpus all` to use the GPU. * With `--no-prefect-server`, each run uses a temporary Prefect server. To report to a Prefect server instead, pass its address, for example `-e PREFECT_API_URL=http://prefect.example.org:4200/api`. ## Prefect server FLIMAnalyzer runs analyses and workflows as [Prefect](https://www.prefect.io) flows. At startup it looks for a Prefect server in this order: 1. The server configured in the active Prefect profile or in the `PREFECT_API_URL` environment variable, e.g. prefect profile use # or export PREFECT_API_URL=https://my-prefect-server/api 2. A server already running locally at `http://127.0.0.1:4200/api`. 3. If none is found, FLIMAnalyzer starts a local server (`prefect server start`) and stops it again when FLIMAnalyzer closes. The server's output is written to `prefect-server.log`. Flow and task runs can be inspected in the Prefect UI of the server in use, e.g. [http://127.0.0.1:4200](http://127.0.0.1:4200) for a local server. To keep a local server running across sessions, start it yourself in a separate terminal with `uv run prefect server start`. Use `--no-prefect-server` to skip starting a server; Prefect then uses a temporary server that only runs as long as FLIMAnalyzer. ## Concurrent and distributed execution Every tool and workflow step runs as a Prefect task. A task starts as soon as the results it needs are ready. Tasks that don't depend on each other run concurrently, without waiting for each other. Tasks that draw figures take turns, because matplotlib's pyplot is not thread-safe. By default, up to one task per CPU core runs at a time, as threads. To change that number: uv run flimanalyzer --execargs="num_workers=4" `num_workers=1` runs one task at a time. Prefect's `PREFECT_TASKS_RUNNER_THREAD_POOL_MAX_WORKERS` setting, if set, is used as the default. FLIMAnalyzer can also use [Dask](https://www.dask.org). Dask support is optional; install it with `uv sync --extra dask` (or `pip install -e ".[dask]"`). On a *single node*, start a local Dask cluster: uv run flimanalyzer -e LocalDaskExecutor --execargs="scheduler=processes,num_workers=8" As a general guideline, adjust `num_workers` to match the number of CPU cores in your system. Use `scheduler=threads` to run the workers as threads instead of processes. To use an existing Dask cluster: uv run flimanalyzer -e DaskExecutor --execargs="address=tcp://:8786" ### Concurrency limits Prefect applies [tag concurrency limits](https://docs.prefect.io/v3/develop/task-run-limits) set on the Prefect server, whichever executor is used. Every task is tagged with its tool's name as shown in the menu (e.g. `Autoencoder: Train`, not the Python class name), also as a step of a workflow; workflow steps can carry more tags, which also name their results folders. For example, to let only one autoencoder training run at a time, also inside workflows: uv run prefect concurrency-limit create "Autoencoder: Train" 1 `uv run prefect concurrency-limit ls` lists the limits, and `uv run prefect concurrency-limit delete ` removes one. ## How to cite If you use FLIMAnalyzer, please cite: 1. **The original publication**, in all cases: Zhang J, Wallrabe H, Siller K, Mbogo B, Cassidy T, Alam SR, Periasamy A. Measuring metabolic changes in cancer cells using two-photon fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy and machine-learning analysis. *Journal of Biophotonics* 18(1), e202400426 (2025). [doi:10.1002/jbio.202400426](https://doi.org/10.1002/jbio.202400426) 2. **The publication closest to the version you used**, plus that release's software DOI, from the table below. Use the newest release that is not newer than your version. The version is shown in the FLIMAnalyzer window title. | Your version | Publication | Software DOI | |---|---|---| | v0.5.0 or later | Alam SR, Siller K, Dreicer R, Periasamy A. Label-free optical biomarker for prostate cancer diagnosis. *Molecular Medicine* 32(1), 165 (2026). [doi:10.1186/s10020-026-01605-2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s10020-026-01605-2) | [10.5281/zenodo.23438157](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23438157) | | v0.4.1 or earlier | Zhang et al. (2025), the original publication above | [10.5281/zenodo.23426564](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23426564) | The concept DOI [10.5281/zenodo.23426563](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23426563) covers all versions archived on Zenodo and resolves to the latest of them. Not every release is archived on Zenodo; the table above lists the versions used in publications. Citation metadata is also in [`CITATION.cff`](CITATION.cff); GitHub shows it under "Cite this repository". ## Development Run the test suite: uv sync --extra test uv run pytest Tests that run flows use a temporary Prefect server and database and do not report to any configured server. The tests run one after another. The GUI tests depend on wxPython's event loop and on timing, so they must not run in parallel. Only the core tests (no GUI) can run in parallel, one process per CPU core, with `pytest-xdist`: uv run pytest -n auto tests/core Build the documentation (output in `docs/_build/html`): uv run --group docs sphinx-build -b html docs docs/_build/html The `docs` dependency group contains only Sphinx and the lightweight packages needed to document the code; `docs/conf.py` imports `flim` from the source tree and mocks wxPython, PyTorch and Prefect. This is also how the documentation is built on Read the Docs (see `.readthedocs.yaml`).

repositories.description: A recommender simulator that scores off-policy evaluation methods against known true answers

readme.excerpt:
# recarena

**How well can you judge a new recommender using only old logs?**

Teams often want to know how a new recommender would perform before showing it to anyone. Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates that from logs of the old system. On real data, the true answer is unknown, so it is hard to tell which estimator to trust.

recarena is a simulator where the true answer is known. It runs each policy directly to get its true value, then scores every estimator against that value.

> Early prototype. The API will change, and the results below come from one simulated setup.

## What's in it

- **Simulated users** with hidden interests that drift, fatigue that builds up, and a chance of leaving after missed recommendations.
- **Slates:** users look down a list and stop at their first click, and they are less likely to look at lower slots.
- **A Gymnasium environment**, `SlateRecEnv`, for training RL agents.
- **Six estimators:** IPS, SNIPS, PDIS, SNPDIS, a direct method (fitted Q evaluation) and doubly robust.
- **Budgets:** each step reports sponsored exposure as a cost, so you can test whether an estimator can tell if a policy stays within a budget.

## Quickstart

```bash
git clone https://github.com/anveshachuri/recarena.git
cd recarena
python -m venv .venv
.venv/Scripts/python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"   # On Linux or macOS: .venv/bin/python
.venv/Scripts/python -m pytest
.venv/Scripts/python -m recarena.benchmark --sizes 200 1000 --seeds 5 --truth 200000
```

Score the estimators yourself:

```python
import numpy as np
from recarena import Catalog, SimConfig, SoftmaxPolicy, collect, estimate_all, true_value

config = SimConfig()
catalog = Catalog.generate(config)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

old = SoftmaxPolicy(catalog, "old")
new = SoftmaxPolicy(catalog, "new", history_weight=1.5, quality_weight=1.2)

logs = collect(config, catalog, old, 1000, rng)
estimates = estimate_all(logs, logs.rewards, new, config.examine_decay, rng)
truth = true_value(config, catalog, new, 200_000, rng)

print("true value:", round(truth.reward, 3))
print({name: round(value, 3) for name, value in estimates.items()})
```

Or train an agent:

```python
from recarena import SlateRecEnv

env = SlateRecEnv()
obs, info = env.reset(seed=0)
obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(env.action_space.sample())
print(reward, info["cost"])
```

## What the stress test found

**No estimator won everywhere.** The results depended on how far the new policy was from the logged one, and on what the model knew.

Results for the two new policies far from the logged one, with 5,000 logged sessions, across 5 catalogs and 10 logged datasets per catalog:

| Scenario | SNPDIS | Direct | DR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Informed model | 18.5% | **2.5%** | 86.1% |
| Uninformed model | 21.6% | **14.4%** | 52.2% |
| Hidden item appeal | 18.3% | **3.5%** | 44.5% |
| Sponsored items drive users away | 17.2% | **2.8%** | 24.0% |
| All of the above | **15.2%** | 22.0% | 35.8% |

*Reward error (RMSE as a share of the true value, lower is better). IPS, SNIPS and PDIS were never the best here, and are in the full results.*

Each estimate was also tested against budgets 10% above and below the policy's true cost:

| Scenario | SNPDIS | Direct | DR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Informed model | 64% | **100%** | 83% |
| Uninformed model | 63% | 55% | **70%** |
| Hidden item appeal | 64% | **100%** | 79% |
| Sponsored items drive users away | 70% | **100%** | 84% |
| All of the above | 62% | 65% | **80%** |

*Share of budget decisions that were correct (higher is better). A method that always gives the same answer scores 50%.*

What this suggests so far:

- **Close to the logged policy, the choice barely matters.** All six estimators were accurate, and all got 100% of budget decisions right.
- **The direct method is only as good as its features.** It stayed accurate with hidden effects when it knew about quality and sponsorship, and it became the wrong choice for budgets when it d

.venv/Scripts/python -m recarena.benchmark --sizes 200 1000 --seeds 5 --truth 200000
```

Score the estimators yourself:

```python
import numpy as np
from recarena import Catalog, SimConfig, SoftmaxPolicy, collect, estimate_all, true_value

config = SimConfig()
catalog = Catalog.generate(config)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

old = SoftmaxPolicy(catalog, "old")
new = SoftmaxPolicy(catalog, "new", history_weight=1.5, quality_weight=1.2)

logs = collect(config, catalog, old, 1000, rng)
estimates = estimate_all(logs, logs.rewards, new, config.examine_decay, rng)
truth = true_value(config, catalog, new, 200_000, rng)

print("true value:", round(truth.reward, 3))
print({name: round(value, 3) for name, value in estimates.items()})
```

Or train an agent:

```python
from recarena import SlateRecEnv

env = SlateRecEnv()
obs, info = env.reset(seed=0)
obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(env.action_space.sample())
print(reward, info["cost"])
```

## What the stress test found

**No estimator won everywhere.** The results depended on how far the new policy was from the logged one, and on what the model knew.

Results for the two new policies far from the logged one, with 5,000 logged sessions, across 5 catalogs and 10 logged datasets per catalog:

| Scenario | SNPDIS | Direct | DR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Informed model | 18.5% | **2.5%** | 86.1% |
| Uninformed model | 21.6% | **14.4%** | 52.2% |
| Hidden item appeal | 18.3% | **3.5%** | 44.5% |
| Sponsored items drive users away | 17.2% | **2.8%** | 24.0% |
| All of the above | **15.2%** | 22.0% | 35.8% |

*Reward error (RMSE as a share of the true value, lower is better). IPS, SNIPS and PDIS were never the best here, and are in the full results.*

Each estimate was also tested against budgets 10% above and below the policy's true cost:

| Scenario | SNPDIS | Direct | DR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Informed model | 64% | **100%** | 83% |
| Uninformed model | 63% | 55% | **70%** |
| Hidden item appeal | 64% | **100%** | 79% |
| Sponsored items drive users away | 70% | **100%** | 84% |
| All of the above | 62% | 65% | **80%** |

*Share of budget decisions that were correct (higher is better). A method that always gives the same answer scores 50%.*

What this suggests so far:

- **Close to the logged policy, the choice barely matters.** All six estimators were accurate, and all got 100% of budget decisions right.
- **The direct method is only as good as its features.** It stayed accurate with hidden effects when it knew about quality and sponsorship, and it became the wrong choice for budgets when it didn't.
- **Reward accuracy doesn't guarantee budget accuracy.** With the uninformed model, the direct method's median error on the sponsored policy's reward was only 2.2%, but it got just 55% of budget decisions right across the far policies, because it can't see which items are sponsored.
- **Doubly robust is usually fine and occasionally terrible.** Its typical error was far below its RMSE, which a few extreme runs dominate. For example, its median error on one policy was 13.6%, while its RMSE was 118.4%.

**Limits of these results:** this is one simulator with settings chosen by its author, and the hidden effects used here may be too mild. The hidden appeal, for example, isn't related to anything the policies favor. The large errors are also noisy with this few runs. These results need more scenarios and independent checking.

Full tables are in [`results/stress_test.md`](results/stress_test.md), and an earlier single-catalog run is in [`results/first_benchmark.md`](results/first_benchmark.md). Reproduce the stress test with:

```bash
python -m recarena.stress --sizes 1000 5000 --catalogs 5 --repeats 10 --truth 500000
```

If it runs slowly, set `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1` and `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` first, because it already runs one job per CPU core.

## How it's tested

The tests compare the simulator with values worked out by hand from every possible slate, check the estimators against hand-calculated answers, and confirm that doubly robust stays unbiased even with a deliberately wrong model.

## Where this is going

The goal is a shared, trustworthy place to answer: **which offline evaluation method can I trust, for which kind of recommender problem, and how would I know?**

| Stage | What it adds |
|---|---|
| Now | One simulator, six estimators, and a stress test |
| Next | Plug-in estimators and user models, so anyone can add one and benchmark it |
| Then | Harder worlds, trained RL agents, warnings for when not to trust an estimate |
| Later | Simulators calibrated to public datasets, and a public leaderboard of methods with reproducible results |
| Open question | Choosing policies under budgets and fairness limits when you can only estimate their effects |

This is a direction, not a promise. If you have a better idea, [open an issue](https://github.com/anveshachuri/recarena/issues). Contributions are welcome, and [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) explains how to start.

## License

Apache-2.0
