repositories.readme_full_content: # Dex **Analytics engineering for your coding agent, with guardrails and lifecycle built into the engine.** Dex lets your agent build your analytics: data warehouse exploration, dbt data transformation and semantic modeling, and schema-drift maintenance. **Built by [Exmergo](https://www.exmergo.com)** [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/exmergo-dex-core?logo=pypi&logoColor=white&color=165dfc)](https://pypi.org/project/exmergo-dex-core/) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache--2.0-165dfc)](LICENSE) [![data-eng-bench](https://img.shields.io/badge/data--eng--bench-57%25-33cf56)](benchmarks/data-eng-bench/README.md) [![ADE-bench](https://img.shields.io/badge/ADE--bench-76%25-33cf56)](benchmarks/ade_bench/README.md) [![CI](https://github.com/exmergo/dex/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/exmergo/dex/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-docs.exmergo.com%2Fdex-165dfc?logo=readthedocs&logoColor=white)](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex) [![LinkedIn](https://img.shields.io/badge/LinkedIn-Exmergo-165dfc?logo=linkedin&logoColor=white)](https://www.linkedin.com/company/exmergo/) [![X](https://img.shields.io/badge/Follow-%40exmergo-165dfc?logo=x&logoColor=white)](https://x.com/exmergo) [![Star the repo!](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/exmergo/dex?style=flat&label=Star%20the%20repo!%20%E2%AD%90&labelColor=555&logo=github&logoColor=white&color=165dfc)](https://github.com/exmergo/dex) ## Install **Any agent** (run in your terminal): ```bash npx skills add exmergo/dex ``` **Claude Code** (run these inside Claude Code, one at a time): ``` /plugin marketplace add exmergo/exmergo-agent-plugins ``` ``` /plugin install dex@exmergo ``` **Codex**: ```bash npx skills add exmergo/dex --agent codex ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > **Dex needs [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) on your `PATH`.** No agent installs > it for you. Run `brew install uv` or `pipx install uv`, or see the > [uv installation docs](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) > for other platforms. `uv` supplies Python and the engine. Use uv 0.13.4 or > later (`uv self update`): earlier releases still trust the emSign CA roots > withdrawn after their keys were compromised. In Claude Code the skills appear as `/dex:explore`, `/dex:transform`, and `/dex:maintain` and trigger on matching intent. Update later with `/plugin marketplace update exmergo`. Codex also gets a native plugin, with no MCP server needed. Any other agent can be pointed at [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md). Run Dex from your project directory, so it finds your `.dex/config.yml` and keeps its cache next to your project. Dex needs an agent with a local shell, so it does not run in claude.ai chat. > [!TIP] > **Skip the first-run wait.** The first command installs the engine, which takes > tens of seconds on a cold `uv` cache. Ask your agent to warm Dex once after > installing, or run the command below in a CI or container build step. Add > `--connector snowflake` (or any connector) to warm one before a project exists. ```bash uv run --no-project --script skills//scripts/run.py --warm ``` What you get: - **Explore** a warehouse you have never seen. Ranked inventory, column profiles built from aggregates, PII flags, verified joins, and an ER diagram. - **Transform** your dbt project and semantic layer. Models, tests, docs, and metrics arrive as reviewable plans and build only on a dev target. - **Maintain** it as the world changes. Schema, volume, grain, and metric-definition drift, each with a proposed fix. Your source data is never written to, and builds run on a dev target only. Cost quoted before any spend. Every change is a diff you review. Works in Claude Code, Codex, or any agent that loads Agent Skills. ## Why > *Most deadly errors arise from obsolete assumptions.* > > Frank Herbert, *Children of Dune* A general coding agent is a good SQL author and a poor analytics engineer. It: - re-learns the schema every session, - has no strategy for a warehouse with thousands of tables, - is blind to what a query costs, - will happily pull personal data into its context, - does not treat a dbt project or a semantic layer as an object to keep coherent over time. Dex owns exactly that loop, and enforces its rules in the engine rather than in a prompt. ## Try it in three commands No warehouse, no credentials, no cloud account, no network. ```bash pip install "exmergo-dex-core[duckdb]" dex demo dex explore map ``` `dex demo` writes a small e-commerce DuckDB warehouse (`dex_demo.duckdb`, 7 tables, 29,512 rows) and a `.dex/config.yml` into the current directory, so every command after it runs with no flags. It refuses rather than overwrite anything. The data comes from a pinned seed, so what you see is what is written here. `explore map` maps all 7 tables, infers 5 joins, flags 6 columns as personal data, and reports 6 data-quality findings. Every command answers with one JSON envelope. An excerpt, for one table: ```json { "identifier": "dex_demo.main.order_items", "row_count": 14000, "grain": null, "data_quality": [ "order_item_id is not unique: 13000 distinct over 14000 rows (1000 rows would have to be removed for it to be unique, so it is unique for 92.9% of rows); joins on it will fan out" ] } ``` ### It is broken on purpose A first run that reports a clean bill of health teaches you nothing, so the demo ships with real defects. Dig into them: ```bash dex explore profile order_items products dex explore relationships --verify dex explore query "select email from customers" ``` - **A broken grain.** A batch was loaded twice, so `order_item_id` is unique for only 92.9% of rows. Dex reports the duplicates and leaves the grain unknown rather than guessing a key. - **A key that mixes id schemes.** `sku` is `90% numeric, 10% 32-character hexadecimal (md5-shaped)`. Cast it to a number and you silently drop 10% of products. - **A join that looks right and is not.** `web_events.customer_id` shares a name with the CRM's key, but verification finds 100% of its values have no match. - **A refusal.** The query firewall will not put `customers.email` into context. `select count(distinct email) from customers` runs, because a statistic is not a value. There is also a table an interrupted load left empty, two columns whose declared type contradicts their content, and two designed PII false positives. See the [`dex demo` reference](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/cli/demo). > [!NOTE] > DuckDB is free and local, so nothing here asks you to confirm a spend. On a > metered warehouse the same commands return an estimate first and run only once > you agree to it. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR Agent[Coding agent] --> Skills[Dex skills] Skills --> Engine[exmergo-dex-core engine] Engine -->|SELECT-only SQL, cost-capped| Warehouse[(Your warehouse)] Engine -->|dbt builds, dev target only| Warehouse Engine -->|one sanitized JSON envelope| Agent Engine -->|plans as diffs| Repo[Your repository: dbt project + semantic layer] Engine <--> Cache[.dex/ cache and snapshot] ``` The skills are thin. All the logic, and every guardrail, lives in one engine (`exmergo-dex-core`) behind a [small command contract](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/reference/command-contract). Your repository is the source of truth on two independent axes: the transformation project (dbt) and the semantic layer. The `.dex/` directory is only a cache. ### Explore Rank what matters, profile selectively, infer and verify joins, answer ad-hoc questions through a PII-aware query firewall, read and query the semantic layer, and draw the map as a Mermaid ER diagram. Fully read-only. [Skill](skills/explore/SKILL.md) · [methodology](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/concepts/methodology) · [commands](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/cli/explore) ### Transform Author and refactor dbt models from staging to marts, with tests and docs, plus the semantic layer on top. Every change is a stored plan you review, then apply. Builds run against a dev target only. [Skill](skills/transform/SKILL.md) · [what Dex writes](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/concepts/dbt-project) · [commands](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/cli/transform) ### Maintain Diff the warehouse, the project, and the semantic layer against the last snapshot, rank the drift by blast radius, and propose the reconciling edits. `maintain verify` checks a project as it stands, with no baseline needed. [Skill](skills/maintain/SKILL.md) · [commands](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/cli/maintain) ### What to commit in `.dex/` Dex keeps its working state in `.dex/`. Most of it is safe to commit; the exception is any file that can carry data values. Commit the lockfile and the config, and keep the exploration cache out of a repo that must not publish data values: | File | Commit? | Can it contain data values? | | --- | --- | --- | | `.dex/config.yml` | Yes | No: connector targets, `pii_overrides` (column names, not values), budgets and limits. Credentials live in environment variables or dbt profiles, never in this file. | | `.dex/snapshot.json` | Yes, like a lockfile | Yes: when snapshotted from a cache it pins the cache's datasets wholesale, including each non-PII column's capped value domain and min/max. A metadata-only baseline (no cache) carries schema and volume only. PII-flagged columns never carry value domains. | | `.dex/cache.json` | Only if values may be public | Yes: column profiles with capped value domains (actual values with counts). Never for PII-flagged columns. | | `.dex/plans/*.json` | Optional, as an audit trail | No warehouse values: the proposed contents of project files. | | `.dex/queries.jsonl` | Optional, as a ledger | SQL text, which may hold literals. | | `.dex/drift.json` | No: regenerate with `maintain check` | Aggregates only: counts, names and schema metadata in drift findings. | For a repo that must not publish data values, ignore the rest: ```gitignore # Dex state that can publish data values, or is local-only output. .dex/cache.json .dex/dex.db .dex/dex.db-journal .dex/queries.jsonl .dex/drift.json .dex/spend.jsonl .dex/spend.lock ``` `.dex/dex.db` is the SQLite backend's equivalent of `cache.json`, so it gets the same caution. `.dex/spend.jsonl` is the billed-command ledger: byte counts, job ids and statement hashes only, never SQL values or credentials, but it is local spend history, so there is no reason to commit it. ### What Dex will never do - **Write to your source data.** Dex's own SQL is SELECT-only. The only writes to your warehouse are the dbt builds you confirm, on a dev target. - **Put personal data in your agent's context.** PII is flagged by column, category, and confidence, and never surfaced. Only a human clears a flag. ([PII policy](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/guardrails/pii-policy)) - **Spend before quoting.** A metered scan returns an estimate and runs only with your confirmation and a budget. ([cost controls](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/guardrails/cost-controls)) - **Change your project behind your back.** Every edit is a diff, and a human edit made since planning is never overwritten. ([source of truth](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/concepts/source-of-truth)) - **Build anywhere but dev.** Prod-looking targets are refused outright. ## Connectors | Connector | Type | Self-hostable | Extra / `--connector` | Cost surfaced as | Credentials from | | --- | --- | :---: | --- | --- | --- | | [**Snowflake**](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/connectors/snowflake) | Cloud warehouse | ❌ | `snowflake` | Warehouse-seconds, with credits | `connections.toml`, `SNOWFLAKE_*` env, or a dbt profile | | [**BigQuery**](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/connectors/bigquery) | Cloud warehouse | ❌ | `bigquery` | Bytes scanned | Application Default Credentials | | [**Databricks**](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/connectors/databricks) | Cloud warehouse | ❌ | `databricks` | Warehouse-seconds, with DBUs | `databricks auth login`, `DATABRICKS_*` env, or a dbt profile | | [**Amazon Redshift**](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/connectors/redshift) | Cloud warehouse, Serverless-first | ❌ | `redshift` | Compute-seconds, with RPU-hours | The AWS credential chain or `REDSHIFT_*` env | | [**ClickHouse**](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/connectors/clickhouse) | Analytical database | ✅ | `clickhouse` | Compute-seconds on Cloud, database-seconds self-hosted | `CLICKHOUSE_URL`, `CLICKHOUSE_*` env, or a dbt profile | | [**Trino**](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/connectors/trino) | Federated query engine (Trino, Starburst Enterprise, Trino on EMR) | ✅ | `trino` | Cluster-seconds | `TRINO_URL`, `TRINO_*` env, or a dbt profile | | [**DuckDB**](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/connectors/duckdb) | Embedded analytical | ✅ | `duckdb` | Free and local | None, just a file path | | [**Postgres**](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/connectors/postgres) | Operational database | ✅ | `postgres` | Database-seconds | `pg_service.conf`, `DATABASE_URL`, `PG*` env, or a dbt profile | Credentials are discovered, never asked for, and never enter the agent's context. Every scan is estimated, confirmed, and capped server-side, and settled spend is recorded in a local ledger ([cost controls](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/guardrails/cost-controls)). Self-hosted databases bill no dollars and are still gated, because an unbounded scan on a production Postgres primary is a real cost too. **Coming next:** MotherDuck, Starburst Galaxy, Microsoft Fabric. ## Semantic layers The semantic layer is its own axis, chosen once per repository in `.dex/config.yml`. With Ossie or SLayer, it needs no dbt project at all. ([overview](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/semantic-layers/overview)) | Semantic layer | Hosted | Queryable | `vendor` / `deployment` | Read through | | --- | :---: | :---: | --- | --- | | **dbt** | ✅ | ✅ | `dbt` / `local` or `dbt_cloud` | MetricFlow locally, run through the Dex connector and its cost guard, or the hosted dbt Cloud Semantic Layer API | | **[Apache Ossie](https://github.com/apache/ossie)** (incubating) | ❌ | ❌ | `ossie` / `local` | Native documents in the repository, no dbt or MetricFlow in the path | | **[SLayer](https://github.com/MotleyAI/slayer)** | ❌ | ✅ | `slayer` / `local` | SLayer model files, validated by one pinned release; SLayer renders, Dex runs it under the cost guard | Ossie is catalog-first because the format specifies interchange metadata and no query runtime, so Dex reads, authors, and checks an Ossie layer but refuses a metric query by name rather than inventing semantics. See the [Ossie page](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/semantic-layers/ossie) and the [Ossie tutorial](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/guides/ossie-semantic-layer). **Coming next:** Cube, Snowflake Semantic Views, Looker / LookML, and Databricks Metric Views. ## See it on a real project **[github-repo-analytics](https://github.com/exmergo/github-repo-analytics)** is a template that tracks GitHub traffic, stars, downloads and contributors for your open-source projects, free on GitHub Actions. Every model and metric was built and is maintained with Dex. Its [audit trail](https://github.com/exmergo/github-repo-analytics/blob/main/.dex/review/README.md) holds the raw envelopes, including the drift Dex blocked. ## The Core Python Library you can use The engine is a plain Python package, `exmergo-dex-core`: ```bash pip install exmergo-dex-core # or: uv add exmergo-dex-core ``` Drive the same loop from Python instead of parsing CLI output: ```python from exmergo_dex_core import DexEngine with DexEngine(connector="duckdb", path="shop.duckdb") as eng: mapped = eng.map() # a DexCache, not a JSON blob rows = eng.query("select status, count(*) from orders group by status") print(mapped.relationship_count, rows.cells) ``` Every guarantee the CLI makes holds here, because it is the same code. An unconfirmed billed call raises `ConfirmationRequiredError` carrying the estimate. By default nothing is written to disk; `DexEngine.from_repo("path/to/repo")` opts in to a project on disk, the way the CLI does. For hosts embedding Dex: - **Values-free mode** keeps every table value out of the model's view, aggregates only. ([values-free mode](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/guardrails/values-free-mode)) - **Per-user credentials**: pass a `ConnectionSource` so each request reaches the warehouse as its own principal. - **Multi-process lifecycles**: export a plan, verify and apply it elsewhere, and get typed evidence of what a build established. ([host integration](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/reference/host-integration)) - **Other formats and stores**: plug in a [project format](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/reference/project-formats) or a [storage backend](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/reference/storage-backends). More in the [package README](packages/dex-core/README.md). ## Benchmarks We run Dex on two public analytics-engineering benchmarks and commit every run's raw per-task results, including the ones that flatter us least. | Benchmark | Setup | Result | Details | |---|---|---|---| | **data-eng-bench** (Snowflake, 103 tasks) | Dex + Claude Sonnet 5 | **57.3%** resolved, 89.7% of assertions pass | [README](benchmarks/data-eng-bench/README.md) | | **ADE-bench** (dbt Labs, 75 tasks) | Dex + Claude Sonnet 5 | **76%** resolved, at 2.5x lower cost than Fable 5 | [README](benchmarks/ade_bench/README.md) | We believe that benchmarks are important, but not as important as user/agent experience. Trust in a diff, cost surfaced before spend, and sensitive data kept out of context. We optimize for that experience and treat these scores as guide posts. ([evaluation](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/reference/evaluation)) ## What Dex sends where - **On install**, `uv` downloads the pinned engine (and a Python 3.11 to 3.14 if you have none) from PyPI or your configured index. - **Your warehouse** gets SELECT-only SQL from Dex, plus the dbt builds you confirm on a dev target, with credentials from your existing credential chain. - **dbt Cloud** is contacted only if you enable the hosted semantic layer. - **dbt-core**, when Dex runs it, sends dbt Labs its own anonymous usage statistics unless you turn them off. `transform deps` downloads the packages your `packages.yml` declares. - **Your repository** holds Dex's state in `.dex/`. dbt writes its usual `target/` and `logs/`. > [!IMPORTANT] > **Dex sends nothing to Exmergo.** No telemetry, analytics, license check, or > update ping. See the [Dex privacy policy](https://www.exmergo.com/privacy/dex). ## Further reading - [Documentation](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex): start here - [CLI reference](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/cli/overview): every command and flag - [Command contract](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/reference/command-contract) and [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md): how any agent drives the engine - [Cost controls](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/guardrails/cost-controls) and [PII policy](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/guardrails/pii-policy): the two guardrails that cut across everything - [Configuration](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/cli/config): read and change `.dex/config.yml` as a confirmed diff - [Connectors](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/connectors/duckdb): setup, cost, and read-only enforcement per warehouse - [Changelog](https://docs.exmergo.com/dex/changelog) - [`references/`](references/): the same material as Markdown, for agents and offline reading ## Dex Enterprise Dex Enterprise runs Dex as automated workflows in your own CI. It turns tickets into draft pull requests with `explore` and `transform`, and runs `maintain` on a schedule to turn drift into draft pull requests for your engineers to review. No Exmergo service sits in the request path, and everything in this repository stays Apache-2.0. [Learn more](https://www.exmergo.com/dex/enterprise). ## Community ### Community Integrations **[dagster-dex](https://github.com/catincloud-labs/dagster-dex)**, maintained by CatInCloud Labs, lets Dex read a Dagster asset graph instead of a dbt project, so exploration and drift maintenance run natively against your orchestrated assets. ### Connect with the Community Join the agent-native data/analytics community! - 🌟 [Star Us on GitHub](https://github.com/exmergo/dex/) - 👾 [Join Our Discord Community](https://www.exmergo.com/discord) - 🔗 [Follow Us on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/exmergo/) - 🐦 [Follow Us on X](https://x.com/exmergo) - 🔨 [Follow Us on GitHub](https://github.com/exmergo/) ## Contributing See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for local setup, linting, the pre-commit hook, and changelog fragments. Every pull request into `main` must pass Lint and CI, and adds a fragment under [`changelog.d/`](changelog.d/) unless no user can see the change. Please also read the [code of conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). ## License Apache-2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) and [NOTICE](NOTICE).

readme.excerpt: # sqlalchemy-cubrid **SQLAlchemy 2.0–2.1 dialect for the CUBRID database** — Python ORM, schema reflection, Alembic migrations, and type mapping for SQLAlchemy and CUBRID-specific types. CUBRID itself is a separate database server that must already be running; installing these packages does not install CUBRID or create a database. New to CUBRID or to SQLAlchemy? CUBRID is a high-performance open-source relational database, widely adopted in Korean public-sector and enterprise applications. [🇰🇷 한국어](docs/README.ko.md) · [🇺🇸 English](README.md) · [🇨🇳 中文](docs/README.zh.md) · [🇮🇳 हिन्दी](docs/README.hi.md) · [🇩🇪 Deutsch](docs/README.de.md) · [🇷🇺 Русский](docs/README.ru.md) [![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/sqlalchemy-cubrid)](https://pypi.org/project/sqlalchemy-cubrid) [![python version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/sqlalchemy-cubrid)](https://www.python.org) [![ci workflow](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/sqlalchemy-cubrid/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/sqlalchemy-cubrid/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![integration-full workflow](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/sqlalchemy-cubrid/actions/workflows/integration-full.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/sqlalchemy-cubrid/actions/workflows/integration-full.yml) [![license](https://img.shields.io/github/license/cubrid-lab/sqlalchemy-cubrid)](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/sqlalchemy-cubrid/blob/main/LICENSE) [![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/cubrid-lab/sqlalchemy-cubrid)](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/sqlalchemy-cubrid) [![docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-GitHub%20Pages-blue)](https://cubrid-lab.github.io/sqlalchemy-cubrid/) --- > **Status: Production/Stable** — `sqlalchemy-cubrid` is a maintained SQLAlchemy dialect for CUBRID supporting SQLAlchemy 2.0–2.1 and CUBRID 10.2–11.4. > **Note:** Versions prior to 1.0.0 used inconsistent numbering (0.x, 2.x). The canonical version history starts at 1.0.0. ## Start here sqlalchemy-cubrid lets SQLAlchemy work with a CUBRID database. CUBRID itself is a separate database server that must already be running; installing these packages does not install CUBRID or create a database. New to CUBRID or to SQLAlchemy? Follow [Your First SQLAlchemy Connection to CUBRID](docs/QUICKSTART.md): it shows what to prepare when you already have a database, how to start a disposable local one with Docker, and takes you on the recommended `sqlalchemy-cubrid[pycubrid]` path to a first query and a first saved row. The rest of this page is reference material for after that first connection works. ## Why sqlalchemy-cubrid? CUBRID is a high-performance open-source relational database, widely adopted in Korean public-sector and enterprise applications. Until now, there was no actively maintained SQLAlchemy dialect that supports the modern 2.0–2.1 API. **sqlalchemy-cubrid** bridges that gap: - Full SQLAlchemy 2.0–2.1 dialect with **statement caching** and **PEP 561 typing** - **Extensive offline test suite** — no database required to run it; CI enforces a minimum 95% line-coverage gate (`--cov-fail-under=95` in the `offline-tests` job, [CI badge above](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/sqlalchemy-cubrid/actions/workflows/ci.yml)) - **Concurrency stress tests** — `QueuePool` sync threaded + asyncio.gather workloads validated against live CUBRID - **SQLAlchemy 2.1-ready compat shim** — private API access wrapped in `_compat.py`; dependency cap `>=2.0,<2.2` covering SA 2.0 and 2.1 - Tested against **4 CUBRID versions** (10.2, 11.0, 11.2, 11.4) across **Python 3.11 -- 3.15** - CUBRID-specific DML constructs: `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, `MERGE`, `REPLACE INTO` - Alembic migration support out of the box - **Three driver options** — pure Python (`cubrid+pycubrid://`, recommended), async pure Python (`cubrid+aiopycubrid://`), or the CUBRIDdb C-extension driver (`cubrid://` / `cubrid+cubriddb://`) ## Support Status - **Status**: Production/Stable [![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/sqlalchemy-cubrid)](https://pypi.org/project/sqlalchemy-cubrid) - Supported matrix: SQLAlchemy `>=2.0,<2.2`, CUBRID `10.2`, `11.0`, `11.2`, `11.4`, Python `3.11`–`3.15` - Ordinary PRs run the full offline suite with the 95% coverage floor on one Ubuntu/Python 3.12 lane; high-risk changes add Python 3.14/CUBRID 11.4 live integration. Main/changed-weekly runs add Python 3.11/CUBRID 10.2 and run the offline suite on the oldest and newest supported Python (3.11, 3.15). The full supported integration matrix remains manual and release-gated. See [CI execution policy](docs/CI_POLICY.md). - An advisory SQLAlchemy pre-release canary logs its resolved version; a passing run alone does not establish 2.2 beta compatibility (see #778) - See [Known Limitations](#known-limitations) for behavior boundaries and unsupported features ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD app["Application"] --> sa["SQLAlchemy Core/ORM"] sa --> dialect["CubridDialect"] dialect --> pycubrid["pycubrid driver"] dialect --> cext["CUBRIDdb driver"] dialect --> aio["pycubrid.aio async driver"] pycubrid --> server["CUBRID Server"] cext --> server aio --> server ``` See [full communication architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md#end-to-end-communication-architecture) for the Broker, CAS and CCI path. ```mermaid flowchart TD expr["SQL Expression"] --> compiler["CubridSQLCompiler"] --> sql["SQL String"] ``` ## Requirements **Python 3.10 support retirement:** Python 3.10 reached upstream end of life on 2026-10-01 ([PEP 619](https://peps.python.org/pep-0619/#310-lifespan)). The 1.8.x and 1.9.x lines support Python 3.10; 1.9.0 carried the advance notice. From 1.10.0 the package requires Python 3.11 or newer, so `pip` on Python 3.10 keeps installing 1.9.x. Upgrade your interpreter, recreate your virtual environment and validate your application before upgrading. - Python 3.11 or later - SQLAlchemy 2.0 – 2.1 - [pycubrid](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/pycubrid) (pure Python, recommended) **or** the official CUBRIDdb C extension built from [cubrid-python](https://github.com/CUBRID/cubrid-python) v11.3.0.51 or later ## Installation ```bash pip install sqlalchemy-cubrid ``` With the pure Python driver (sync and async): ```bash pip install "sqlalchemy-cubrid[pycubrid]" ``` The `[pycubrid]` extra supports both `cubrid+pycubrid://` and `cubrid+aiopycubrid://`. It includes SQLAlchemy's `asyncio` extra (`greenlet`); `greenlet` may need build tools if a compatible wheel is unavailable. With Alembic support: ```bash pip install "sqlalchemy-cubrid[alembic]" ``` With the CUBRIDdb C-extension driver (the bare `cubrid://` URL), build CUBRIDdb from [cubrid-python](https://github.com/CUBRID/cubrid-python) v11.3.0.51 or later; see [Driver Compatibility](docs/DRIVER_COMPAT.md#building-cubriddb-from-source). > **The `[cubrid]` and `[cubriddb]` extras are deprecated.** They install the > `CUBRID-Python` package from PyPI, whose newest release is 9.3.x (2015). That release is > untested with this dialect: it returns `BIGINT` as `str` and fails parts of the > integration suite. The dialect warns (`SAWarning`) at the first connection when it > finds a CUBRIDdb older than 11.3. For new projects, use the recommended pure-Python > `[pycubrid]` driver (the `cubrid+pycubrid://` URL). To select the CUBRIDdb C-extension > driver explicitly, use the `cubrid+cubriddb://` URL. ## Quick Start These short examples assume a running database named `demodb` and a `dba` account whose password is `password`; replace the URL with your own values. The [first-connection guide](docs/QUICKSTART.md) instead uses a local lab database, `testdb`, with no password. The ORM example creates a `users` table; the async insert example creates and drops a table of its own. ### Core (Connection-Level) ```python from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text engine = create_engine("cubrid+pycubrid://dba:password@localhost:33000/demodb") with engine.connect() as conn: result = conn.execute(text("SELECT 1")) print(result.scalar()) ``` ### ORM (Session-Level) ```python from sqlalchemy import create_engine, String from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, Session, mapped_column class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass class User(Base): __tablename__ = "users" id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True, autoincrement=True) name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100)) email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(200), unique=True) engine = create_engine("cubrid+pycubrid://dba:password@localhost:33000/demodb") Base.metadata.create_all(engine) with Session(engine) as session: user = User(name="Alice", email="alice@example.com") session.add(user) session.commit() ``` ### Async The async driver is `cubrid+aiopycubrid://`. Both examples below are complete programs: save each under the name given and run it with `python`. Their code runs inside `async def main()`, started by `asyncio.run(main())`; in an ordinary script, `await` or `async with` outside a function is a `SyntaxError`. Each creates its engine inside the running event loop and always awaits `engine.dispose()`. Save this as `async_first_query.py` and run `python async_first_query.py`: ```python import asyncio from sqlalchemy import text from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession, create_async_engine async def main() -> None: # Create the engine inside the running event loop, and always dispose of it. engine = create_async_engine("cubrid+aiopycubrid://dba:password@localhost:33000/demodb") try: async with AsyncSession(engine) as session: result = await session.execute(text("SELECT 1 + 1")) print(result.scalar()) finally: await engine.dispose() if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) ``` It prints `2`, the value the database computed. #### Async insert with PK retrieval CUBRID has no `RETURNING` clause. For ORM inserts, call `await session.flush()` inside the transaction block: it sends the INSERT and populates the auto-increment PK on the object before the commit. Save this as `async_insert_id.py` and run `python async_insert_id.py`. It creates its own table, `sqlalchemy_async_example_notes`, inserts one row, reads it back through a new session and drops the table again, also when a statement fails or the run is interrupted with Ctrl+C. If a table of that name already exists, it stops at the first statement with `Class dba.sqlalchemy_async_example_notes already exists` and leaves that table alone. ```python import asyncio from sqlalchemy import String, select from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession, create_async_engine from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass class Note(Base): # A table that belongs to this example; the comment marks it as such. __tablename__ = "sqlalchemy_async_example_notes" __table_args__ = {"comment": "created by the sqlalchemy-cubrid async README example"} id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True, autoincrement=True) note: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100)) async def main() -> None: engine = create_async_engine("cubrid+aiopycubrid://dba:password@localhost:33000/demodb") try: async with engine.begin() as conn: # checkfirst=False: stop with an error instead of reusing an existing table. await conn.run_sync(Base.metadata.create_all, checkfirst=False) try: async with AsyncSession(engine) as session: async with session.begin(): # commits when the block ends note = Note(note="saved from asyncio") session.add(note) await session.flush() # sends the INSERT and sets note.id, before the commit print(f"Inserted id={note.id}") note_id = note.id async with AsyncSession(engine) as session: # a new session sees the committed row saved = await session.scalar(select(Note.note).where(Note.id == note_id)) print(f"Read back: {saved}") finally: # Drop only the table this run created. async with engine.begin() as conn: await conn.run_sync(Note.__table__.drop) finally: await engine.dispose() if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) ``` It prints the generated id, which can differ between databases and runs, and the row the new session read: ```text Inserted id=1 Read back: saved from asyncio ``` If the process is killed outright between creating and dropping the table (for example with `kill -9`), the table stays behind and the next run stops at `already exists`. Its comment, `created by the sqlalchemy-cubrid async README example`, identifies it; drop it with `DROP TABLE sqlalchemy_async_example_notes` once you have checked that. For raw Core inserts where you need the auto-increment PK, run `SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID()` after the statement (see [Known Limitations](#known-limitations)). ## Features - Type mapping for SQLAlchemy standard and CUBRID-specific types — numeric, string, date/time, bit, LOB, collection, and JSON types - SQL compilation -- SELECT, JOIN, CAST, LIMIT/OFFSET, subqueries, CTEs, window functions - DML extensions -- `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, `MERGE`, `REPLACE INTO`, `FOR UPDATE`, `TRUNCATE` - DDL support -- `COMMENT`, `IF NOT EXISTS` / `IF EXISTS`, `AUTO_INCREMENT` - Schema reflection -- tables, views, columns, PKs, FKs, indexes, unique constraints, comments - Alembic migrations via `CubridImpl` (registered automatically when the dialect loads) - Three CUBRID MVCC isolation levels — `READ COMMITTED` (default), `REPEATABLE READ`, `SERIALIZABLE` - Async support — `create_async_engine("cubrid+aiopycubrid://...")` via pycubrid.aio ## Known Limitations - **No `RETURNING`** — `INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE ... RETURNING` not supported; for ORM use `await session.flush()` to populate `id` on the object (see [Async Quick Start](#async)), or for Core use `cursor.lastrowid` / `SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID()` after the statement - **No sequences** — CUBRID uses `AUTO_INCREMENT` only - **Single effective schema** — CUBRID exposes one schema per connection (the current user's schema); `get_schema_names()` reports that one schema and every reflection method honours `schema=` consistently (the default schema is reflected; any other schema yields no tables/views). Owner-qualified cross-schema reflection is not supported. - **Uncommitted DDL holds schema locks** — CUBRID DDL is transactional (`ROLLBACK` undoes it; only client autocommit, which the dialect turns off, commits it early), so by default a whole Alembic upgrade is one transaction (`transactional_ddl = True`) and keeps the tables it touches locked until it commits; use `transaction_per_migration=True` for long or large-table migrations - **SQLAlchemy 2.0–2.1 only** — capped at `<2.2`; SA 2.2 compatibility shims exist, but the advisory pre-release canary has not yet proven installation or compatibility of a published 2.2 beta (see #778) ([details](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)) - **Async requires pycubrid >= 1.8.0,<2.0** — the `cubrid+aiopycubrid://` driver needs the async-capable pycubrid package line currently supported by this project - **CARDINALITY() broken** — `func.cardinality()` raises `CompileError` with workaround guidance; the CUBRID server has a [known bug](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/.github/issues/3) - **Reserved words auto-quoted** — Column names matching CUBRID reserved words (`day`, `count`, `value`, etc.) are automatically double-quoted in DDL; see [reserved word list](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/.github/issues/5) - **Timezone type reflection** — CUBRID's `TIMESTAMPTZ`, `TIMESTAMPLTZ`, `DATETIMETZ` and `DATETIMELTZ` reflect as distinct SQLAlchemy types (`sqlalchemy_cubrid.types.TIMESTAMPTZ`/`TIMESTAMPLTZ`/`DATETIMETZ`/`DATETIMELTZ`, each with `timezone=True`) rather than collapsing into plain `TIMESTAMP`/`DATETIME` (#181, #442); see [Type Mapping](docs/TYPES.md#type-reflection-ischema_names-only) ## Documentation | Guide | Description | |---|---| | [Your First Connection](docs/QUICKSTART.md) | Start here: prepare a database, first query, first saved row, first-connection problems | | [Connection](docs/CONNECTION.md) | Connection strings, URL format, driver setup, pool tuning | | [Type Mapping](docs/TYPES.md) | Full type mapping, CUBRID-specific types, collection types | | [DML Extensions](docs/DML_EXTENSIONS.md) | ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, MERGE, REPLACE INTO, query trace | | [Isolation Levels](docs/ISOLATION_LEVELS.md) | The three CUBRID MVCC isolation levels, configuration | | [Alembic Migrations](docs/ALEMBIC.md) | Setup, configuration, limitations, batch workarounds | | [Feature Support](docs/FEATURE_SUPPORT.md) | Comparison with MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite | | [ORM Cookbook](docs/ORM_COOKBOOK.md) | Practical ORM examples, relationships, queries | | [Development](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md) | Dev setup, testing, Docker, coverage, CI/CD | | [Driver Compatibility](docs/DRIVER_COMPAT.md) | CUBRID-Python driver versions and known issues | | [Troubleshooting](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md) | Common issues, error solutions, debugging techniques | | [Async Connection](docs/CONNECTION.md#async-connection) | Async engine setup with `cubrid+aiopycubrid://` | ## Compatibility Matrix | Component | Supported versions | |---|---| | Python | 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14, 3.15 | | CUBRID | 10.2, 11.0, 11.2, 11.4 | | SQLAlchemy | 2.0–2.1 | | Alembic | >=1.7.2 | | pycubrid (sync) | >=1.8.0,<2.0 | | pycubrid (async) | >=1.8.0,<2.0 | ## FAQ ### How do I connect to CUBRID with SQLAlchemy? ```python from sqlalchemy import create_engine engine = create_engine("cubrid+pycubrid://dba:password@localhost:33000/demodb") ``` The recommended way is the pure-Python `pycubrid` driver: `create_engine("cubrid+pycubrid://dba:password@localhost:33000/demodb")`. The driver requires no CUBRID native libraries. The `[pycubrid]` extra also installs `greenlet` for SQLAlchemy's async bridge; it may require build tools when no compatible wheel is available. The bare `cubrid://` URL uses the supported CUBRIDdb C-extension driver, which must be built from cubrid-python v11.3.0.51 or later (the PyPI `CUBRID-Python` 9.3.x release that the deprecated `[cubriddb]` extra installs is untested); to select it explicitly and unambiguously use `cubrid+cubriddb://`. ### Does sqlalchemy-cubrid support SQLAlchemy 2.0–2.1? Yes. sqlalchemy-cubrid is built for SQLAlchemy 2.0–2.1 and supports the 2.0-style API including `Session.execute()`, typed `Mapped[]` columns, and statement caching. ### Does sqlalchemy-cubrid support Alembic migrations? Yes. Install with `pip install "sqlalchemy-cubrid[alembic]"`. The CUBRID migration implementation registers itself when the dialect loads, so the default `env.py` works unchanged with synchronous URLs; for `cubrid+aiopycubrid://`, use Alembic's async template (`alembic init -t async`). CUBRID DDL is transactional, so by default a failed `alembic upgrade` is rolled back whole, version bump included; set `transaction_per_migration=True` to commit after each revision for long or large-table migrations. ### What Python versions are supported? Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 (standard GIL builds). ### Does CUBRID support RETURNING clauses? No. CUBRID does not support `INSERT ... RETURNING` or `UPDATE ... RETURNING`. Use `cursor.lastrowid` or `SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID()` instead. ### How do I use ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE with CUBRID? ```python from sqlalchemy_cubrid import insert stmt = insert(users).values(name="Alice").on_duplicate_key_update(name="Alice Updated") ``` ### What's the difference between `cubrid://` and `cubrid+pycubrid://`? `cubrid://` uses the C-extension driver (CUBRIDdb) which requires compilation. `cubrid+pycubrid://` uses the pure Python driver, which requires no CUBRID native libraries. The `[pycubrid]` extra includes `greenlet`, whose installation may require build tools when no compatible wheel is available. `cubrid+aiopycubrid://` uses the async variant of the pure Python driver for use with `create_async_engine` and `AsyncSession`. > **Recommendation:** for new projects prefer `cubrid+pycubrid://` (pure Python driver, no CUBRID native libraries). The `[pycubrid]` extra's `greenlet` dependency may need build tools. Use `cubrid+cubriddb://` with CUBRIDdb built from cubrid-python v11.3.0.51 or later when you specifically need the C-extension driver. ### Does sqlalchemy-cubrid support async? Yes. Use `create_async_engine("cubrid+aiopycubrid://...")` with the pycubrid async driver. Requires `pycubrid>=1.8.0,<2.0`. Both pycubrid dialects use native `Connection.ping(False)` / `AsyncConnection.ping(False)` for `pool_pre_ping`, and all Core and ORM features work with `AsyncSession`. ## Related Projects - [pycubrid](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/pycubrid) — Pure Python DB-API 2.0 driver for CUBRID - [cubrid-cookbook-python](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/cubrid-cookbook-python) — Production-ready Python examples for CUBRID ## Roadmap See [`ROADMAP.md`](ROADMAP.md) for this project's direction and next milestones. For the ecosystem-wide view, see the [CUBRID Labs Ecosystem Roadmap](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/.github/blob/main/ROADMAP.md). ## Contributing See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for guidelines and [docs/DEVELOPMENT.md](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md) for development setup. ### First contribution New to CUBRID? Pick the repository that matches what you want to work on: - Documentation and runnable examples: [cubrid-cookbook-python](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/cubrid-cookbook-python) - Pure-Python driver fixes: [pycubrid](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/pycubrid) - SQLAlchemy dialect fixes: [sqlalchemy-cubrid](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/sqlalchemy-cubrid) Most first issues can be developed and tested with the offline checks in CONTRIBUTING.md — no Docker or CUBRID server needed. Live CUBRID verification can be completed by CI and maintainers. Browse open [`good first issue`](https://github.com/cubrid-lab/sqlalchemy-cubrid/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22+no%3Aassignee) tasks. ## Security Report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting (email is the fallback) -- see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). Do not open public issues for security concerns. ## Disclaimer > This project is part of [CUBRID Lab](https://github.com/cubrid-lab), an independent open-source initiative for CUBRID developer tooling, and is not affiliated with, sponsored by, or endorsed by CUBRID Corporation or the official CUBRID project. ## License MIT -- see [LICENSE](LICENSE).

# h-ssh `h-ssh` runs commands across a fleet of network devices: one device or three hundred, Juniper, any SSH host, or a console still speaking telnet. Devices are worked in parallel, results are collected per device, and one dead box does not sink a run: every run probes the boxes first (unless you say `--no-probe`), without logging in, so a dead one is a FAIL within seconds, and an edit does not go on without a box the probe found dead unless you say so. The per-device session is a solved problem; what is left is everything around it: the thread pool, per-device result collection, a rate limiter (`--safety-file`) so a router that already failed is not hammered, and a record of what changed (`--audit-log`). That is the part h-ssh provides. On Junos, everything goes through PyEZ over NETCONF, reads and writes alike, which gives one session, real RPC errors, and the lock, diff and rollback that config changes need. Every edit is probed for reachability (unless `--no-probe`) and prompts before it commits; with `--audit-log` it lands in a JSONL audit trail. `--commit-confirmed` puts the device back the way it was if you never confirm. ## Features - **Four transports, one interface.** Juniper (PyEZ over NETCONF), any SSH host through paramiko or the system `ssh` binary, and raw-socket telnet with IOS-, Junos-, Arista- and NX-OS-flavoured prompt handling. Same flags whichever you point it at; the ones only a Junos transport can honour (`--dry-run` on an edit, `--show-diff`, `--commit-confirmed`, and over NETCONF `--comment`, `--format`, `--rollback`, `--commit-status`) are refused on the others device by device: such a device is a FAIL with the reason, nothing is sent to it, and the run exits 1; never faked. - **Parallel by default.** Devices are worked concurrently behind an `asyncio` semaphore, `--workers 8` out of the box. - **One command or many, one device or many.** `--batch` runs several commands per device on a single connection; `--job` takes a JSON file with different commands — and different modes — per device, readable from a file or stdin. - **A dead box costs seconds, not a worker.** Every run starts with a probe (`--no-probe` skips it) — a TCP connect and the SSH banner, no login, 100 boxes at a time — and goes to the boxes that answered; `--probe` alone is a health check of the fleet, with each box's TCP handshake round trip as the kernel measured it and the time its sshd took to answer. See [The probe](#the-probe). - **Writes are gated.** The probe's question before a partial deployment, `y/N` confirmation, `--dry-run` that shows the diff without committing and `--commit-confirmed N` for changes that undo themselves unless you confirm within N minutes (both Junos), and an opt-in per-device rate limit and cooldown (`--safety-file`). - **Templates instead of memorised syntax.** `-sC bgp` resolves through a per-vendor JSON template library — *per target*, so the same shortcut sends a Junos router and an EOS switch each their own command. Drop your own in `~/.h-ssh/commands/{dialect}.json` (`junos`, `ios`, `nxos`, `eos`, `none`) to add or override; `junos`, `eos` and `none` ship one. - **Built to be scripted.** `--json` on stdout, a structured summary line on stderr, meaningful exit codes, and credentials from `HSSH_USER` / `HSSH_PASSWORD` — or import `hssh` and skip the CLI entirely. A whole fleet run fits in one YAML file (`--run fleet.yaml`) that a pipeline step or a jump-host session runs as it is. - **Built for a maintenance, not just a run.** A session pool keeps one NETCONF session per router open for a whole script; `rpc()` and `--format json|xml` return the router's own data instead of CLI text; `begin()` holds a diffed candidate open until a gate decides; `--rollback N`, commit comments, `--commit-status` and `guarded_commit()` cover the commit-confirmed lifecycle without a `| match` in sight. - **Two runtime dependencies — or none.** `paramiko` and `junos-eznc` come with the package. Telnet is a raw socket (no stdlib `telnetlib`, so it still works on Python 3.13+), and the `openssh` transport drives the system `ssh` binary, so a checkout on a locked-down jump host with nothing installable still runs shows and edits over `ssh`. ## How it works ``` hosts / devices.csv / --job per device, up to --workers at once ────────────────────────────────── ───────────────────────────────────── │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ probe, no login │──▶ a dead box: FAIL in seconds │ TCP + SSH banner │ (an edit asks before it goes │ 100 boxes at once │ on without one) └───────────────────────┘ │ the boxes that answered │ ┌─ junos PyEZ over NETCONF (830) ▼ │ show/edit → PyEZ NETCONF ┌───────────────────────┐ │ lock → load → diff │ safety gate (opt-in) │ │ → commit → unlock │ rate limit 10/device │──▶ workers ──┼─ ssh exec_command │ cooldown 120s on fail │ │ │ --safety-file, flock'd│ ├─ openssh the ssh binary, no deps └───────────────────────┘ └─ telnet raw TCP + prompt match │ │ └──────────── every edit ──────────────────┴──▶ --audit-log (JSONL) ``` On Junos, show commands run through PyEZ `Device.cli()` over one NETCONF session (a batch shares it); a reply whose text opens with the CLI's refusal (`error: could not resolve file: ...` as the ``, where most refusals come back as an RPC error) is a failure, `'CMD' was refused by the device: ...`, as on the text transports, and is not tried again; a transaction's `tx.show()` raises it too. The NETCONF port defaults to 830 for every Junos call; set the target's port to use NETCONF on 22. Config changes lock the candidate, load, diff, run `commit_check`, commit, and unlock, rolling back if any step fails. Confirming a commit-confirmed (`-eC "commit"`) first reads the commit history: with no commit-confirmed waiting (the timer expired, or it was confirmed already) the device fails with *nothing to confirm* and nothing is sent, because a plain commit there would hide that the change is already gone. It locks too, so another user's uncommitted edits in the shared candidate refuse it — nothing sent, retried like any other lock refusal — instead of riding along with the confirmation. The "don't forget to confirm" reminder prints only when at least one device actually armed a timer. A commit whose reply never arrives is reported as *outcome unknown* and is never retried or rolled back automatically — check the device (and any commit-confirmed timer) first. The NETCONF session verifies the router's host key by default since #150 (a default change: before it, the password went to whoever answered on the port, a router whose key had changed included), on the store the `ssh` transport keeps: `HSSH_NETCONF_HOSTKEY=accept-new` (the default) pins an unknown router in `~/.h-ssh/known_hosts` on first contact, under `[HOST]:PORT`, and refuses one whose key is not the one pinned there or in `~/.ssh/known_hosts` before the password goes (`host key verification failed for HOST:PORT: its key is not the one pinned in FILE (or ~/.ssh/known_hosts); if the router was re-keyed, remove its line`; a router the two files disagree on is refused too); `yes` refuses an unknown router as well (`not pinned in ~/.h-ssh/known_hosts or ~/.ssh/known_hosts`); `no` is the opt-out to the old behaviour, for a re-keyed router that must not stop a maintenance; anything else is refused, and the variable is read per call. `~/.ssh/known_hosts` is read as the `ssh` transport reads it: its `@cert-authority` lines are passed over, and a key it marks `@revoked` is refused (`host key verification failed for HOST:PORT: its key is marked @revoked in FILE`). With a password, no `~/.ssh/id_*` key and no agent is tried first. A session that does not open is reported by what happened, not by PyEZ's label (which calls anything that fails within 3 s *refused*): `connection refused by HOST:PORT` or `no route to host HOST:PORT` (what the OS answered the TCP connect, where ncclient says only "Could not open socket"), `TCP connect to HOST:PORT timed out after Ns`, `HOST:PORT is not an SSH server: the banner is not text`, `HOST:PORT dropped the session before login after Ns (sshd connection limit?)`, `no SSH banner from HOST:PORT within Ns`, `no SSH session to HOST:PORT within Ns: the banner came, but key exchange did not finish`, `host key verification failed`, `authentication failed for USER at HOST:PORT`, `cannot resolve HOST`, and `local open-file limit reached (ulimit -n N): this machine had no descriptor for a session to HOST:PORT; nothing was sent` when this process is out of descriptors, for the socket (which ncclient swallows, so it read *connection refused* for a port that was listening) or for what the session opens after it; the system's file table full (ENFILE) says `fs.file-max, not ulimit -n` instead. That one is this machine's limit, not the device's answer: a `hssh.errors.OpenFileLimitError` (a `NotAppliedError` and a `LocalError`), not tried again, and no `--safety-file` cooldown for the device. A `delete` of a statement the device does not have is a no-op (`warning: statement not found` is the one load warning that is ignored, so a broadcast of deletes stays idempotent); every other warning still fails the device. `--session-timeout` is one deadline for the whole session set-up — TCP connect, SSH banner, key exchange, authentication — not PyEZ's connect timeout followed by paramiko's own 15 s banner, 15 s key-exchange and 30 s authentication timeouts, and the router's NETCONF hello after it has `--session-timeout` of its own. Within that deadline `--connect-timeout` (3 s) bounds the TCP connect and the banner together, so a router that does not answer, or accepts TCP and then says nothing, costs 3 s an attempt and is tried again (see [Failure handling](#failure-handling)); a slow key exchange, login or hello still has the session timeout. An IPv6 literal cannot be used on this transport at all (PyEZ refuses the bare form, ncclient cannot resolve the bracketed one); it is reported once, as such. ## Install One line, no package manager. It needs `python3` 3.10 or newer with its venv module (Debian/Ubuntu: `sudo apt install python3-venv`) and `git`: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/h-network/h-ssh/develop/install.sh | sh h-ssh --list-vendors ``` The installer puts h-ssh in a Python environment of its own, `~/.h-ssh/venv`, with every transport (paramiko and PyEZ come with it), and links `h-ssh` and `h-ssh-store` into `~/.local/bin`, creating that directory when it is missing; if it is not on your `PATH` yet the script says so and how to add it. Your config, inventory, shortcuts and profiles live next to the environment under `~/.h-ssh` (the result store is `./h-ssh.db` in the directory you run from, unless you name another), and pip's download cache lands in its usual place (`~/.cache/pip` on Linux). Running the same line again upgrades, whatever the version number says. It installs the `develop` branch; a knob on the `sh` side of the pipe picks another branch or tag: `curl -fsSL … | H_SSH_REF=main sh` for the release branch. `H_SSH_REPO`, `H_SSH_HOME`, `H_SSH_BIN` and `H_SSH_PYTHON` are the others, see the script's header. Removing it: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/h-network/h-ssh/develop/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall ``` takes the environment and the two links away and leaves `~/.h-ssh` otherwise alone; it never touches an `h-ssh` in `~/.local/bin` that it did not put there (a pipx or uv install, your own wrapper), and neither does an install. Read the script first if you like: a page of POSIX sh that does what this paragraph says. If you already use [pipx](https://pipx.pypa.io) or [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), the same thing in their words: `pipx install git+https://github.com/h-network/h-ssh.git` or `uv tool install git+https://github.com/h-network/h-ssh.git` (the default branch, `develop`; add `@main` for the release branch). For working on h-ssh itself: ```bash git clone -b develop https://github.com/h-network/h-ssh.git && cd h-ssh python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate pip install -e '.[dev]' # the package, editable, plus pytest, pytest-cov and ruff ``` The checkout's `./h-app/h-ssh.py` is the same CLI without installing, on an interpreter that has `paramiko` and `junos-eznc`; the `openssh` and `telnet` transports need neither. The store reader has no script there: `PYTHONPATH=h-app python3 -c 'from hssh.store import main_sync; main_sync()' runs` is `h-ssh-store runs`. ## Quick start ```bash # a show on two routers typed bare: the host is the name, --transport the driver; you are the user # you are logged in as, the password is asked for (keys and agents need nothing) h-ssh --transport junos 10.0.1.1 10.0.1.2 -sC bgp # the same, named, the vendor on the target, as another user h-ssh --user admin -sC bgp R1:10.0.1.1:junos R2:10.0.1.2:junos # ... or from a CSV inventory, as JSON (the sample inventory in a checkout has junos, openssh and ssh rows) h-ssh --user admin --json -sC "show version" --devices h-app/devices.csv # compare one command's output across the fleet: each device against the first that answered, in # target order (bare hosts, then --target; or the inventory's rows) h-ssh -sC bgp --diff R1:10.0.1.1:junos R2:10.0.1.2:junos # config change — look before you leap (no host typed: the inventory is ~/.h-ssh/devices.csv, or # ./devices.csv; these are Junos lines: an ssh or openssh row fails --dry-run and --commit-confirmed, # and gets the set line as a command) h-ssh --user admin -eC "set system ntp server 10.0.0.1" --dry-run h-ssh --user admin -eC "set system ntp server 10.0.0.1" -y # a change that rolls itself back in 10 minutes unless you confirm h-ssh --user admin -eB configs/all.set --commit-confirmed 10 -y # several commands per device, one connection h-ssh --batch commands.txt R1:10.0.1.1:junos h-ssh --profile junos-health R1:10.0.1.1:junos # a named command set, yours or shipped (--list-profiles) # watch: the same read again 30 s after each tick, every tick kept in the store, only what changed is printed h-ssh -sC "show bgp summary" --every 30 R1:10.0.1.1:junos R2:10.0.1.2:junos # a console server still speaking telnet h-ssh -sC "show version" SW1:10.0.0.1:5000:telnet-ios # is every box there? one line each, no login (the same probe runs before every run) h-ssh --probe # every run is kept in ./h-ssh.db (a --probe too), as the devices answered; read it back h-ssh-store runs h-ssh-store output R1 20261027-0930 # R1's reply in that run: an id from the list, or a unique prefix ``` Targets are typed bare on the command line, before or between the flags (not right after a `--commit-confirmed` that has no N: the target would be read as the minutes). A host alone (`10.0.1.1`, `cr1.example.net`, `[2001:db8::1]`) is a device named after itself on `--transport`; `NAME:HOST`, `NAME:HOST:VENDOR`, `NAME:HOST:PORT` or `NAME:HOST:PORT:VENDOR` name it (`NAME:HOST:VENDOR:PORT` works too; the confirm hint writes a job's targets that way), an IPv6 host in brackets, `R1:[2001:db8::1]:junos`. A port needs a name: `10.0.1.1:830` is read as `NAME:HOST`, a device named `10.0.1.1` on host `830`; write `R1:10.0.1.1:830`. `--target SPEC` is the same thing as a flag (repeatable; it wants the name). With any target typed the inventory file is not read; without one it is `--devices`, else `~/.h-ssh/devices.csv`, else `./devices.csv`. A CSV inventory accepts `name,ip`, `name,ip,vendor` or `name,ip,vendor,port`, or one bare hostname per line; headers or none (a header is a first row whose first column is `name`; any other first row is a device), and `#` comments, full-line or trailing. A UTF-8 BOM from Excel or Notepad is skipped. A fifth column, a port outside 1..65535 or a port that is not a number is refused naming the row, so a typo never turns into the wrong device. Each device is listed once, a device being its host and the port its transport uses, written or not (`R1:10.0.0.1:junos` and `R2:10.0.0.1:830:junos` are one router): the same row twice, one name on two hosts, or one host under two names is refused before anything runs (exit 2, naming the duplicate). A job file may repeat a device (its entries run in file order; on `junos` they share one NETCONF session, on the other transports each entry logs in again), but not use one name for two hosts or one host under two names. **A target that doesn't declare a vendor gets `--transport`**, which defaults to plain `ssh` — the transport that assumes least, since its show and edit paths are both `exec_command`. Declare `junos` on the target to get NETCONF, or set it once with `--transport junos` (or `transport = junos` in `~/.h-ssh/config`; either takes only `junos`, `ssh`, `openssh` or `telnet`, so another driver, `telnet-ios` or `junos@ssh`, goes on the target or the CSV row) for an inventory of `name,ip` rows; a vendor on the target itself always wins. Command shortcuts resolve per target against that vendor, so one `-sC bgp` across a mixed inventory sends each device its own command. ### Authentication ```bash h-ssh --user admin -sC bgp # SSH agent / key, or type it at the prompt export HSSH_USER=admin HSSH_PASSWORD=secret # a pipeline: from the environment, nothing to type ``` There is no `--password` flag. h-ssh reads `HSSH_PASSWORD` when it is set, which is how a pipeline hands over the secret for that one process (from a vault, from the scheduler); otherwise, when stdin is a terminal, it asks, and Enter skips the password for keys or an agent; with neither there is no password. A variable that is set but empty refuses a pipeline run (exit 2) rather than falling back to keys without a word. A flag would show the password to every user on the host (`ps`, `/proc//cmdline`), leave it in the shell history, and put it in the command line `--store` keeps. Your own user password belongs in neither a file nor a shell profile; the environment variable is for an account made for automation. h-ssh alone reads it: no `ssh` process the `openssh` transport runs inherits it, nor a `ProxyCommand` one of them runs (a process of the same user can read another's environment from `/proc//environ`), and the password itself reaches `ssh` through an `SSH_ASKPASS` helper that prints a 0600 file in a private 0700 directory, made for the call and removed with it (the login and the commands that ride its session; an edit typed into `ssh -tt` has it until the prompt is seen), never through the environment either. The same `ps` exposure holds for what the `openssh` driver sends: a show, and each line of an `openssh` edit, runs as the `ssh` process's argument, so a config line is readable from `ps` for the life of that process (a dialect's edit over the OpenSSH binary, `junos@openssh` and the like, is typed into `ssh -tt` instead); push secrets over NETCONF or paramiko, not over `openssh`. A password means the same on every transport: it is the credential, and no `~/.ssh/id_*` key and no agent key is offered first (`openssh` passes `PubkeyAuthentication=no` and `IdentitiesOnly=yes`), so a wrong password is a failed login on `junos`, `ssh` and `openssh` alike, never an OK by way of a key. Without a password the keys and the agent are what you log in with. The username is plain text. Telnet types it at the `login:` prompt as it is, where a line break would end it and run the rest as commands once the login succeeds, so one with a control character in it (a line break, an ESC, a Tab) is refused before a run that logs in starts, on every driver: exit 2, naming where it came from (`--user`, the run file's `user`, `HSSH_USER` or the config file), without quoting it. The password is checked where it is typed: `telnet` and its flavours refuse one with a control character other than a Tab before they connect, a FAIL of that device tried once, and the other drivers hand it to the SSH login as it is (see [Transports](#transports)). ## Modes | Flag | Mode | What it does | |---|---|---| | `-sC` | Show | Run a show/display command (or a template name): one line of text, so a line break or another control character in it is refused (exit 2). A command that acts on the device (`request …`, `clear …`) is sent once and never retried, and refused under `--format` (exit 2, nothing sent) | | `-eC` | Edit command | Apply one config line to every target; a control character other than a line break (an ESC, a NUL, a ^C) is refused (exit 2). A Tab passes here; a driver that types at a CLI refuses it before it connects (see [Transports](#transports)). One with nothing in it but blank lines and comments for a target's dialect (`-eC '# x'`, and `-eC '! x'` to an IOS-shaped one, comments as for `-eD`) is refused too (exit 2, nothing sent) | | `-eD` | Edit directory | Per-device config from `.set` files: blank lines and full-line comments are skipped, `#` on every driver and `!` too on an IOS-shaped dialect (`ios@…`, `nxos@…` and `eos@…`, so `telnet-ios`, `telnet-nxos` and `telnet-arista` as well); nothing else is touched, so `community ab#12` goes as written, and a `!` line goes to the plain `ssh`, `openssh` and `telnet` drivers as written. A device without its `.set` ends the run before anything is sent (exit 2, naming it); `--allow-missing` skips those devices instead and reports them as skipped (exit 3); it is for `-eD` and changes nothing beside another edit, and on a run with no edit (a show, a batch, `--commit-status`, `--probe` alone, a job of shows) it is refused (exit 2), as `--comment` is. A `.set` with nothing in it but blank lines and comments for its device's dialect ends the run the same way on every driver, `--allow-missing` or not, and so does one with a control character other than a line break in it (an ESC, a ^C, a DEL), as `-eC` does, naming the file and the line | | `-eB` | Edit broadcast | One config file applied to all targets (comments as for `-eD`; a file with nothing else in it for a target's dialect, naming those targets when not all of them, or with a control character other than a line break, ends the run before anything is sent, exit 2) | | `--batch` | Batch | Several show commands from a file, one connection per device. Every line is held to `-sC`'s rules: one line of text, and a line that acts on the device makes the batch a single attempt and is refused under `--format` (exit 2, nothing sent). A file that cannot be read (not UTF-8, no permission) is exit 2 saying why | | `--profile` | Batch | The same, by name: a command set of yours in `~/.h-ssh/profiles/NAME.txt` (or `NAME`; a name with a `/` is a path), or one that ships (`junos-health`, `junos-snapshot`); `--list-profiles` shows both. A profile is a batch file, one command per line, `#` comments, the first comment its description; one that cannot be read is listed as unreadable, with the reason | | `--job` | Job | Per-device commands *and* modes from JSON — file or `-` for stdin; each entry's `target` is `NAME:HOST[:VENDOR][:PORT]`, as for `--target` (a bare host is refused). A job's targets are its entries: a target typed beside it (a bare host, `--target`), a `--devices`, or the `devices` of a run file it is typed beside is refused (exit 2, nothing sent) | | `--rollback N` | Rollback | Return every target to rollback N (0–49): the same lock → diff → commit check → commit → unlock as an edit, so `--dry-run` shows the diff of going back and `--commit-confirmed` arms the timer (NETCONF `junos` only) | | `--commit-status` | Commit status | `show system commit` as data per target: sequence, time, user, comment, and the pending commit-confirmed timer (NETCONF `junos` only) | | `--probe` | Probe | Alone, with no command: every box checked without logging in, one line each with its result and times, a summary, kept in the store; exit 0 when every box is live, 1 when one is dead, 3 when none is but one was not probed, 4 when the store could not keep it. See [The probe](#the-probe) | | `--run FILE` | Run file | Any of the above but `--profile` and `--probe` alone, described in one YAML or JSON file: devices, commands, options, outputs (a profile's file can go in as `batch:`; `--profile` or `--probe` typed next to `--run` still work). A flag typed next to it wins over the file whatever its value, and a target or a `--devices` typed next to it replaces the file's `devices`; a `--job` typed next to a file that holds `devices` is refused (exit 2). See [Run files](#run-files) | `-sC`, `-eC`, `-eD` and `-eB` are also `--show-command`, `--edit-command`, `--edit-dir` and `--edit-broadcast`; `-y` and `-v` are `--yes` and `--verbose`. ```json [ {"target": "R1:10.0.1.1:junos", "show": "show bgp summary"}, {"target": "R2:10.0.1.2:junos", "show": "show version"}, {"target": "R3:10.0.1.3:junos", "edit": "set system host-name R3-new"} ] ``` ```bash ./h-app/h-ssh.py --user admin --job jobs.json --json -y cat jobs.json | ./h-app/h-ssh.py --user admin --job - --json -y # the job is on stdin: an edit cannot be confirmed there, and no password is asked (HSSH_PASSWORD, or keys) ``` An entry may also carry `"port": 830` to override the target's port. A `show` is one line of text and an `edit` has no control character but its line breaks, as for `-sC` and `-eC`, and neither is whitespace alone; nor is an `edit` nothing but blank lines and comments for its target's dialect (`#`, and `!` for an IOS-shaped one). Each is refused before the password is asked or anything is sent (exit 2). A job with an edit entry asks the usual `y/N` unless `-y` is given, and the question goes to stdout, so a `--json` run wants `-y`. A device may appear in more than one entry. Its entries run one after another, in file order, so a show listed after an edit sees the edit, and each is audited with its own mode and payload. Other devices, two routers behind one address on two ports too, run beside them. With `--save-output DIR` each entry is saved to a file of its own: the device's first entry keeps `DIR/.output`, its later ones go to `DIR/.2.output`, `DIR/.3.output` and so on, in file order. A job that would put two results in one file that way (a device named `R1.2` beside a second `R1` entry) is refused before the password is asked or anything is sent (exit 2). The store numbers a device's entries the same way: `h-ssh-store output R1 --seq k` reads the entry saved as `R1.output` (k=0) or `R1..output`; the file adds the DEVICE/HOST/MODE/VENDOR header, and for a failed entry it holds the ERROR line that `output` prints on stderr with exit 1. `--show-diff` previews a job's edits one by one, each a dry run on the device as it is now, while the run that follows applies a device's entries one after another. A device's later edit would be previewed without the ones before it, so a job with more than one edit entry for a device is refused with `--show-diff`, naming the device, before the password is asked or anything is sent (exit 2). Put a device's edits in one entry: an `edit` may hold several lines. ### Watching: `--every` `--every SECONDS` runs the same read again, SECONDS after the previous tick finished (one second to a day), until Ctrl-C or `--times N`. Reads only (`-sC`, `--batch`, `--profile`), and the store must be on: every tick is a run in the store, and the ticks are compared through it. `--json` and `--raw` are refused with it: a watch prints tick lines, and a pipeline reads the ticks from the store (`h-ssh-store export`). The password is asked once, before the first tick. The screen gets one line per tick and, for every device whose reply changed since the tick before, the difference: ``` tick 1 14:02:10: 250 OK, 0 failed; baseline kept as run 20261025-140210-3f1a tick 2 14:02:43: 250 OK, 0 failed, 1 changed --- cr17: show bgp summary --- 2026-10-25T14:02:10 +++ 2026-10-25T14:02:43 @@ -3,2 +3,2 @@ 10.9.9.9 65000 Establ -10.9.9.8 65000 Establ +10.9.9.8 65000 Active ``` A device that fails on a tick shows as `OK -> FAIL (reason)`; every tick is probed first, so a box that went away since the tick before shows as `OK -> FAIL (probe: …)` within seconds. A tick the store could not keep in full says so on its line, in the warning's words: `baseline not kept (N of M results were not kept: why)` in place of the baseline's run id, `; N of M results were not kept: why` after a later tick's count; what the store lost is still compared, as the tick got it. With `--diff` every tick also prints how each device's reply differs from the first device's, as a single run does. The structured summary line still goes to stderr once per tick, and any two ticks can be compared later with `h-ssh-store diff DEVICE RUN_A RUN_B`. Ctrl-C between ticks stops the watch and says how many ticks are kept, and how many were not kept in full. The exit code is the worst tick's, in this order: `130` > `4` > `2` > `1` > `3` > `0`. A device that failed on one tick is exit `1` however clean the ticks after it, and a tick that cannot start ends the watch with `2`, as when the store was deleted or replaced since tick 1: a watch keeps all its ticks in one store. ## The probe Every run starts by asking each box whether it is there, at the protocol level and without logging in: a TCP connect to where the run will connect (the port its transport uses, 830 for `junos`, 22 for `ssh` and `openssh`, the target's own when it names one, or what your ssh configuration says: see *Where the run goes* below), the server's identification line read and checked to start with `SSH-` (an SSH server speaks first; lines it sends before that one are passed over, as paramiko and OpenSSH pass them over, up to 100 lines of 255 bytes), and the connection closed. No key exchange, no login, no credential. `telnet*` (frozen) has no banner to check: a TCP connect is all it is asked, and so is a `junos` target on port 23, which PyEZ reaches as a console over telnet. It is plain TCP, so no root is needed. Each box gets one result: | Result | What happened | |---|---| | `live` | the box answered with an SSH banner, `SSH-2.0-…`, which is kept as its sshd's version string | | `refused` | the TCP connect was refused (`connection refused by HOST:PORT`) | | `no route` | the network said there is no way to the box (`no route to host HOST:PORT`, `network is unreachable for HOST:PORT`), or the OS refused the connect otherwise (`TCP connect to HOST:PORT failed: …`) | | `name not found` | the name did not resolve (`cannot resolve HOST`, `name lookup for HOST failed: …` in the resolver's words, or `name lookup for HOST did not answer within Ns`); a name no resolver takes, `10.0.0..1` or a label over 63 characters, says why (`cannot resolve 10.0.0..1: label empty or too long`) | | `timed out` | no TCP answer within `--connect-timeout` (`TCP connect to HOST:PORT timed out after Ns`) | | `silent` | TCP accepted, and no banner within `--connect-timeout` (nothing at all, or the start of one and no more), or the connection closed without a word (a NAT or load balancer answering for a dead box, an sshd that hangs or is at its `MaxStartups`) | | `not SSH` | something else answered (`HOST:PORT answered '220 mail.example ESMTP', not an SSH banner`): a line and no `SSH-` line after it, or bytes that cannot begin one; a server that greets and then waits for the client is known when `--connect-timeout` runs out. A server that waits for the client to speak first, a web server say, sends nothing and is `silent` | | `error` | the probe itself failed on something it did not expect (`the probe of HOST:PORT failed: …`); that box counts as dead, and every other box is probed as usual | | `not probed` | the probe did not ask: the box is reached through a `ProxyJump` or a `ProxyCommand`, its ssh configuration cannot be read, or the safety gate holds it (a cooldown, or a corrupt safety file, which holds every box), or this machine had no file descriptor to spare for the probe's socket (`ulimit -n`, or `fs.file-max`: a Fleet's pooled sessions can hold many), which says nothing about the box. It is not dead: the run goes to it as with `--no-probe` | Every result but `live` and `not probed` is a dead box. The TCP connect and the banner get `--connect-timeout` each (3 s, never more than `--session-timeout`; a name's lookup too), a box that fails is tried once more half a second later, and at most 100 boxes are probed at once whatever `--workers` says, fitted to the open-file limit as the workers are (one descriptor each; a `WARNING` says when fewer run). A box that refuses or does not resolve is known in about half a second (it is asked twice), one that does not answer in about two connect timeouts (6.5 s at the defaults), and no worker waits for it: without the probe the run spends three connect timeouts and the pauses on it, about 10 s of a worker at the defaults. **Before every run, on by default:** `-sC`, `--batch`, `--profile`, `--job`, `--commit-status`, `--rollback`, every edit, `--dry-run` and `--show-diff`, and every tick of `--every`. The run goes to the boxes that answered; a dead one is a FAIL of that run with the probe's reason, in `--json`, `--log`, the audit log and the store like any failed device, and exit 1 (a device failed); it is not touched again in that run, so it starts no `--safety-file` cooldown either (the gate counts the run's own logins). A box not probed is run as without the probe. The progress output gets one line for the probe, and the stderr summary `probe_ms`, the time it took: ```console $ h-ssh -sC "show version" cr1:10.0.1.1:junos cr2:10.0.1.2:junos cr3:10.0.1.3:junos ... Probe: 3 box(es) in 0.5s: 2 live, 1 dead (refused 1), 1 slow (above 10 ms: cr2 10.7 ms) [03:02:44] cr1 STARTED [03:02:44] cr2 STARTED [03:02:44] cr3 FAIL ERROR: probe: refused (connection refused by 10.0.1.3:830) [03:02:44] cr2 OK [03:02:44] cr1 OK Done. Failures: 1 ``` **Where the run goes.** The probe asks the host and port the run will connect to. `openssh` reads your ssh configuration (`~/.ssh/config`, `/etc/ssh/ssh_config`), so for an `openssh` box the probe asks `ssh -G`: its `HostName` and `Port` are where the box is asked, and a box reached through a `ProxyJump` or a `ProxyCommand` is `not probed` (`reached through ProxyJump bastion (ssh -G)`), since the probe cannot see past the jump host; the run goes through it as it always did (an edit too, with no check before it, as under `--no-probe`). `junos` (PyEZ and ncclient) reads `~/.ssh/config` for `HostName`, `Port` (over the target's own) and `ProxyCommand`, not `ProxyJump`, and the probe reads it the same way (`reached through ProxyCommand (~/.ssh/config)`); a `junos` target on port 23 is a console PyEZ telnets to, at the host as given, so only the file's `Port` applies to it. `ssh` (paramiko) and `telnet*` read no ssh configuration: the target's host and port are what the probe asks. A configuration that cannot be read (a line `ssh -G` refuses, a `Port` that is no number) leaves the box `not probed`, with the words why, and the run says what its transport makes of it. **Before an edit** the probe replaces the old pre-flight, which waited `--session-timeout` per box and tried twice. When boxes the edit goes to are dead, an edit does not go on without them unless you say so (a dead box a `--job` only reads is a FAIL of the run, as in a show, and asks nothing): - at a terminal, h-ssh names them with their reasons and asks `Continue with the N reachable? [y/N]`. `y`: the reachable boxes get the change and the dead ones are skipped: each has its entry, `SKIPPED` on screen (`probe: refused (…); skipped`), the verdict says `skipped as unreachable: N`, and the exit code is 3, nothing failed but not everything ran. Anything else: nothing is sent, exit 2; - without a terminal the edit is refused, exit 2 (`ERROR: N device(s) unreachable: …`, or with `--json` the object `{"error": …, "unreachable": [names], "reasons": {name: why}}`), unless `--skip-unreachable` is given, which goes on with the reachable boxes without asking, at a terminal too; the skipped ones make the exit code 3. Without a terminal an edit that commits needs `-y` first (it is refused before the probe otherwise), so a pipeline gives `-y --skip-unreachable`; - `-y` confirms the edit; it never accepts a partial deployment by itself, so the question is asked with `-y` too, and without a terminal `-y` alone is refused; - with every box dead the edit is refused (exit 2) and nothing is asked; - a `--dry-run` rehearses the edit, the question included: it is asked and stopped the same way (it still needs neither `-y` nor a terminal to start); `--show-diff` is probed before its previews and previews only the boxes that will get the change. An edit the probe stopped leaves an audit entry per dead box (`preflight probe failed: refused (…) (aborted)`). **`--probe` alone**, with no command, is the health check: one line per box with its result, the handshake's round trip and the banner time, the banner or the reason, and the slow tag; then a summary.
