No password is read or asked for, and no transport needs to be installed: ```console $ h-ssh --probe cr1:10.0.1.1:junos cr2:10.0.1.2:junos cr3:10.0.1.3:junos cr4:10.0.1.4:junos sw1:10.0.1.5:telnet-ios Probe: 5 box(es), 5 at a time, 3s for the TCP connect and 3s for the banner cr1 live connect 0.4 ms banner 7.2 ms SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6 cr2 live connect 10.7 ms banner 16.5 ms SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6 slow: answered in 10.7 ms (above 10 ms) cr3 refused connection refused by 10.0.1.3:830 cr4 timed out TCP connect to 10.0.1.4:830 timed out after 3s sw1 live connect 0.3 ms TCP only, no banner to check Probe: 5 box(es) in 6.5s: 3 live, 2 dead (refused 1, timed out 1), 1 slow (above 10 ms) ``` It exits 0 when every box is live, 1 when one is dead, 3 when none is but one was not probed (4 when the store could not keep it), and the stderr summary gains `slow` (a box not probed is in `skipped`). `--json` prints the records instead, one per box: `device`, `host`, `port`, `vendor`, `ok`, `result`, `connect_ms`, `banner_ms`, `banner`, `reason`, `slow`, `duration_ms`. The check is kept in the store as a run of mode `probe`, one row per box with the record as JSON, so `h-ssh-store failed` lists every box that is not live with its verdict and `h-ssh-store field connect_ms` the round trips. The rows are written before the report is printed: a Ctrl-C while it prints costs at most the report, never the record, and closes the run as interrupted; a reader that leaves early (`| head`) costs the rest of the report and nothing else, the run closed whole with its own exit code (the screen is best effort in every mode: see [Output](#output)). `--probe` with a command probes before the run even where the config file says `probe = no` or a run file `no-probe`. **Two times per live box, one sample each.** The connect time is the TCP handshake's round trip as the kernel measured it (`TCP_INFO`'s `tcpi_rtt` on Linux, exact however many probes run at once; where `TCP_INFO` is missing, the wall time of the connect, which also counts this program's own waiting). The banner time is the wall clock from the finished handshake to the banner line, and shows how fast sshd answers (healthy cRPDs take 7 to 8 ms). A box whose round trip is above 10 ms is tagged `slow: answered in 10.7 ms (above 10 ms)`; the tag is information, never a failure, and does not change the exit code. The threshold is yours: `--slow MS` (`--slow 25` on a network where 10 ms is normal), `slow =` in `~/.h-ssh/config`, `slow:` in a run file, `slow_ms=` for the library. The tag goes on the kernel's round trip, not on the banner time: a stopwatch is not precise when many probes run at once. **What it does not tell:** whether the NETCONF subsystem works (the NETCONF hello comes after login) or whether the credentials do. A live box can still fail the run. **What it costs:** one extra pre-auth SSH connection per box per run, per tick for `--every`. That counts against a Junos `system services ssh rate-limit` and `connection-limit` (and sshd's `MaxStartups`); on the router it shows as an SSH connection closed before login (OpenSSH logs `Did not receive identification string from …` or `Connection closed by … [preauth]`), never as a failed login. Where that matters, or when you know every box is up and accept the risk, `--no-probe` skips it for one run, `probe = no` in `~/.h-ssh/config` for every run, `no-probe: true` in a run file, and `Fleet(..., probe=False)` in the library. Without it a dead box costs `--connect-timeout` per attempt during the run (see [Failure handling](#failure-handling)), and an edit has no reachability check before it starts. A box the `--safety-file` gate holds is never probed (`not probed`, `safety gate: cooldown active (Ns remaining)`, or for every box `safety gate: safety file corrupted (fail-closed): …` when the file is corrupt), on a run, a tick or `--probe` alone, so the rate-limit the gate spares stays spared; the run's gate turns it away as before (exit 3). ## Transports A target names a *driver*: one dialect (what the device speaks) on one transport (how it is reached). The canonical name is `dialect@transport` — `junos@netconf`, `ios@telnet` — and the short names in the table below (`junos`, `ssh`, `openssh`, `telnet`, `telnet-ios`, …) are aliases of canonical ones; the `@ssh` and `@openssh` rows are canonical names themselves. Both kinds work in a target, a CSV and a job file. The driver declares what it can be asked (`hssh.drivers`): where it does not list `--rollback`, `--format`, `--comment`, `--commit-status`, `--dry-run` on an edit or `--commit-confirmed`, each device fails with the reason before a session is opened (exit 1); only the probe has connected to it, and an edit has still asked its questions. | Vendor | Transport | Library | Show | Edit | |---|---|---|---|---| | `junos` | NETCONF | junos-eznc | PyEZ `Device.cli()` | PyEZ lock/load/diff/commit | | `ssh` | SSH | paramiko | `exec_command` | `exec_command` | | `openssh` | OpenSSH client | built-in | `ssh host cmd` | `ssh host cmd` | | `junos@ssh` | SSH, Junos CLI | paramiko | exec channel | shell: `configure exclusive` / `show \| compare` / `commit`, `--dry-run`, `--commit-confirmed`, `-eC commit` | | `ios@ssh`, `nxos@ssh` | SSH, IOS-shaped CLI | paramiko | exec channel | shell: `configure terminal` … `end` | | `eos@ssh` | SSH, EOS CLI | paramiko | exec channel, `--structured` via `\| json` | shell: `configure terminal` … `end` | | `junos@openssh`, `ios@openssh`, `nxos@openssh`, `eos@openssh` | the same dialects over the OpenSSH binary | built-in | `ssh host cmd` (`\| json` for `eos@openssh --structured`) | `ssh -tt host` shell, the same edit sequences | | `telnet` | Raw socket | built-in | raw TCP | config mode | | `telnet-ios` | Raw socket, IOS prompts | built-in | raw TCP | `configure terminal` | | `telnet-junos` | Raw socket, Junos prompts | built-in | raw TCP | `configure exclusive` / `commit` | | `telnet-arista` | Raw socket, EOS prompts | built-in | raw TCP | `configure terminal` | | `telnet-nxos` | Raw socket, NX-OS prompts | built-in | raw TCP | `configure terminal` | Every transport runs a batch on one session per device. A dialect over SSH or telnet is typed at by one CLI engine (`hssh/transports/cli.py`): it logs in, learns the device's own prompt, answers paging, and runs the edit sequence the dialect describes (a candidate diffed and committed or discarded for Junos, lines applied in config mode for the IOS-shaped ones). Only telnet has a login dialogue for it to answer (`login:`, `Password:`). Over SSH the session has logged in before the shell opens, so the engine reads the banner to the prompt and types neither the username nor the password, whatever the banner ends with: a banner ending in `Password: ` gets nothing, and the password cannot come back in a reply, to the screen, `--log`, the audit log or the store. A shell that asks for credentials after SSH has logged in (a console server's port) gets none and fails as a login that shows no prompt. A login ends at a prompt that is the last line, with nothing after it, once the device has said nothing more for 0.15 s. A banner line that ends in `NOC-DESK>` is not the device's prompt once its line break has come, however long the pause after it, and a read that stops right after such a line (or one that is all `NOC-DESK>`) is read past when the banner goes on within that time. When the device pauses longer right after it, before the line break, the login ends there. A line that is all `NOC-DESK>` is then learned as the prompt, and every command fails on its timeout, nothing applied. One that only ends in it costs an SSH shell nothing: the shell echoes every line typed, so the first command after the login, always one of the engine's own (`configure exclusive`, `configure terminal`, `show system commit`), is read through its echo and then its prompt, the device's prompt is learned from it, and the rest of the banner is never taken for its reply. Over telnet, where the device need not echo, the rest of the banner is read as the first reply and each later reply as the one before, so a refused line can come back APPLIED. An empty `show | compare` is `NO CHANGES` (the note Junos prints above `[edit]` while a commit confirmed waits, `# commit confirmed will be rolled back in 4 minutes`, is the prompt's, not a diff): the candidate is discarded and no `commit` is typed, plain or confirmed, as NETCONF aborts on an empty diff, so no timer is armed over nothing and no other user's pending commit-confirmed is confirmed by it. Shows over SSH use an exec channel, one command per channel; only edits and confirms open a shell. Over the OpenSSH binary the shell is `ssh -tt -e none` (no escape character, so a typed line that starts with `~` goes to the device as it is), with a password still handed over through `SSH_ASKPASS`, never typed at a prompt. The plain `ssh`/`openssh` drivers (dialect `none`) never open a shell. The engine types plain text only. A CLI acts on a control character as it arrives (^C drops the line typed so far, ^U kills it, DEL rubs out a character, a Tab completes the word), and what is left of the line runs as typed, a `commit` too, under `--dry-run` as well. So `edit()` refuses a payload with a C0 or C1 control character, DEL, a Tab or a byte that is not UTF-8 in a line, and `confirm()` a `comment=` with one of those, a line break or a double quote (which would end it on the commit line), or, as every commit comment, with no text or over 512 bytes (it is typed stripped): a `ValueError` before the device is contacted, nothing sent. The CLI refuses a control character in `-eC`, `-eD`, `-eB` or a job on every driver before the run starts (exit 2) and lets a Tab through: it is text to `junos`, whose `load set` reads it as a space, and to the plain `ssh` and `openssh` drivers, which type at no CLI. A set file indented with Tabs works there and is a FAIL, nothing sent, on `junos@ssh`, `junos@openssh`, `telnet-junos` and every other driver that types at a CLI. A show over telnet with a Tab in it, or a batch with such a line, is refused before the socket is opened, `show()` and `show_batch()` for a library caller too. The telnet login dialogue is held to the same rule: a username with a control character or a Tab in it, or a password with a control character (a Tab is text at a password prompt), is refused by the telnet drivers before they connect, a `ValueError` for a library caller too, and the engine types neither at a login prompt. None of these refusals is tried again. `h-ssh --list-vendors` prints the registry: every driver a target may name, its aliases, transport, dialect, the formats `--format` can ask it for, what it supports, and where it came from (`built-in`, or the package that registered it: see [Adding a vendor](#adding-a-vendor)). `h-ssh --list-commands --transport junos` lists the `junos` shortcut library the same way. `--transport` takes only `junos`, `ssh`, `openssh` and `telnet`, and the last three list the `none` library, so the `eos` library and a package dialect's are read in their JSON files. Telnet is a prompt match on a raw socket, so it is strict about what it has not seen. A read that reaches its timeout or loses the connection is an error, never a partial reply passed off as the device's answer, and a `login:`/`Password:` prompt back after the password is a failed login, reported once — not the command typed in as a username. A port that prints nothing until Enter — a console-server line left at a prompt — gets one Enter once the session timeout is up, before silence counts as a failed login. A telnet command the device sends once the session is open (`IAC WILL ECHO` after `Password: `, say) is negotiation, not text: it is left out of what is read, so the prompt before it is still the last line, and a reply holds none of it. The prompt is learned at login (`lab@R1` or `Router`, with its config-mode suffix) and ends a reply only as its whole last line, from the start with nothing after it, never as the echo of what was typed: a description ending in `>`, a community ending in `#` or a reply line `uplink to BackupRouter>` cannot be taken for the prompt and shift every later reply. A reply with output of its own is read on until the device has said nothing more for 0.15 s after its prompt (0.3 s after a refusal: a CLI on a pty refuses the Enter again after redrawing the line), so a reply line that is the prompt itself (`Router>`) does not end it when the reply goes on within that time (unless it is the reply's first line: a reply that is only the echo and a prompt so far is not waited on, as each set line's is not); output that comes within that time with no prompt after it (a console's syslog line without `logging synchronous`) leaves the reply with none, and it fails on the command's timeout. A prompt the dialect cannot name (`RP/0/RSP0/CPU0:R1#` is no IOS prompt name) is not learned: the dialect's own pattern stays, which only has to end the line, so on such a device a reply line `uplink to BackupR1#` with a longer pause after it still ends the reply, the rest of it read as the next command's. A reply that is only the echo and the prompt, with its `[edit]` banner (`{master}[edit]` on a router with two routing engines, and the note of a pending commit confirmed above it), as each line of an edit is, is not waited on, and a long edit costs no more. On an SSH shell the echo is also the line as the CLI drew it, when that is the reply's one line of text (a keyword Junos completed as it was typed, a long line an IOS-shaped CLI scrolled), or the line as the terminal shows it after Junos redrew it (a line longer than the 80-column pty of `junos@openssh`, scrolled to `...` and its end); over telnet, where the device need not echo, only the line typed is, and a line echoed otherwise is waited on for the 0.15 s. The echo is the reply's first line of text: a line break the device sends before it leaves it out of the reply all the same. No wait runs past the command's timeout. `telnet-junos` edits enter `configure exclusive`, as the NETCONF driver's lock does: a refused lock is reported before any `set` line is sent, and `commit` and the dry run's `rollback 0` only ever touch this session's candidate, never another user's pending changes. `-eC "commit"` confirms a pending commit-confirmed with one bare `commit` in exclusive mode; a line inside a config payload whose first word is `commit` (`commit;` too, the set-syntax guard's own spelling), or `com`, `comm` or `commi`, which the CLI completes to it, is refused before the device is contacted, on every Junos driver that types at the CLI and for a library caller too. A commit whose reply never arrives is *outcome unknown* here too; one answered with `commit complete` that then takes the session with it — a management address, the telnet service — is still reported as committed, the closed session releasing the lock. ### `ssh` — paramiko, for anything that speaks SSH The default transport runs each line as its own `exec_command`. A command that exits non-zero is a failure, not output: an edit stops at that line and reports it, a batch marks the entry `ok: false` with the first line the device said about it (stderr, or stdout where the device puts its errors). So is a session lost before the command finished — the connection gone before the device ended its output — whatever the device had sent by then, an exit status too (OpenSSH's sshd, Junos's included, sends the status as soon as the command exits, with up to 2 MB of the reply still to come): `connection to HOST lost before 'CMD' finished`. A read is tried again, an edit line is FAILED with its outcome unknown and never sent again, a batch marks that entry `ok: false`. A device that ends its output, or closes the command's channel on a session that stays up, without an exit status, as some network OSes do, has answered. Host keys are pinned on first contact in `~/.h-ssh/known_hosts` (created 0600), and `~/.ssh/known_hosts` is honoured too. The policy is the same `HSSH_HOST_KEY_POLICY` the `openssh` transport reads: `accept-new` (default) pins an unknown host, `yes` refuses one, `no` only warns; it is read per call, and `ask`, `off` or anything else is refused. A host whose key has changed is refused under every policy, before any credential is sent — after a re-image, remove its line from `~/.h-ssh/known_hosts` — and so is a key `~/.ssh/known_hosts` marks `@revoked`. A host the two files hold different keys for is refused as well, whichever key it shows (paramiko reads `~/.ssh/known_hosts` first and the pin file only for a host absent there, so one key taken through `openssh` or a manual `ssh` overrode the pin, #150): one of the files is wrong, and the message names both (the names compared as the `openssh` transport's check compares them: see there for what it covers). Its `@cert-authority` lines are passed over: paramiko cannot check a host certificate, so a host known only through its CA is an unknown host here (`accept-new` pins its key; the `openssh` transport checks the certificate). A pin is written to a new file renamed over the old one, with the old one's mode and group and its other lines byte for byte, under a file lock a reading run waits for, and the host is looked up again under that lock: a host another run pinned meanwhile is checked against that pin, never pinned over. Another run's lock is waited for as long as that run keeps pinning, since every pin changes the file; one held for `--session-timeout` with the file unchanged (a run stopped with Ctrl-Z in the middle of a pin) fails the device, not retried, with `/home/you/.h-ssh/known_hosts is locked by another h-ssh run (one stopped with Ctrl-Z while it pinned?); resume or end it`, and the devices queued behind it fail with it rather than wait again. A line of `~/.h-ssh/known_hosts` that holds no pin — too few fields, a key that is not base64 or not a key of its type, a key type paramiko does not know, a hashed name that is not `|1|salt|hash`, a marker — is not dropped, which would pin that host again on trust: the connection is refused before anything is sent, naming the file, the line number and the line. In `~/.ssh/known_hosts` such a line is passed over, as OpenSSH passes it over, and so is a marker OpenSSH does not have; an `@revoked` line that cannot be read is refused the same way, so a revocation is never dropped, but one with a key type paramiko does not know is passed over, since paramiko can never be shown that key. The TCP connect and the SSH banner get `--connect-timeout` between them; running out there is `TCP connect to HOST:PORT timed out after Ns` or `no SSH banner from HOST:PORT within Ns`, and is tried again. A refusal, no route or a name the resolver says does not exist is said as the OS said it (`connection refused by HOST:PORT`, `no route to host HOST:PORT`, `cannot resolve HOST`, where paramiko said `[Errno None] Unable to connect to port 22 on HOST`) and is not; a lookup that failed otherwise, a resolver that did not answer in time above all, is said in its words too (`name lookup for HOST failed: Temporary failure in name resolution`) and is tried again, an edit too: nothing was sent. The key exchange gets `--session-timeout`, not paramiko's fixed 15 s; one that has not finished by then is `no SSH session to HOST within Ns: the banner came, but key exchange did not finish`, as on `openssh`, and is not retried. A server that drops the session there sooner (within half the session timeout) is `HOST dropped the session before login after Ns (the banner came, but key exchange did not finish)`: a read is retried, an edit is not. ### `openssh` — for hosts where you cannot install anything `openssh` needs no Python packages at all. It drives the system `ssh` binary: `subprocess` for key auth, and `SSH_ASKPASS` for password auth, because OpenSSH refuses to read a password from a pipe. The password reaches OpenSSH through a helper it execs itself, on a channel the session never touches — never through the terminal, where device output and auth prompts would share one stream. The helper reads it from a 0600 file in its own 0700 directory, kept for the call alone (the login and the commands that ride its session; an edit typed into `ssh -tt` has it until the prompt is seen); no `ssh` process, and no `ProxyCommand` one runs, has it in its environment (see [Authentication](#authentication)). Each call logs in once, on an OpenSSH `ControlMaster` (`ssh -N`, which goes to the background once the session is up), and every command, a lone show's too, runs through it as an `ssh` of its own: a batch has one TCP connection and one authentication, and each command still comes back cleanly separated. OpenSSH prints the server's login message (its SSH banner, a Junos `system login message`) on the stderr of the ssh that logs in; that stderr is the login's own, read only to say why a login failed, so the message is in no command's `STDERR:` block, store row or verdict, and one that starts with `error:` fails no show (a command that finds the shared session ended between two commands logs in by itself, as each one did before, and its stderr has the message again). OpenSSH's `ConnectTimeout` bounds the TCP connect and the banner, and it is `--connect-timeout`; nothing in OpenSSH bounds a key exchange that hangs after the banner, so the driver keeps its own clock: ssh's `-v` log (written to a private file with `-E`, never mixed into the device's output) says how far the connection got and when the session is up. No TCP connection, or no banner, within `--connect-timeout` is `TCP connect to HOST:PORT timed out after Ns` or `no SSH banner from HOST:PORT within Ns` (the same words when ssh's own `ConnectTimeout` fires first), and is tried again; a session that is not up within `--session-timeout` is abandoned then (`no SSH session to HOST within Ns: the banner came, but key exchange or authentication did not finish`), and `--command-timeout` starts the moment the session is up, not at process start. Through a `ProxyJump` or a `ProxyCommand` the connect timeout covers reaching the device's banner through the jump, as OpenSSH's own does: raise it for a slow jump host. A batch is one `ssh` per command through that login, so a batch whose login runs out of its connect phase before any command ran ends there, as one failure, instead of spending a connect timeout on every command; a login that fails otherwise is that command's failure, and the next command logs in again, as it does after a command whose session was lost; once a command has its result, the results stand, and a later command whose connect runs out (the session it rode lost, and its own connect unanswered) is that command's failure. ssh's own diagnostics come from that log (a failure of ssh's own is its exit 255); the `STDERR:` block of an output is the device's, and a command that exits non-zero fails in the device's words, `exit N from 'CMD': ` and the first line it said, never read as ssh's: a device's `Permission denied` is not a failed login. A session lost under a command takes the login's master with it, and the command's `ssh` exits 255 with nothing in its log: with the master gone (`ssh -O check`) that is `connection to HOST lost before 'CMD' finished`, as on `ssh`, never the first line of the reply cut short, so a read is tried again and an edit line is FAILED with its outcome unknown and never sent again; an exit 255 with the master still up is the device's own. One case is not seen: a session lost after the device's exit status arrived (OpenSSH's sshd sends it as soon as the command's process ends, ahead of the reply's tail) lets the master pass that status on, the command's `ssh` exits with it, and the reply may be cut short with no word of it; the `ssh` driver, which reads the channel itself, sees that case too. Password auth needs OpenSSH 8.4+ for `SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=force`; older clients are refused rather than silently falling back to a terminal prompt. Key auth has no such floor. Use it on locked-down jump hosts — no package index, no `ensurepip`, no root — where `pip install paramiko` is not on the table but `ssh` is already there: ```bash ./h-app/h-ssh.py --target R1:10.0.1.1:openssh -sC "show version" --user admin ``` It inherits your `~/.ssh/config`, so jump-host `ProxyJump` stanzas and per-host identities work with no extra flags; without a password it also uses your keys and agent (with one, the password is the credential: see [Authentication](#authentication)). The probe reads the config too, through `ssh -G`: a `HostName` or `Port` there is where it asks the box, and a box behind a `ProxyJump` or `ProxyCommand` is not probed but run (see [The probe](#the-probe)). Host keys are checked against the store the `ssh` transport keeps, `~/.h-ssh/known_hosts` (made 0600; a first contact's pin goes there) and then `~/.ssh/known_hosts`, under `HSSH_HOST_KEY_POLICY`, read per call, whatever `StrictHostKeyChecking` or `UserKnownHostsFile` your config sets: `accept-new` (default) pins an unknown host, `yes` refuses one, and `no` is OpenSSH's `accept-new` as well, since OpenSSH's own `no` lets a changed key through (the one difference from the `ssh` transport's `no`: a first contact is pinned), so a changed key in either file is refused under every policy; `ask`, `off` or anything else is refused (#150: passed through, `ask` with a password put the yes/no question to the askpass helper, which answered with the password, thousands of times). A host the two files hold different keys for is refused before the ssh that logs in runs (once a session, not once a command), as the `ssh` transport refuses it, since OpenSSH would take a match in either file. That check looks the host up under the name OpenSSH looks it up under, as `ssh -G` reports it: a `HostKeyAlias` from your config, else the `HostName` with the `Port` in effect (`[name]:port` off port 22, a `Port` stanza counting where the target names none), so a stanza that moves the box moves the check with it; a configuration `ssh -G` refuses fails the device with ssh's words (`SSH transport failed: ssh -G HOST: ...`), as the login would have. What the check compares, in both files, is exactly this: a line whose name is that name written plainly, the `[host]:port` form included, compared case-insensitively as OpenSSH compares it (`router`, `ROUTER` and `[Router]:2222` name one host), and a line whose name is hashed (`|1|…`, as `HashKnownHosts` writes it) by OpenSSH's hash, of the name lowercased. It does not compare a line whose name is a pattern (`*.example.com`, `router?`, a `!` negation), a hashed name made from the name in another case, the entry OpenSSH keeps for the address under `CheckHostIP`, or a host known through a `@cert-authority` line: those lines are OpenSSH's alone to match, so a conflict that reaches the host only through one of them is not refused by this check. A key `known_hosts` marks `@revoked` is said as such (`its key is marked @revoked in ~/.ssh/known_hosts`), with no advice to remove its line. Two limits of the plain `openssh` driver, both deliberate: `--structured` falls back to text (`eos@openssh` has it, through `| json`), and `--commit-confirmed` is rejected rather than silently ignored, as it is on every driver but the four Junos ones (`junos`, `junos@ssh`, `junos@openssh`, `telnet-junos`), which can arm a rollback timer; dropping the timer without saying so would be worse than refusing. On `eos@openssh` (and `eos@ssh`, `telnet-arista`) an edit is typed in config mode, as for IOS: `configure terminal`, the lines, `end`. Each line is live once it is typed; there is no session diff and nothing to roll back. A refused line stops the edit there, since the next line would be typed in whatever mode the device is left in (a `shutdown` after a refused `interface Gi0/9` shut the interface before it): `end` is typed and the edit fails, naming the line and the device's complaint, the lines applied before it, which stay applied, and the lines not sent. A line is refused as the dialect's `refused` says, a line of the reply that starts with `%` or `ERROR:` for these (`% Invalid input …`, `%Inconsistent address and mask`, `ERROR: The secret you entered is not a valid encrypted secret.`), not by an `error` or a `%` anywhere in it; a syslog message the device prints meanwhile (`%LINK-3-UPDOWN: …`) is not a refusal. A line the device took with a warning or a note (`%Warning: portfast should only be enabled …` and the `%Portfast has been configured …` under it, `% Warning: use /31 mask …`, `%Default route without gateway …`, the others the dialect's `informational` names, below) is applied and the edit goes on. A clean edit prints `(config applied)`, and each warning or note under it, after the line it answered. ## Adding a vendor A vendor is a driver: a dialect (what the device speaks) on a transport (how it is reached). The built-ins are declared in `hssh/drivers/__init__.py`; a package installed next to h-ssh declares its own through the `hssh.drivers` entry-point group, so an internal package can ship a dialect, or a driver pairing one with an existing transport, without a fork of h-ssh. Four pieces and one test run. **A dialect file.** A `Dialect` (`hssh/dialects/base.py`) is everything h-ssh knows about the device and nothing about connections; `hssh/dialects/ios.py` is the smallest that defines its own CLI, and `nxos.py` and `eos.py` reuse it in a few lines. A field h-ssh adds goes after the ones it had, so a dialect that gives its fields in order, not by name, keeps each where it was. | Field | What it is | |---|---| | `name` | the half of a driver name before the `@` (`ios` in `ios@ssh`), and the stem of the operator's shortcut file | | `title`, `description` | the name as printed to the operator, and one line on the dialect | | `refused` | a compiled regex (`re.MULTILINE`) for a line in which the CLI refused a command: for IOS a line that starts with `%`, a space after it or not, or with `ERROR:`, but for a syslog message (`%LINK-3-UPDOWN: …`, a facility, a severity, a mnemonic and a colon). On an exec channel (`ssh`, `openssh`) every reply is read with it: a show whose reply opens with such a line is a failure, not output, and the plain drivers' line-by-line edit stops at the line that got one. Typed at a CLI (a shell on `ssh` or `openssh`, `telnet`), a candidate edit checks each line's reply with it and discards the candidate after the last line; a lines edit checks each line's reply with it too, stops at the first refused line and types `end`, and fails naming that line, the lines applied before it and the lines not sent; a telnet show is not checked. A dialect on `ssh`, `openssh` or `telnet` must have one | | `informational` | a compiled regex (`re.MULTILINE`) for a line in which the CLI took a command and warned about it, though `refused` may match it: for the IOS-shaped dialects IOS's `%Warning: …` and `% Warning: …`, the `%Portfast has been configured …` under its portfast warning, its notes on a default route out of an interface (`%Default route without gateway …`) and on a command it calls obsolete (`%Command accepted but obsolete …`), what it says as it makes RSA keys (`% The key modulus size is 2048 bits`, `% Generating 2048 bit RSA keys …`) and as a switch leaves a VLAN's mode (`% Applying VLAN changes may take few minutes. …`), and its note that a VRF enabled or disabled on an interface removed the interface's addresses (the line after it puts them back). Such a line is no refusal: a lines edit goes on, and prints it under `(config applied)` after the line it answered, in quotes. `None`, the default and Junos's and `none`'s: every line `refused` matches is a refusal | | `is_read` | `command -> bool`: a read is retried and allowed under `--format`, anything else is sent once. The default takes `show …` and `get-*`; a command with a line break in it is never a read, whatever the dialect says | | `comments` | what starts a full-line comment in an edit payload besides h-ssh's own `#`, which is one on every driver: `("!",)` for the IOS-shaped dialects, `()` (the default) for Junos and `none`, to which a `!` line is a line. Such a line is never sent, and an edit of nothing but those, `#` lines and blank lines is refused before the device is contacted (`comment_prefixes` is the whole set) | | `check_edit` | `(payload, allow_commit) -> (ok, why_not)`: the guard an edit payload must pass before any device is contacted (Junos's set-syntax rule; `allow_commit` is False for `-eD`/`-eB` files). `None` means no guard | | `cli` | a `CliSyntax`, for edits over a transport that types at the device (a shell on `ssh` or `openssh`, `telnet`): the prompt regexes (`prompt`, `prompt_name`, `prompt_tail`: `prompt_name`'s group 1 is the name the device's prompt line starts with, and the prompt learned from it is that name at the start of a line, then `prompt_tail`, the whole line; a prompt it cannot name leaves `prompt`, which need only end the line), `config_enter`/`config_exit`, and for a dialect with a candidate configuration `compare`, `discard` and `commit` (plus `context`, a line Junos prints with its prompt: `[edit]`, `{master}[edit]` with two routing engines, and the `# commit confirmed will be rolled back in 4 minutes` above it while a timer runs; every such line at the end of a reply is the prompt's, and a reply of the echo, those lines and the prompt is not waited on for more). `None`: the dialect shows over `ssh` and `openssh` (an exec channel) but cannot edit, and cannot be used on `telnet`, where a show is typed at the CLI too | | `commit_pending` | a regex whose group 1 is the minutes left on a pending commit-confirmed, as `show system commit` prints them; `-eC commit` confirms only when it finds one | | `shortcuts` | the stem of a shipped library, `hssh/dialects/.json` — built-in dialects only, see below | ```python # acme_hssh/__init__.py — an IOS-shaped switch, shows and edits over paramiko import re from hssh import drivers from hssh.dialects.base import CliSyntax, Dialect from hssh.drivers import Driver CLI = CliSyntax(prompt=re.compile(r"[\w\-\.]+(\([^\s()]+\))?[>#]\s*$"), prompt_name=re.compile(r"^([\w\-\.]+)(\([^\s()]+\))?[>#]\s*$"), prompt_tail=r"(\([^\s()]+\))?[>#]\s*$", config_enter="configure terminal", config_exit="end") DIALECT = Dialect("acme", "AcmeOS", "Acme switches: an IOS-shaped CLI", refused=re.compile(r"^\s*% ", re.M), cli=CLI) DRIVERS = [Driver(DIALECT, drivers.SSH, frozenset({"show", "show_batch", "edit"}))] ``` **A `Driver` on a transport.** `Driver(dialect, transport, supports, aliases=())`. The transport is one of `drivers.SSH`, `drivers.OPENSSH`, `drivers.NETCONF` and `drivers.TELNET` (frozen: it takes a dialect, nothing else), or a `Transport` of the package's own, `Transport(name, description, module, install, default_port, formats=("text",), banner=b"SSH-", pooled=False, frozen=False, ssh_config=None, console_port=None)` (give the ones after `default_port` as keywords), whose `module` meets the contract below. The probe asks every box for `banner` before each run, so a transport that is not SSH sets `banner=None` (a TCP connect only), or every box is dead to the probe; `ssh_config` (`"openssh"` or `"paramiko"`) says which ssh configuration the transport follows, so the probe asks where it connects. `supports` is the set of words the runner may ask for: `show`, `show_batch`, `show_structured`, `rpc`, `edit`, `rollback`, `confirm`, `commit_status`, and the policies `dry_run`, `commit_confirmed` and `comment`. A word the driver does not list is refused by name on each device before a session is opened (the device fails; only the probe has reached it), so list what the transport's module really does for this dialect. The `ssh` and `openssh` modules show on an exec channel for any dialect with a `refused`, edit through the CLI engine for one with a `cli`, need a candidate (`compare`, `discard`, `commit`) for `dry_run` and `commit_confirmed`, and a candidate and `commit_pending` for `confirm`, which reads `show system commit` first, as Junos prints it; `show_structured` there is EOS's `| json`, and `rpc`, `rollback`, `commit_status` and `comment` are NETCONF's. `Driver` itself refuses nonsense (`rpc` on a text-only transport, a policy without `edit`). An alias is another name a target may carry (`telnet-ios` for `ios@telnet`) and must be free. **A JSON of shortcuts.** `-sC bgp` resolves against the dialect's library: for a built-in dialect the file next to it, `hssh/dialects/.json`, and for every dialect the operator's `~/.h-ssh/commands/.json` and `~/.h-ssh/commands/.json` on top, later files overriding earlier entries. A built-in dialect names its library by stem (`shortcuts="junos"`); a dialect from another package names its own file by path (`shortcuts=str(Path(__file__).with_name("acme.json"))`), and the operator's `~/.h-ssh/commands/acme.json` still goes on top. The format is `hssh/dialects/junos.json`'s — a name, the command, a description, and for NETCONF an optional `structured` binding: ```json { "version": {"command": "show version", "description": "Software version and uptime"}, "bgp": {"command": "show ip bgp summary", "description": "BGP neighbor summary"} } ``` **The entry point.** In the package's own `pyproject.toml`: ```toml [project.entry-points."hssh.drivers"] acme = "acme_hssh:DRIVERS" ``` It names a `Driver`, a list of them, or a callable returning either. Installed next to h-ssh, the package's drivers load after the built-ins, and `acme@ssh` works in a target, a CSV row, a job and a run file like any built-in name (`--transport` keeps its four choices). `h-ssh --list-vendors` shows it with where it came from: ```console $ h-ssh --list-vendors name aliases transport dialect formats supports source junos@netconf junos netconf junos text,xml,json comment commit_confirmed commit_status … built-in none@ssh ssh ssh none text edit show show_batch built-in … acme@ssh - ssh acme text edit show show_batch acme-hssh (entry point acme) ``` An entry point is taken whole or not at all. One whose import raises, that hands over something that is not a `Driver`, or that claims a name or alias already registered is listed by name at the end of that output — `broken entry point 'acme': ImportError: …` — never as a traceback, and the rest still load. A target that names one of its drivers is then `ERROR: Unknown vendor 'acme@ssh'.` (exit 2); `--list-vendors` says why. The registry is `hssh.drivers`: `DRIVERS`, `SOURCES` and `BROKEN` are what `--list-vendors` prints, and `load()` rebuilds them. **The contract test run.** `pytest h-app/tests/drivers/test_contract.py` puts every registered driver through `hssh.drivers.contract.violations()`: the module behind the driver has an `AVAILABLE` flag and a function for each capability declared — `show`, `show_batch`, `edit`, … — that takes what the runner passes: `host, user, passwd`, then the command, commands, payload or rollback number, then `session_timeout, command_timeout` (and `commit_confirmed` for an edit), with `port=` and `vendor_hint=` as keywords, and `connect_timeout=` to a function that takes it (the built-in SSH transports' all do; one without it is called as before); `binding=` on `show_structured`, `fmt=` on `rpc` and on the `rpc_batch()` that must sit next to it, `dry_run=` and `commit_confirmed=` on `rollback`; `dry_run=` and `expected_diff=` on `edit` for a driver that declares `dry_run`, and `comment=` on `edit`, `confirm` and `rollback` for `comment`. A capability declared and not backed would otherwise fail on the first device with a `TypeError` where a refusal should have been. Run it with the package installed; for one that is not, build the entry point in a test and hand it to `drivers.load([...])`, as `h-app/tests/test_entry_points.py` does with the packages under `h-app/tests/fixtures/`. ## Defaults Typing `--user` on every run gets old. `~/.h-ssh/config` holds per-user defaults: ```ini # ~/.h-ssh/config user = EF workers = 16 retries = 0 session_timeout = 5 connect_timeout = 2 command_timeout = 15 transport = openssh slow = 25 # the probe's slow tag, in ms probe = yes # no: skip the probe before every run, as --no-probe does for one ``` Precedence is flag → config file → built-in default. A value given on the command line always wins; of the file's keys only `user` and `store` have an environment step: `--user` falls back to `HSSH_USER`, then the file's `user`, then the name you are logged in as, like ssh; `--store` falls back to `HSSH_STORE`, then the file's `store`, then `./h-ssh.db` (see [The result store](#the-result-store)). `--audit-log` and `--safety-file` have no key in the file and fall back to `HSSH_AUDIT_LOG` and `HSSH_SAFETY_FILE`. The password has no flag and no file entry: `HSSH_PASSWORD` when set, else the prompt. A key the file does not set keeps its built-in default: `workers` 8, `retries` 2, `session_timeout` 30, `connect_timeout` 3, `command_timeout` 20, `transport` ssh, `slow` 10, `probe` yes. Keys may be written with `-` or `_`. An empty value is not a flag left out. `--devices`, `--user`, `--config`, `-eD`, `-eB`, `--batch`, `--profile`, `--job`, `--run`, `--comment`, `--save-output`, `--log`, `--store`, `--audit-log` and `--safety-file` refuse `''` in one line naming the flag (exit 2), so a pipeline's `--audit-log "$AUDIT"` with the variable unset cannot turn the `HSSH_AUDIT_LOG` audit trail off, `--config ''` does not read the default file and `--user ''` does not log in as `HSSH_USER`. An empty `HSSH_AUDIT_LOG` or `HSSH_SAFETY_FILE` is no audit log and no safety file, as an unset one is. `transport` is the vendor for targets that don't declare one — `name,ip` inventory rows, a target without one (`10.0.1.1`, `R1:10.0.1.1`), or a job entry without a vendor. The example above runs those through the system `ssh` binary; a vendor on the target itself always wins. It takes `junos`, `ssh`, `openssh` or `telnet`, as `--transport` does; a driver such as `eos@ssh` goes on the target. `connect_timeout` is what a device that does not answer costs you: a dead or blackholed address, or a port that accepts TCP and never sends the SSH banner. It bounds the TCP connect and the banner together on `junos`, `ssh` and `openssh`, 3 s by default and never more than `session_timeout`, and such a device is tried again after half a second and then a second, so three attempts take about 10 s, where it cost 30 s on `junos` and `openssh` and about 94 s on `ssh`. A healthy sshd sends its banner within about 100 ms of the TCP connect (the lab's cRPDs did, 254 at once), so 3 s leaves room; raise it for a slow link or a jump host. It is also each wait of [the probe](#the-probe) before the run. `session_timeout` (30 s) is what the key exchange, the login and the NETCONF hello get once the device has answered, and all of a telnet login. `command_timeout` (20 s) is what each command or operation gets once the session is up. `slow` is the probe's threshold in milliseconds (10 by default, fractions allowed): a live box whose TCP handshake took longer is tagged slow, information only. `probe = no` (`yes`, `no`, `true`, `false`, `on`, `off`, `1`, `0`) skips the probe before every run; `--probe` with a command still probes that run, and `--probe` alone is unaffected. **Passwords are never read from this file.** A config file on a shared jump host is the wrong place for a secret; a `password`, `passwd`, `secret`, `token` or `pass` line is refused with exit 2 naming it, exactly as in a run file. Use the prompt or keys, and `HSSH_PASSWORD` for a pipeline. `--config PATH` points at a different file, and that path must exist: a typo is exit 2, only the default path may be absent. Every line is `key = value`; a line that is not is exit 2 naming it, as is a value outside the flag's range (`workers` 1..256, `session_timeout`, `connect_timeout` and `command_timeout` 1..86400, `retries` 0 or more, `slow` above 0 up to 86400000) or a `probe` that is not yes or no. A key h-ssh does not know (`worker = 16`) is ignored without a word, so check the spelling. The flags are held to the same ranges, and a usage error prints one line, not the usage block. ## Run files A pipeline step does not want fifteen flags, and neither does a jump host at three in the morning. A run file is the whole run in one YAML (or JSON) file: ```yaml # fleet-bgp.yaml devices: inventories/ax.csv # a CSV path, or an inline list (below) transport: junos user: h-lab # never a password: see below workers: 64 retries: 1 session-timeout: 15 format: xml commands: # a batch, one session per device - show bgp summary - show route summary log: runs/bgp.jsonl audit-log: audit.jsonl ``` ```bash h-ssh --run fleet-bgp.yaml # on the jump host: asks for the password once HSSH_PASSWORD=... h-ssh --run fleet-bgp.yaml --json > out.json # in a pipeline: no terminal needed h-ssh --run fleet-bgp.yaml --dry-run # a flag on the command line wins over the file ``` Every key is named after a flag, written with `-` or `_` (`show` for `-sC`, `edit` for `-eC`), and gets the flag's validation: a transport outside the list, `workers: 0`, `format: csv`, an unknown key or an empty path, `user` or `comment` (`audit-log: ''`, which would otherwise turn off the `HSSH_AUDIT_LOG` trail) is exit 2 naming the key, and so is a `comment` that `--comment` refuses (a YAML block of two lines, `comment: |`; the line break a block ends with is stripped, as `show`'s is). `--store`, `--no-store`, `--every`, `--times`, `--profile`, `--job`, `--target` and `--config` have no key; give them on the command line. Precedence is command line → run file → environment → `~/.h-ssh/config` → built-in default, so a `--dry-run` from a pipeline variable overrides whatever the file says. A flag typed on the command line wins whatever its value, the default's own included: `--format text` beside `format: xml` asks for text, `--devices devices.csv` beside `devices: prod.csv` reads `devices.csv`, and an `--audit-log` equal to `$HSSH_AUDIT_LOG` beside `audit-log:` writes where the flag says. A target typed on the command line (bare or `--target`) or a typed `--devices` replaces the file's `devices`, an inline list or a path alike, and one line on stderr says so (once for a whole `--every` watch): `Run file 'fleet-bgp.yaml': 'devices' is ignored; --devices on the command line wins.` A `--job` typed beside a file that holds `devices` does not replace them: a job's targets are its entries, so the run is refused (exit 2, nothing sent) rather than run on the job's devices with the file's `yes` and timer: `ERROR: run file 'fleet-bgp.yaml': 'devices' beside --job: a job's targets are its entries.` Relative paths in the file (`devices`, `batch`, `edit-dir`, `edit-broadcast`, `log`, `audit-log`, `save-output`, `safety-file`) resolve against the file's own directory, so a run directory with its inventory and set files moves as one. Three keys have no flag of their own. A file holds `commands` or `jobs`, not both; with `jobs` the targets are the entries', the file's `devices` is not used, and a target typed beside the file (bare or `--target`) or a `--devices` is refused, exit 2: `ERROR: --target beside a run file's 'jobs': a job's targets are its entries.`, as beside a `--job` file: ```yaml devices: # inline targets instead of a CSV - R1:10.0.1.1:junos - {name: R2, host: 10.0.1.2, vendor: junos, port: 830} commands: [show version, show route summary] # an inline --batch ``` ```yaml jobs: # the entries a --job file holds - {target: "R1:10.0.1.1:junos", show: show bgp summary} - {target: "R3:10.0.1.3:junos", edit: set system host-name R3-new} commit-confirmed: 10 # a file that commits needs a timer (below) ``` The rest are the flags: `show`, `edit`, `edit-dir`, `edit-broadcast`, `batch`, `rollback`, `commit-status`, `comment`, `show-diff`, `dry-run`, `commit-confirmed`, `yes` (or `assume-yes`: YAML reads a bare `yes:` as a boolean, both spellings work), `structured`, `format`, `json`, `raw`, `diff`, `verbose`, `save-output`, `log`, `audit-log`, `safety-file`, `retries`, `workers`, `session-timeout`, `connect-timeout`, `command-timeout`, `transport`, `user`, `allow-missing`, and the probe's `no-probe`, `slow` and `skip-unreachable` (`--probe` alone has no key: a run file runs commands; `--probe` typed on the command line probes a run whose file says `no-probe`, as any flag wins). Two rules the file cannot bend: - **No credential, ever.** `password`, `passwd`, `pass`, `secret` and `token` keys are refused before anything runs. The password comes from `HSSH_PASSWORD` or the prompt when stdin is a terminal, exactly as without a file, so a run file can live in git or on a shared jump host. - **Changes need a timer.** A run started with `--run` that commits (an `edit`, `edit-dir`, `edit-broadcast`, `rollback` or job edit in the file, or `-eC`, `-eD`, `-eB`, `--rollback` or a `--job` file's edit on the command line) must set `commit-confirmed` in the file or on the command line, or be a `dry-run`; otherwise exit 2. A confirm (`edit: commit`) needs no timer. Nobody watches a pipeline, and an unattended commit without a rollback timer is the one thing it must not be able to do by accident. The `y/N` question and `-y` work as they do for flags, and the banner names the file, the device count and the timer. The other way round, a file that only reads takes no `commit-confirmed`, `skip-unreachable` or `allow-missing`: exit 2, as for the flags. The file is declarative: no variables, loops or templating. A pipeline that needs them generates the file. YAML needs PyYAML, which comes along with junos-eznc, so every install has it; a JSON run file needs nothing. ## Output | Flag | Prints | |---|---| | *(none)* | one status line per device, plus the verdict and diff under it for edits | | `-v` | status plus a framed block per device | | `--raw` | device output only: no banner, progress lines or summary on stdout | | `--json` | one object per device (per entry for a `--job`): `device`, `host`, `vendor`, `ok`, `duration_ms`, then `command` and `output` for a show (a job's show entry too), a `commands` list (one entry per command) for `--batch`, `output` alone for an edit, a `commits` list for `--commit-status`, `error` for a failure; with `--diff` on a show or a batch the objects come in target order and, when two or more are `ok`, each of those has a `diff` against the first of them, the baseline: the unified diff or `(identical)`, for a batch a list of `{command, diff}` (`(baseline)` on the baseline itself). `--probe` alone prints the probe's records instead (see [The probe](#the-probe)) | | `--diff` | after the results, each device's reply against the first one in target order that answered (bare hosts, then `--target`; or the inventory's rows): the unified diff, or `(identical)`; for a batch, command by command. A show only (`-sC`, `--batch`, `--profile`): with an edit, a job, `--rollback`, `--commit-status` or `--probe` alone it is refused (exit 2, nothing sent), a run file's `diff` too | | `--format json\|xml` | the router's own JSON or XML reply instead of CLI text (the NETCONF `junos` driver only; `junos@ssh`, `junos@openssh` and every other driver refuse it, nothing sent, a FAIL of that device): pretty-printed wherever output is printed; in `--json`, `output` carries the JSON as data and the XML as a string. Reads only: a `-sC` or a batch line that is not a read is refused before anything is sent (exit 2), under `--dry-run` too | A reader that stops early (`h-ssh ... | head`) is not an error and gets no traceback, and it does not end the run: the screen is best effort. The first write to stdout or stderr that fails, because the reader left or the file can take no more (a full disk), mutes that stream for the rest of the run, which goes on to its end, every device run and recorded (the store, the audit log, `--log`), and exits with its own verdict (`1` for a failed device). Before #153 the exception out of a progress line ended the run while the commits in flight finished on the routers unreported, unlogged and unaudited, the devices still queued never ran, the run row stayed open (`?/?`) and the exit was 0 or a traceback; a reader that left during the `--json` report kept exit 0 with a failed device in it and the row open. paramiko's transport thread logs a full traceback when a device closes the connection mid-handshake; the CLI keeps that off the screen (the one FAIL line already says so) unless `-v` is given. Under `Fleet` it stays off stderr too while logging is not set up (paramiko's and ncclient's loggers get a `NullHandler`, no level is changed); set logging up and those records go where you send them. `--raw` is the pipe-friendly one: no banner, no progress lines, no summary. Each device gets a `name:` line and its output (an edit's output is its verdict and diff); failures go to stderr, and so does the closing `Done.` line when something failed or was skipped (`Done. All devices OK.` is not printed), so for a show `--raw > out.txt` keeps the file clean even on a partial run. A show adds nothing else to stdout but the `Resolved 'version' -> 'show version | no-more' (junos)` line a shortcut produces (and `--diff`'s block, when asked for). An edit also prints to stdout its probe line (and the boxes found dead), `Ready to execute on N device(s).`, the confirmation (and `Aborted by user.` when it is not answered y), `--show-diff`'s previews, the commit-confirmed reminder and, when the probe stops it, `ERROR: N device(s) unreachable: …` with its `Aborting …` line. ```console $ h-ssh -sC "show version | match Junos:" --raw cr1: Junos: 24.2R1-S2.5 cr2: Junos: 24.2R1-S2.5 ``` `--raw` is exclusive with `-v` and with `--json`; asking for either pair is an error rather than a silent preference (`--json -v` is accepted: the JSON is printed as without `-v`, which only lets paramiko's and ncclient's log records, their tracebacks among them, through to stderr). The command echo (`$ show version`) belongs to the framed view — `--raw` and `--json` both drop it, and `--json` reports it as its own `command` field instead of repeating it inside `output`. `--save-output DIR` makes DIR, and any parent it has to make, 0700 (a DIR that is there is left as the operator made it, with a `WARNING: --save-output DIR is not private` when group or others can read it: its files are 0600 either way, their names are not) and writes one file into it per device that ran or that the probe found dead (0600, never redacted; none for a device the safety gate held back or `--allow-missing` left out, nor for `--probe` alone): `NAME.output` holds the DEVICE/HOST/MODE/VENDOR header, then the reply or the `ERROR:` line; a batch that ran is `NAME.json`, its commands as JSON (one that failed before it ran, or that the probe found dead, gets `NAME.output`); a job's later entries for one device go to `NAME.2.output`, `NAME.3.output`, … in file order (see [Modes](#modes)). A `--show-diff` preview is not saved: the files are the run's, so an answer other than y at its question, or a preview that failed, leaves the files in DIR as they were. DIR is proven writable before the first device, as the audit log is (a test file, and every result's file name against what the file system takes), so a run never commits what it could not save (exit 2). A file that still cannot be written once the result is in (a directory or a FIFO in its place, a planted symlink, a disk that filled) is that result's loss, never the device's failure: the result is shown, stored and audited as any other, the device is not cooled, a `WARNING` names the file as it happens and says at the end how many of how many were not saved, the summary line carries `not_saved`, and the exit code is 4. ### The result store Every run is kept. The store is `h-ssh.db` in the directory you run from, so the evidence sits with the job (`cd customer-x && h-ssh ...`); `--store PATH`, `HSSH_STORE=PATH` or `store = PATH` in `~/.h-ssh/config` name another file, in that order of precedence (a leading `~` is your home directory in each of them), and `--no-store` keeps nothing of one run. One SQLite file, run after run: one row per command per device — run, device, seq, host, vendor (as the target names it: `junos`, `eos@ssh`), the command as sent, when, OK or not, the duration (a batch's on its first row), the error, the format (`text`, `xml`, `json`) and the device's own reply. A show is one row, a `--batch` one row per command in order, an edit one row with the payload as the command and the verdict (the diff, the commit line) as the output, `--commit-status` the history as JSON, a `--job` one row per entry (a device the job names twice has `seq` 0 and 1, in file order), `--probe` alone one row per box with its probe record as JSON (a box that is not live is a failed row). A second table, `runs`, has one row per run (an `--every` watch adds one per tick): when it started and finished, the mode (`show`, `show-batch`, `edit-cmd`, `edit-dir`, `edit-broadcast`, `rollback`, `commit-status`, `job`, `probe`), what it was about, the whole command line, who ran it and from where, and the counts. A read's row is opened before its probe, so a read stopped there by Ctrl-C is kept as an interrupted run, every device skipped. An edit's is opened once the edit is past its questions (the probe's, `Proceed with changes?`, `--show-diff`'s `Commit these changes on all devices?`): an edit stopped before that (an answer other than y, an edit the probe stopped, a `--show-diff` preview that failed, a Ctrl-C) committed nothing and is no run, so it leaves no row. Everything is kept as it came: a snapshot one may have to restore from is not edited, so nothing in the store is redacted, and a `show configuration` keeps its hashes, and a Junos `$9$` secret is reversible, so the store, its exports and `--save-output` files hold the equivalent of the passwords in it: keep them as you keep those; escape sequences and control characters are taken out of a reply as a terminal is shown it, by `h-ssh` and by `h-ssh-store` alike, never out of the record: the store, `--log`, `--json` and the audit log hold the same bytes whether the run was started from a terminal or a pipe, the reply's own line endings included (a show over SSH from a device that ends its lines with CRLF keeps them there and on `--raw` to a pipe; telnet hands its lines over with LF), and `h-ssh-store` hands a pipe or an `export --out` file the rows as they were kept. The file is made 0600 at the open whatever it was (a 0644 `h-ssh.db` made by hand, or by the `sqlite3.connect` snippet above before the first run, is made private, and so are a `-wal` and `-shm` left beside it), in directories made 0700, must be this user's own regular file (one owned by another user is refused, `owned by another user`, as a symlink in its place is), and is checked, once SQLite has it open, to be the file that was made private. Its directory must be yours too, and not one other users can write (a symlink one of them plants between the open and SQLite's own, which reopens the file by name, would otherwise send the run's writes elsewhere): a directory owned by another user, or group- or world-writable without the sticky bit, is refused (`its directory DIR is writable by other users`); a sticky one such as `/tmp/yourjob`, where others cannot rename a file that is not theirs, is fine. Its tables are made before the first device, after the checks that need no file: a store that cannot be written is no run (exit 2, nothing sent), because a run nobody can look up afterwards is not worth having. A run refused before it starts leaves no store file: one those checks refuse never opens it (`--raw -v`, an edit with no terminal and no `-y`), and a store the run made is taken away again when the run stops after it with nothing kept in it (a `--safety-file` or `--save-output` that cannot be used, Ctrl-D or Ctrl-C at the password prompt); one that was there stays as it was. A store that fails during the run (the disk fills, someone deletes or replaces the file) does not stop the devices' replies from being shown; the loss is said as it happens, counted at the end with its reason, and the run exits 4. The store holds its directory open, so a job directory renamed during the run (`mv customer-x customer-x-done`) loses nothing. A file overwritten in place (same inode) is the one case that goes unnoticed. Writes are one transaction per device result, in WAL mode with `synchronous=NORMAL`: a row costs about a tenth of a millisecond, a 250-device run adds a few tens of milliseconds, the file never corrupts and every commit survives the process dying; only a power cut can lose the last commits. Two h-ssh runs may write one store at the same time, including two that create it at the same instant; a writer waits up to ten seconds for the other's commit before it gives up. The store holds output and nothing else: no parsing, no normalising, no per-command schema — what is done with the replies is the reader's business. `h-ssh-store` is the reader that ships; it looks where the run wrote (`--store PATH`, given before the command: `h-ssh-store --store PATH runs`; `HSSH_STORE`; `store` in `~/.h-ssh/config`, never in a file a run named with `--config`; else `./h-ssh.db`): | Command | Prints | |---|---| | `runs [--last N]` | the last 20 runs (`--last N` for another number), newest first by the instant they started (ids and `started` are local time, which a DST fall-back puts out of order): id, start, mode, user, targets/ok/fail (`/int` after an interrupted run, `?` where a run's row was never closed), what it was about | | `failed [RUN]` | the failed rows of a run (default: the last), with the device's error line; exit 1 when there are any | | `output DEVICE [RUN] [--seq N]` | one reply, as the device gave it (`--seq` picks a batch's command or a job's entry); the error on stderr and exit 1 for a failed row | | `grep PATTERN [--run RUN] [--device D] [--command C] [-i]` | the lines of stored replies that match a regex, with run, device and command: every run unless `--run`, rows that succeeded only, `--command` matched exactly; exit 1 when no line matches | | `field PATH [--run RUN] [--device D] [--command C]` | a dotted path into JSON replies (`--format json` shows, commit histories): the device's structure read, not parsed; exit 1 when no reply has the path | | `diff DEVICE RUN_A RUN_B [--seq N]` | one device's reply in two runs as a unified diff; exit 1 when they differ (lines are compared without their line endings) | | `history DEVICE [--command C] [--last N]` | the newest 50 stored results for a device (`--last N` for another number), newest first | | `slowest [RUN] [--last N]` | the 20 slowest results (`--last N` for another number), of a run or overall | | `export [RUN] [--all] [--device D] [--command C] [--format csv\|jsonl] [--out FILE]` | the rows as they are, for a spreadsheet or a notebook: CSV (a multi-line reply is one quoted cell, the default) or JSON Lines; one run (default: the last) or the whole store; exit 1 when no row matched; with `--out`, the file written 0600 as `--log` is (whatever mode a file there had; a symlink is not followed, a FIFO or anything but a regular file or a character device such as `/dev/null` is refused, and so is the store or a file SQLite keeps beside it under any name, a hard link included), `N rows written to FILE` on stderr. The file itself is plain SQLite, so `pandas.read_sql("SELECT * FROM results", sqlite3.connect("h-ssh.db"))` works as well | A run is named by its id or any unique prefix of it (`20261024-1730` when only one run started then). Anything else is a `sqlite3 h-ssh.db` query away: the schema is two tables, documented at the top of `hssh/store.py`. The reader never writes the store, though where it may, SQLite leaves an empty `-wal` and a `-shm` beside it. A finished store in a directory the reader cannot write to (an archived job directory, a read-only mount, another user's directory) is read as it is, without SQLite's locks; one with WAL frames or a rollback journal still beside it is not, since the file alone is not the whole store (a run killed before it closed the store leaves rows in its `-wal`: the error says to copy the store with its `-wal` to a directory you can write). A run that writes such a store while it is read could make rows go missing or repeat, so the reader looks again when it is done and says so: `ERROR: PATH was written while it was read as it is; the output may miss or repeat rows, read it again`, exit 2. `grep`, `field` and `export` take the rows as they come, so a store of hundreds of megabytes costs no more memory than a small one. They read while they print, so one left open on a store a run is writing (`h-ssh-store grep ... | less` beside an `--every` watch) keeps SQLite from recycling the run's `-wal`: it grows by what the run writes meanwhile, and goes when a run closes the store after the reader has exited. A reader that stops early (`h-ssh-store ... | head`) is no traceback, as with `h-ssh`: exit 0, or the verdict the command had before it printed (`failed`, `diff`, `output` of a failed row). What the reader cannot do (no store at the path, a run that matches nothing or several, an `--out` file it cannot open or write, or one that is the store itself) is one `ERROR:` line on stderr and exit 2. ```console $ h-ssh --devices core.csv -sC "show bgp summary" $ h-ssh-store runs run started mode user targets/ok/fail command 20261024-173057-e45e 2026-10-24T17:30:57 show h-lab 10/10/0 show bgp summary $ h-ssh-store diff cr1 20261024-1730 20261023-0905 ``` ## Failure handling A device that black-holes packets used to cost the full timeout three times over. Before the run [the probe](#the-probe) finds it without logging in, and the run does not spend a worker on it; what fails once a run is under way, with the probe skipped or after it, is classified before anything is retried: | Failure | Behaviour | |---|---| | A box the probe found dead before the run — refused, no route, a name that does not resolve, no TCP answer or no SSH banner within `--connect-timeout`, something other than SSH on the port, the probe failing on something it did not expect | a FAIL of the run at once, in the probe's words (`probe: refused (connection refused by HOST:PORT)`), not tried by the run: the probe asked twice, half a second apart. An edit asks first, or stops (see [The probe](#the-probe)) | | No answer in the connect phase — no TCP answer, or no SSH banner, within `--connect-timeout` (`TCP connect to HOST:PORT timed out after Ns`, `no SSH banner from HOST:PORT within Ns`) | retried on `junos`, `ssh` and `openssh`, `--retries` times, after 0.5 s and then 1 s; nothing was sent, so an edit is retried too (a show that acts on the device keeps its one attempt). `telnet*` (frozen) keeps `--session-timeout` for its connect and retries the socket's bare `timed out` after 1 s and then 3 s, for a read only: a telnet edit is not tried again | | A clear answer in the connect phase — refused, no route, network unreachable, a name that does not resolve (`connection refused by HOST:PORT`, `no route to host HOST:PORT`, `cannot resolve HOST`, after `NETCONF connect failed: ` on `junos`; on `openssh` `Connection refused by HOST.` and `Cannot resolve HOST.`; on `telnet*` the socket's own words) | fail immediately (on `telnet*` an unresolvable name is still retried: the socket's bare `Name or service not known` matches no marker). On `ssh` only a name the resolver says does not exist is `cannot resolve HOST`; a lookup that failed otherwise, a resolver that did not answer in time above all (`name lookup for HOST failed: Temporary failure in name resolution`), is retried after 1 s and then 3 s, an edit too | | A key exchange that `--session-timeout` ran out on after the banner (`no SSH session to HOST within Ns: the banner came, but key exchange did not finish`) | fail immediately | | A device that drops the session before login (`HOST dropped the session before login after Ns (…)`, an sshd at its connection limit) | on `ssh` a read is retried after 1 s and then 3 s, an edit is not; on `junos` it fails at once | | Authentication, host key, rejected command | fail immediately | | The request itself is wrong — `--structured` on a command without a binding, no password and no key to offer (`ssh`), a user or host name OpenSSH refuses, a `known_hosts` line that cannot be parsed, a pin file another h-ssh run keeps locked (`ssh`: `/home/you/.h-ssh/known_hosts is locked by another h-ssh run …`), a host PyEZ does not accept | fail immediately: the same call cannot come out differently | | This machine out of descriptors opening a session (`junos`: `local open-file limit reached (ulimit -n N): …`) | fail immediately, with no cooldown: the next attempt meets the same limit, and the device did nothing | | Failures *after* connecting — command timeout, reset, broken pipe, a session lost before the command finished (`ssh`, and `openssh` unless the exit status had already come: `connection to HOST lost before 'CMD' finished`) | retried, `--retries` times (default 2), after 1 s and then 3 s | The split is whether the device answered. A box that does not answer at all — a dead or blackholed address, or a port that accepts TCP and never sends the SSH banner (a load balancer or NAT answering for a dead box, an sshd that hangs or is still booting, something else on the port) — costs `--connect-timeout` an attempt, and the next attempt may find it up: three attempts at the defaults take about 10 s (3 s each, and the two pauses), where it cost 30 s on `junos` and `openssh` and about 94 s on `ssh`. A healthy sshd sends its banner within about 100 ms of the TCP connect (the lab's cRPDs did, 254 at once), and the connect timeout never exceeds `--session-timeout`. A clear answer is the same answer next time and fails once. Once a session exists, a read failure may well be transient, so those still get retried. **Edits are different:** a config push is retried only when the driver reports that nothing reached the device: a connect phase that got no answer, a resolver that did not answer (`ssh`), a NETCONF session lost before the lock or before the commit, and for Junos a candidate-lock failure, over NETCONF or a refused `configure exclusive`. Any other failure — above all a timeout around a commit — is reported once and left for you to check. (A none-dialect edit over `openssh` sends each line as its own `ssh`: a connect that runs out after a line was applied is reported, not retried, and after Ctrl-C it is a failure, not interrupted: lines reached the device.) Retrying an authentication failure cannot succeed either, and on a fleet it spends three real login attempts per device against accounts that may lock out. Those stop at one. `--workers` defaults to 8; when the fleet is more than four waves of workers and `--workers` is under 64, the banner says so with a hint (`Hint: 250 devices at 8 workers is 32 waves; --workers 64 would be 4 (one session per router either way)`), since the workers spread over routers and each router still sees one session. It is honoured literally, up to 256, within the open-file limit: an in-flight NETCONF session costs about six descriptors, so the soft limit (`ulimit -n`) is raised towards the hard one when it is short, which needs no privilege, and only what is still short lowers the workers, with one warning naming the limit and the number run. A `--job` runs on the session pool, where a `junos` device keeps its session (about four descriptors) from one entry to the next and lets it go after its last entry: the sessions kept between entries are counted too (a device's session in flight once, as its worker's, the pool counting as the fit does, so none of them is closed while the limit holds them all), and when even the hard limit cannot hold them no worker is taken away and no router failed for it: the pool closes its least recently used idle session before it opens another (a later entry on that device logs in again), and the warning says how many it keeps. The vendor calls block, so each in-flight device holds a thread; h-ssh sizes the executor to `--workers` rather than leaving it at asyncio's default of `min(32, cpu+4)`, which on a 2-vCPU jump host is **6 threads no matter what you asked for** — and a device that does not answer holds one of those six through every attempt. Ctrl-C stops starting new devices and lets the calls already in flight run out: a commit that was on its way to a router is reported, logged and audited like any other, never dropped. Nothing is tried again after it: the attempt in flight is that device's last, so an edit whose connect runs out after Ctrl-C is not sent again once you have stopped the run. The run then reports how many devices completed (`Interrupted. Completed 1 of 3 device(s).`, on stderr) and exits `130`; the devices that had not started are `skipped` in the summary and in the run row (#153: they were counted nowhere). A second Ctrl-C does not end the run either, whenever it comes (while a result is being printed too, and on Python 3.10, whose own handler raised at the first Ctrl-C, the same as on 3.11 and later): it says how many devices are still in flight (`Interrupted again: 2 device(s) in flight are waited for and recorded; the run ends when they have.`), and the run ends when they have, their results reported, logged and audited (before #153 it raised out of the run and cancelled the in-flight devices while their commits finished on the routers, with no report, no audit entry and no row: the run said `Completed 0 of 4`). Output already written to stdout stays valid, so a truncated `--raw` run cannot look like a complete one. A device that was still being connected to when Ctrl-C came, and whose connect then ran out on its own, is reported as `INTERRUPTED` rather than `FAIL`: nothing reached it and the operator stopped the run. Its entry carries `interrupted: true`, its error starts with `interrupted while connecting:`, the notice says `; N interrupted while connecting`, and the summary gains an `interrupted` count. With `--json` there is no notice: the array holds only the devices that completed, the summary's `targets` is that count, and the exit code is still `130`. A Ctrl-C during the probe stops a read before any device is started (`Interrupted. Completed 0 of 3 device(s).`, exit `130`): it is kept in the store as an interrupted run with every device skipped, and the summary's `skipped` counts them. An edit stopped there committed nothing and leaves no run (see [The result store](#the-result-store)). ## Safety Layered. Three automatic layers — the probe's question, confirmation, syntax guard — run for a write only (the probe itself runs before every run); the reply verdict and the result store work for every mode; the opt-in ones (`--safety-file`, `--audit-log`, `--log`) apply to every mode once given. | Guard | Flag | Behaviour | |---|---|---| | Probe | *(automatic)*; `--no-probe`, `probe = no`, `--skip-unreachable` | Before every run, edits included (`--dry-run` and `--show-diff` too): a TCP connect plus, for `junos`/`ssh`/`openssh`, the SSH banner (not for a `junos` console on port 23, which is telnet), so a port that merely accepts and closes is not a device; no login. It asks where the run will connect (`HostName` and `Port` from the ssh configuration on `openssh` and `junos`); a box behind a `ProxyJump` or `ProxyCommand`, or one the safety gate holds, is not probed and runs as without it. `--connect-timeout` for the connect and for the banner, a box that fails asked once more, 100 at a time. An edit (a `--dry-run` too) with a dead box it goes to (a `--job`'s box with only shows is a FAIL, as in a show) asks `Continue with the N reachable?
